The crucial treasure fleets from the Americas, which funded Philip’s campaigns, would have fallen prey to English and Dutch privateers with little escort.
This loss of revenue, combined with the humiliation of a second naval disaster, would have crippled Spanish military operations in Flanders and the Mediterranean,
likely forcing Philip to sue for peace on much more favorable terms for Elizabeth I.
The much-feared resurgence of a Spanish Armada would have been postponed for years, perhaps indefinitely,
denying Catholic reaction the naval instrument it needed to challenge the Protestant ascendancy.
In Portugal, the English fleet and army intended to back the claimant Dom António, Prior of Crato,
and a successful seizure of Lisbon could have sparked the widespread aristocratic and popular revolt that the expedition’s planners hoped for.
Portuguese resistance to Habsburg rule was real but lacked a decisive spark;
an English-led capture of the capital with a legitimate claimant in tow would have provided it.
An independent, Anglophile Portuguese kingdom would likely have been restored under Dom António or another anti-Spanish native ruler,
instantly stripping Philip of his most valuable Atlantic ports—Lisbon, Oporto, and the Azores—
and giving England a permanent ally with bases across the Lusophone world.
The broader ripple effects are equally profound.
The Dutch Revolt would have received a massive boost:
with Spain’s fleet broken and its treasury drained,
the Army of Flanders would struggle to hold back the United Provinces,
potentially leading to a quicker Dutch victory and an earlier recognition of their de facto independence.
England, enriched by captured treasure and a secure Portuguese alliance,
might have avoided the later strain of the Nine Years’ War in Ireland and the eventual succession crisis.
The early dissolution of the Iberian Union would also mean that Portugal’s overseas empire—from Brazil to the East Indies—remains separate from Spanish control,
drastically altering the trajectory of colonial rivalries:
the Dutch and English might have faced a weaker, divided Iberian presence,
accelerating their own commercial expansion,
while Spain, stripped of Portuguese resources, might cling more tenaciously to its American possessions
but with less capacity to guard them.
In short, a successful English Armada in 1589 would have ended the Anglo-Spanish War within a year or two on overwhelming English terms,
broken the Spanish monopoly on Atlantic power a generation early,
and restored an independent Portugal under strong English influence.
The sixteenth-century contest between Habsburg hegemony and Protestant seapower would have tilted decisively toward the latter,
setting the stage for a very different seventeenth century in Europe and beyond.

items.question: What If Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774?
human_answers: This is why it might have been shortsighted for the British Empire to put so much investment in achieving the total conquest and liquidation of the French Colonial position in the Ohio Country and Canada in the 1754-1763 timeframe, to disproportionate benefit of their Colonial 'Fortunate Sons'. While for Britain, it had the side benefit of defeating French forces, which feels nice, and drawing French fleets out for fights they would lose, and capturing some value from the fur trade, Britain particularly "got over its skis" in providing all this support for the Colonies *without* first compelling the Colonies, then under some fears for their frontier populations, to revise their Charters to accept the principle and practice of taxation by the Westminster Parliament, as a regular, reliable contribution to common defense of the empire, its frontiers, and its trade-based prosperity. Instead, by 1763, Britain brought home French North America like Christmas toys and puppies on its own schilling (though Colonial Assemblies chipped in some from their allowance, but often got reimbursed). But then, late 1763 turned out to be a cold, cold, bitter post-Christmas January hangover, when London Parliament started to tell the Colonies, "now start paying tax for all your presents........oh and by the way, sorry, can't let you play with the new Christmas puppy (settle the new lands in the Ohio, west of the Alleghenies), because it turns out the puppy bites and scratches and we can't afford to keep going to the clinic." ---The Americans certainly were not going to react well to the new message of 'fun's over, time to pay up'. While Britain and the American colonies had certain minimum legal rights, even for tenant farmers (still far less than for small freeholders though) I certainly do not think the three protections you mentioned were observed universally, neither in Britain nor even in all the Colonies, in the 1700s pre and post independence. Making this assertion might be a bit of falling for and repeating English/British self-congratulatory propaganda. Evictions were a fact of life in the English-speaking world in the 1700s and all other centuries. The 1700s were known for the enclosure of common lands [yes, that by itself is not eviction but can lead to starvation-inducing poverty even if one is in a cottage, but it can also lead to failure to meet rent obligations and consequent eviction] and consequent driving of English peasants from the countryside to create an ever increasing town and urban laboring population for industry. White tenants on southern landholdings in the Colonies could be subject to evictions as could tenants in Hudson Valley patroonships. Yes, I'm thinking this is descriptive of the Scandinavian situation until after 1800, or nearly that late, which made it, legally speaking more like serfdom systems East of the Elbe than like tenancy systems in Britain or Western Europe. Serfs lacking really any rights of appeal or any rights at all, whereas tenants in England, parts of France, and I would think the Low Countries and Switzerland would have some rights of appeal, even though their landlords would have superior rights through the 1600s and 1700s.

If the British objective was to set off a full-scale war in every colony right off the bat in which they would lose that is exactly what they should do. The British had no means to do what you're suggesting. The incident that set off the fighting was the British trying to disarm the colonists. In the first year of the war the British lost control in all 13 Colonies. Britian had to spend a year mobilizing an army 1/3 of which were German mercenaries for the invasion of the New York. After winning a number of tactical victories they were unable to bring a single colony back under their control. At no time were they ever able to bring even 10% of the population under occupation. After 1777 all they could hold were coastal enclaves, although there was fratricidal warfare in Georgia & South Carolina. They could hold no territory without the Presence of British or Hessian regulars. Loyalist forces were weak everywhere. The coastal enclaves they held became shells eventually with most of the people leaving, and little trade with the interior. What had brought about the war were British policies to control American trade to force them to trade only with England. That alienated the merchant class. Planters had to sell into a closed market were the buyers set the price, and controlled credit terms. That alienated the planter class. They tried to strangle early industrialization so the colonies could only sell raw materials, and buy English finished goods. That alienated the rising manufacturing class. They blocked westward expansion beyond the Proclamation Line. That alienated the landed class. The overall effect was to squeeze specie out of the colonies creating a growing barter system which alienated everyone. Closing courts, and assemblies, and finally trying to disarm the militia left the colonies with the choice of ether abject surrender or rebellion. It wasn't easy but the British Crown went from being very popular in 1765 to every colony taking up arms against them in 1775.

There are tons of things they could do. They could dissolve the militias and ban the Americans from owning weapons. They could introduce an actual tax to fund a permanent military presence - the Americans paid no land rent, only tarriffs. They could abolished the American right to elect judges and sheriffs, instead appointing crown loyalists by decree. They could have given soldiers immunity from local prosecution and law enforcement, instead tasking their commanding officers (who would of course do pretty much nothing) with upholding the law for their soldiers. They could have created an American trading company owned by the crown and banned Americans from any imports and exports except through this company and cracked down on smuggling. The facts are that the Americans enjoyed the most liberal and democratic system in the world at the time of their revolt. They wanted something even more democratic and liberal. But to most people at the time, especially colonial subjects, they would seem like spoiled toddlers throwing a tantrum. Swedish peasants paid roughly 30-40% of the value of an average harvest in land rent at this time. Icelanders could only trade with the very corrupt royal Danish tradign company, which paid aroudn 5% of the value of their wool and forced the Icelanders to buy moldy flour in return. Austrian and Prussian peasants were banned from owning arms, and their courts were handled by government-appointed bailiffs, unless nobility had the right to neck and hand (to be police, prosecutor, judge and executioner all in one, Judge Dredd style) on their estate.

This is a quote from Wikipedia, as of January 20th, 2026: "With the ascension of peace in 1763 the army was dramatically reduced to a peacetime home establishment of just over 11,000 men, with a further 9,750 for the Irish establishment and 10,000 for the colonies. This meant 20 regiments of infantry totaling just over 11,000 men were stationed in Great Britain, 21 regiments were stationed in Ireland, 18 regiments were stationed in the Americas, and 7 regiments were stationed in Gibraltar. Alongside this, the army could call on 16 regiments of the cavalrymen and 2,712 men in the artillery. This gave a theoretical strength of just over 46,000 men exclusive of the artillery." British Army during the American Revolutionary War - Wikipedia en.wikipedia.org Source as listed in the footnote is here: The British Army at the Start of the Revolution - AmericanRevolution.org Learn about the formation and makeup of the British Army at the start of the American Revolution, with this book chapter from E. Curtis, Ph.D. www.americanrevolution.org "The English establishment comprised 25,871 infantry organized into 46 regiments and 20 independent companies; 4,151 cavalry organized into 16 regiments; and 2,256 artillerymen organized into one regiment of 4 battalions." "The Irish establishment consisted of 13,423 infantry divided into 28 regiments; 2,718 cavalry divided into 12 regiments; and 228 artillerymen embodied into one regiment of four companies. "Such were the numbers of the British army in 1775 and such they had approximately been ever since the close of the Seven Years’ War. "An examination of the location of the British army in 1775 reveals the fact that while small detachments of it were to be found in many distant quarters of the globe, the bulk of it was distributed unequally among three different countries. There were roughly speaking 15,000 men in England, 12,000 in Ireland, and 8,000 in America. The remaining 10,000 were distributed among the West Indies, Africa, Minorca, Gibraltar, and Scotland." Each regiment had a listed strength of 477 men. The British concentrated four of these, or just under 2,000 men, in Boston in 1773 to close the port and essentially establish martial law in Massachusetts. This was achieved by moving them New York City, where these regiments had been stationed. The other 6,000 to 8,000 men to cover Canada, Fort Ticonderoga, the forts around the Great Lakes, Florida, Jamaica, and the West Indies. After abandoning Boston, in 1776 the British increased the size of their army from roughly 45,000 to 60,000 troops, mainly be recruiting in Germany. Out of these, they were able to concentrate about 40,000 to take New York, including troops that had been sent to and which failed to take Charleston. Another 10,000 or so chased the Americans out of Canada. Peak strength of the Briitsh army during the American War of Independence was around 80,000. Note that the British were expecting a rematch with France during this time. In fact, Amherst, the commander of the British army, pointed out that the British simply didn't have the strength to garrison the thirteen colonies and advised against trying to reconquer them. The point is that in 1773, the British had the strength to do a show of force in Boston only. And since 90% of the disturbances were coming from New England, the calculation had to be that this would be sufficient. It was only in New England where the situation was turning violent, and it was only after the formation of the Continental Army, and armed clashes between British and American troops, that they declared all thirteen colonies to be in rebellion and started expanding the army. And they really had to wait for the situation to turn that bad to be able to do that.

People in general don't see stuff like that in objective terms. What people see is that suddenly the government made it more expensive or difficult for them to conduct the usual business of life (which was the effect of all the legislation regarding the colonies from 1763 on) and of course they will complain about it, regardless of how good they have it on a cosmic scale. You might as well tell workers in a first world country that they shouldn't go on strike because slavery is still practiced in certain places. That's a very bad idea, because, you know, there are still hostile natives in the borders . In order to not to lose the territory to them, they'd have to station a permanent army all over the border, and that most likely would end up being more expensive than just let the settlers take care of their own defense. And that's not even going into the possibility of slave rebellions in the places where slavery is still legal...
items.original_question: What if Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774? As the title suggests, I've been trying to figure out what an earlier beginning to the American Revolutionary War might entail. As to how this happens specifically, military action was advocated as soon as news of the tea party reached London by some hard-line MPs such as Germain OTL. Some thoughts: - This happens before the Continental Congress even assembles, so everything might happen much more hastily. There probably is much less wrangling over things like sending an olive branch to the King and instead a more decisive stance taken on independence. - With the states forced to pick sides immediately, I think it's highly likely that Georgia remains decidedly loyalist, which has very interesting implications for the US post-independence Other than that, my knowledge on the American Revolutionary War is very much limited and it'd be great to have some input on this scenario. Cheers!

items.model_answer: If Britain had launched an aggressive military campaign against the American colonies in 1774 instead of relying on legislative punishment, the most likely outcome would have been a rapid radicalization of colonial resistance and a far bloodier start to armed conflict, but not a swift British victory. The preemptive use of force to seize rebel leaders, powder stores, and arms caches might have netted some tactical successes—Samuel Adams, John Hancock, or other prominent agitators could have been captured, and poorly defended provincial stockpiles destroyed. Yet such moves would have inflamed a population already seething from the Intolerable Acts, transforming simmering discontent into open, widespread revolt years ahead of schedule. The colonial network of committees of correspondence was already in place, and the 1774 Powder Alarm had demonstrated that thousands of militiamen would mobilize at a moment’s notice. An early offensive would have triggered these spontaneous musters into pitched battles, forcing Britain into a protracted counterinsurgency without the political groundwork to isolate the rebellion. Moderates who still hoped for reconciliation would have been silenced, and the Continental Congress, meeting that autumn, would likely have become a de facto war council, unifying the colonies behind a common defense. While British regulars might have won initial engagements, their limited numbers—barely 4,000 troops in Boston—would have been dangerously overextended trying to hold key towns while facing a hostile countryside adept at irregular warfare. Crucially, the earlier onset of violence would have upended the careful diplomatic timeline that later secured French support; instead, a premature anti-British uprising might have looked more like a series of scattered insurrections, potentially delaying or diminishing European intervention. In the long run, however, the core grievances of self-governance and representation would have remained unresolved, meaning any short-term British military advantage would only have postponed a deeper, perhaps even more bitter, struggle for American independence.

edus.text: If Britain had launched an aggressive military campaign against the American colonies in 1774 instead of relying on legislative punishment,
the most likely outcome would have been a rapid radicalization of colonial resistance and a far bloodier start to armed conflict,
but not a swift British victory.
The preemptive use of force to seize rebel leaders, powder stores, and arms caches might have netted some tactical successes—
Samuel Adams, John Hancock, or other prominent agitators could have been captured,
and poorly defended provincial stockpiles destroyed.
Yet such moves would have inflamed a population already seething from the Intolerable Acts,
transforming simmering discontent into open, widespread revolt years ahead of schedule.
The colonial network of committees of correspondence was already in place,
and the 1774 Powder Alarm had demonstrated that thousands of militiamen would mobilize at a moment’s notice.
An early offensive would have triggered these spontaneous musters into pitched battles,
forcing Britain into a protracted counterinsurgency without the political groundwork to isolate the rebellion.
Moderates who still hoped for reconciliation would have been silenced,
and the Continental Congress, meeting that autumn, would likely have become a de facto war council,
unifying the colonies behind a common defense.
While British regulars might have won initial engagements,
their limited numbers—barely 4,000 troops in Boston—would have been dangerously overextended trying to hold key towns while facing a hostile countryside adept at irregular warfare.
Crucially, the earlier onset of violence would have upended the careful diplomatic timeline that later secured French support;
instead, a premature anti-British uprising might have looked more like a series of scattered insurrections,
potentially delaying or diminishing European intervention.
In the long run, however, the core grievances of self-governance and representation would have remained unresolved,
meaning any short-term British military advantage would only have postponed a deeper, perhaps even more bitter, struggle for American independence.

items.question: What If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union?
human_answers: Also, with or without overseas colonies, Communist France / Germany would be in a relatively poor position to defend themselves, as their territory is relatively small, so they can't trade space for time, or evacuate their industry far behind the frontlines (the way Russia did), and most of their core industrial and agricultural are close to borders or to coasts. They also would also be outnumbered by their combined enemies (eg. Communist France having to fight an anti-communist coalition of Britain, Germany and other countries), while the USSR actually outnumbered the Axis in WWII (and always had more reserves). Communist France would be very vulnerable to an Anglo-German invasion, with the British blockading the country and possibly landing in Brittany, Normandy, Picardy and/or Nord-Pas-de-Calais, and the Germans invading from the east (possibly with Italians and Spaniards also attacking, and those attacks could probably be contained thanks to the Alps and Pyrenees, but would divert men away from the main fronts). Communist Germany would essentially be in the same position as OTL WWI Germany, stuck between the Anglo-French and Russians. Now, a Franco-German communist union already has more potential. In addition, if France and Germany become a communist state together, there's a strong possibility that other nations will join them. Belgium and Netherlands are quite likely give their position, and also Italy, Spain and Portugal, due to their economical conditions and political instability.

Leading up to WW1, moat of the communist parties of the great powers were following the line of the second international, and therefore we're unable to seize power, the exception being of course the Russians. Had lines equivalent to those of Lenin prospered in the communist parties of other great powers, it is likely that any number of them could have had a successful communist revolution during or immediately after WW1. Germany is the most obvious candidate, as they had a big revolution irl even though it failed. Italy is another candidate, and to a lesser extent France. However, any of these countries would have issues with surviving alone under siege socialism as the Russians did. It was assumed at the time that a revolutionary state could only survive with the export of the revolution, lest it be surrounded and defeated by hostile imperialist powers. Stalin proved this wrong, Russia did benefit from it's unique geography in this sense. Could greater German industrial power make a German Soviet Republic defensible? I'd argue yes. Whilst Russian geography helped defensible, it was the economic boom, industrialisation, and enthusiasm of the people that helped it survive imperialist intervention. History ahs shown how enthusiastic armies fighting for a cause can and do defeat foreign powers. France is far more vulnerable to attack than Russia, and yet the French revolutionary wars showed how successful a mobiles french populace could be against the powers of the day. Whilst Germany does not have all the strategic depth and resources of Russia, could Britain France and Russia really afford fulls cake invasions just after WW1? They would run the risk of Revolution spreading among their own tired soldiers. AS for exporting revolution, depending on timing, an established communist Germany could be in a good position to support revolutions in Hungary and Finland , to give a couple of examples.

I think the stickiest element here is the combo of ideology and great/superpower status necessary to mimic the Soviets. If all that was needed was a large and relatively undeveloped country, China or India are easy picks. The problem is ideology. China only went communist in OTL because of the Soviets. No Soviets, no communist China (or India). These places could hypothetically adopt some other far-left socialist ideology, but it probably wouldn't be identifiably Marxist. Meanwhile, if all that was needed was ideology, many other European countries could conceivably fulfill the role. But if, say, France and France alone went communist, they would be considered threatening, but their industry was already decently developed and central planning isn't exactly good at innovating. Their threat level would not be able to rise much compared to the Soviets who had the wiggle room of being able to look at more developed countries and copy their homework. The Soviets also had a massive pool of labor and natural resources that France would lack. A France that probably lost its colonies and has a lagging industry is a middling concern, ultimately. Ditto with Germany. What's really needed, IMO, for another communist entity to arise to pose a similar threat to the Soviets is a multinational revolution in places where Marxism had decent traction. This means multiple Western European countries experiencing revolution and then deciding to cooperate heavily. Alternatively, a multinational coalition of revolutionary socialist states in South America (which must include Brazil since it has the largest population) could potentially adopt a similar role to the Soviets, although they'd be working with both a somewhat smaller population than the Soviets and a less developed industry than Western Europe. As an outside bet, maybe a revolutionary Spain somehow inspires its former colonies to follow suit and they join hands? Wouldn't need Brazil if you could pick up most of Hispanic America.

I do agree to some extent. Germany and France, though geopolitically disadvantaged, both demonstrated explosive potential for modernization. France, during the Napoleonic Wars, nearly conquered Europe by maximizing the advantages of advanced military doctrines, exceptional leadership, and the power of the nation-state. It’s interesting to think, though, how things might have unfolded if Napoleon had pursued democratic ideals rather than imperial ambitions. What if, instead of installing his relatives as kings, he had focused on exporting republicanism to other nations? Germany also revived after its defeat in World War I, almost conquering Europe by defeating France in just six weeks. However, their ideology, which was not universal but rather intended for domestic consumption, was deeply flawed in terms of fairness and equality. However, there is an issue with the immediate post-World War I period. It was the time when Germany's political system was most vulnerable, yet it was also the period when Germany faced the greatest risk of invasion. If the Kiel mutiny had led to a communist regime in Germany, the Entente Powers would likely have continued the war, eventually attempting to capture Berlin. Indeed, the Soviet Union only became one of the dominant global powers after World War II. Before that, it primarily focused on spreading communism in its neighboring countries.

I think Tsarist Russia was the only country able to become a truly 'marxist' superpower. And even they immediately morphed into a 'Marxist-Leninist' and eventually 'Stalinist' one-party state. If for some reason the Russian Revolution never happened, failed, or never became 'Marxist', Marxism as we know it would remain a political philosophy rather than an ideology, although it would be embraced by various socialist or workers-right parties in the various European parliamentary systems. The closest to a 'soviet-style' communist state I can think of would be Mao's China in the 1940's/1950's where due to it effectively still being run by the last remaining pre-WWII era warlord, China would still be. One-party state with the one party adhering to Chinese-style communism. Before that, any country where the Socialist/communist parties gain a majority in the democratic parliament would be the 'communist' world leader, be it Labour Britain, France, Weimar Germany or even a USA with a pro-labour pro-social(ist) president.
items.original_question: If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union? In OTL, the Soviet Union was essentially the leader of communism, the state that embodied and exported the ideology. In France, after the birth of the “first republic in Europe,” the country faced massive wars against the old Western monarchies. As a result, although Napoleon, an extraordinary hero, almost succeeded in conquering Europe, France ultimately fell. Soviet Russia also faced a similar crisis. After the October Revolution, the first communist state was born, and the great powers, much like the monarchies a century before, sought to destroy Soviet Russia. However, unlike France, Soviet Russia survived the Russian Civil War. Afterward, the Soviet Union was no longer simply "Communist State A." They developed the potential of the land that was Russia. They transformed the underdeveloped economy of the Russian Empire into one of growth. Using that newfound capability, they exported revolution to various countries around the world. From Eastern Europe to Asia, the surrounding countries of Russia were all affected by communism. Furthermore, after 1945, they became a superpower alongside the United States, exporting revolution globally. Let’s consider a historical counterfactual. After Alexander II, the imperial succession changed. Unlike in OTL, Tsarevich Nicholas survived, and instead of the reactionary Alexander III, he ascended the throne. This alternate Nicholas II continued the reforms initiated by Alexander II, complementing, improving, and strengthening them. Unlike in OTL, Russia underwent a different trajectory. The Russian Empire was preserved, and Soviet Russia never came into being. In this scenario, which country could have replaced the Soviet Union? Which nation would need to become communist in order to "survive against surrounding capitalist powers" and "become a great power capable of exporting revolution?" Sometimes, in alternate history works (especially in game mods by Paradox Interactive), there are many timelines where a socialist revolution occurs in a country other than Russia. However, in my view, it’s questionable how many countries could do what the Soviet Union did. France? Germany? They have many geopolitical enemies. Even if they were to become communist after World War I, could they, like the Soviet Union, export revolution worldwide and become a superpower? It seems more likely that they would struggle just to survive. Britain, the United States? In OTL, Marx argued that a sufficiently developed capitalist system was necessary for a communist revolution to occur, with Britain being his example. Britain was also the world’s leading superpower at the time. However, a communist revolution did not occur in Britain. Because capitalism was so advanced, ironically, the entrenched privileges of the system were also too strong. British socialists who advocated for a revolutionary overthrow of the system did not have the power to challenge the entrenched elites, while others accepted the system and sought reforms within it. Ultimately, the conditions I believe are necessary for a "Soviet candidate" are as follows: 1. Geopolitically, it must be easy to defend. The country should be able to secure its borders and have a strategic position that allows for long-term survival and expansion. 2. It must have the potential to become a great power. The country needs the necessary resources, population, and industrial capacity to rise as a major global player. 3. Capitalism cannot be overly developed, and the elites must be driven toward 'system overthrow' rather than 'system compliance.' There must be enough dissatisfaction with the existing system to foster a desire for revolution, not merely reforms within the system. These are the core elements for a country to replicate the role of the Soviet Union. Where, besides Russia, could there be a land or country that fits these conditions? As a side note, it doesn’t necessarily have to be pure communism in this alternative Soviet ideology. It could be something like Maoism, syndicalism, or a unique form of socialism tailored to the needs of that country.

If the Russian Revolution had not succeeded, the most plausible candidate to form a Soviet-style union would have been **Germany**. The German Revolution of 1918–1919 brought the country to the brink of a socialist takeover, with workers' and soldiers' councils (the equivalent of soviets) seizing power in many cities. The Spartacist uprising aimed to establish a dictatorship of the proletariat, and for a time, Bavaria actually became a short-lived Soviet Republic. Germany also possessed the industrial strength, Marxist intellectual tradition, and deep social unrest—fueled by defeat in World War I—that Lenin saw as prerequisites for revolution. 

Unlike Russia, Germany was at the heart of industrialized Europe, and a successful German socialist state might have quickly federated with soviet-style governments in Austria, Hungary, or even breakaway regions of the collapsing Austro-Hungarian Empire, forming a multi-national "Union of Socialist Republics" in Central Europe. The ideological gravitation of Marx's own expectation that revolution would begin in advanced capitalist nations makes Germany the strongest counterfactual birthplace for a Soviet-like entity.

items.question: What If the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe?
human_answers: Yeah, Medieval Europe in a lot of ways was already influenced by steppe culture like the Huns, Magyars, Avars. This is most obvious in the way these cultures introduced the stirrup and revolutionized cavalry warfare in the political and social structure. IMO knighthood would probably not have developed in its recognizable form without these cultures. I guess what I was thinking is that with the Alans, it wouldn’t just be inherited bits and pieces . A stable Alan kingdom could’ve institutionalized that heritage in law, military organization, and diplomacy in ways that a post-Hunnic and Avar kingdom probably wouldn’t. And yeah, I didn’t mean “Zoroastrian” in the sense of fire temples and Avesta orthodoxy. More like echoes of older Iranian cosmology or ritual that might’ve persisted under the surface alongside Christianity, at least in the early centuries. Basically, I think the difference is between having remnants of a steppe culture floating around versus having it as the living core of a political state right in the middle of medieval Western Europe. That alone could’ve made for a noticeably different flavor in the region’s history.

Looking at the map I wonder if we would see the Alans have their focus in what is Portugal especially when the Muslims go a-conquering. Also I wonder with this arrangement would we see a Alanic-Latinite language develop since it does seem that the elite would speak Alanic while the lower classes would speak some flavour of vulgar latin. A scenario where high register words that the ancestral Alans cared about, like rulership (leader, group meeting, horse, that kinda stuff) and normal stuff stays roughly Hispanic. It probably would have a reduced grammar too and be completely different from what we see in English, so that's fun to see. All the talk about knighthood also is highly ironic because it ultimately evolved into one of the best ways to defend against steppe raiders, and the diffuse way that every noble defended their lands via castle did stop steppe invasions alongside other factors.
items.original_question: What if the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe? Most people normally associate the Völkerwanderungen period with the mass migration of Germanic tribes into the Roman frontiers. But a large number of non-Germanic people also joined these groups. One of them were the Alans an Iranian people who crossed the Rhine in the winter of 406 along with the Vandals, Suebi, Goths Burgundians etc. and fanned out into Roman Gaul . They would eventually form a kingdom in North Africa alongside the Vandals. But what if Instead of getting absorbed by the Vandals and the Franks, and disappearing into history, they had actually carved out a stable kingdom, say in southwestern Gaul ? What would that look like? An equestrian -based kingdom with a mix of Iranian steppe traditions and local Roman and Germanic culture. Their language and customs might’ve stuck around longer, even mixing with early medieval Christianity or holding onto some older beliefs. I think that this Alan kingdom could’ve complicated Frankish expansion, maybe even keeping Charlemagne from totally dominating Western Europe or at least delaying it? Their military skills might have decided the outcome in battles and diplomacy, and their cultural blend could’ve made medieval Europe way more diverse , for example maybe in unique artistic terms, linguistic influence and traditions. They don't necessarily have to dominate Europe, but form a lasting kingdom long enough for their language, culture, military tradition, religion to make an impact. The whole medieval map could’ve looked very different, and who knows, maybe Zoroastrian-inspired beliefs and horse culture would still echo in some French villages today.

items.model_answer: If the Alans had forged a lasting kingdom in Western Europe, the continent’s cultural and political trajectory might have been profoundly different. Likely centered in the fertile lands they originally roamed—such as the Rhine valley, Gaul, or the Loire basin—an Alan state would have embedded an Iranian-speaking, originally steppe-nomadic elite atop a Romanized or Germanic population. Over generations, this ruling class would gradually blend but leave a distinctive mark: Alanic place names, a unique fusion of equestrian warrior culture with late Roman administrative practices, and a church possibly shaped by their early Arian Christianity (or later conversion to Catholicism with syncretic elements). items.question: What If Partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th Century?
human_answers: Where would the Dutch stand on this? I'm guessing they don't want to see France gain anything in the Low Countries. But, would it be better to swallow a bitter pill in order to make gains themselves and not be left out in the cold getting nothing? The Dutch are past their prime as a power, but I guess they're still something, if not much. Financially, France is on so-so footing, having recovered from the double beat down of the WoSS, then the Mississippi Bubble burst. Britain is usually seen as being on firm financial footing. Spain is typically meh, while Austria typically needs propping up. I'm guessing Britain/France holds the upper hand in the finance department. Britain, although not yet the naval powerhouse of a century later, is undoubtedly the supreme naval power of these four countries. On land, Spain is rather meh. France has its ebbs and flows, and I'm not sure which way the tide is going in the late 1720s. Austria has Eugene, but I'm thinking he's aging. Overall, with Britain and France in bed together, I think they hold the upper hand. The Dutch siding with B/F would seal the financial and naval superiority. The Ottomans have to figure in there, too. I don't really follow their history, but I know they went at it against Austria a bunch. The German realm will get involved. I'm not sure if Austria can invoke HRE involvement, but I'm thinking the usual some Germans in one camp, some in the other, will be the case. It is my impression that Spain thought Austria was going to be more of an active ally, while Austria didn't agree. The buffoon Spain sent to negotiate the alliance sold Philip/Elizabeth on it being much more than it really was. Thus Austria basically laughed at Spain's request for assistance when the bullets started flying. This situation would need to be remedied. Perhaps Britain/France having the audacity to divvy up Austrian soil might do the trick.

Since the ducy of Luxembourh and her city and Namur were quite strategical and important stronghold, the British and Dutch might ask Dunkirk in return for it, even Lille, since this was an imprtant strongh old as well. The earlier Townsend agrement of 1709 was torpedood by the British since it would gieve the Dutch republic too much marked and trade. well if it happens, France has just gained without a fight a direct border with Holland and the rest of the HRE ( making its ability to influence and successfully intervene militarily even greater than Otl ) to remove the Habsburgs from its border ( which in the long run will be more good for Austria than for others, since he will be able to concentrate exclusively on the fight against France on the Italian front, he will consider the Rhine as a minor front for his troops ( since there will be contingents from the entire empire for that ) to weaken Holland ( Catholics will not want to stay in a country that discriminates against them) all thanks to English stupidity which in doing so has lost the only ally on the continent may contain French hegemonic aspirations ( because I doubt France and England will be friendly to each other in the long run )

This partition plan (Stanhope and Townshend) would require worse Anglo-Austrian relations. Britain would have to be convinced that Austria is the biggest threat to the European balance of power and stability. So had Emperor Charles VI gone ahead to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos, then we would see a more solidified Anglo-French alliance as a counterweight. A Bourbon-Hapsburg alliance would reshuffle the post-Utrecht European order and a war could be a real possibility (Europe plunged into a wider war during the OTL Anglo-Spanish War of 1727). After the war, this partition plan could be the basis of peace negotiations (if the Anglo-French alliance gained the upper hand), and Austria could be compensated with Tuscany like in OTL. Personally, I am more interested in James Stanhope's first idea of giving Austrian Netherlands to Leopold or Francis of Lorraine. Suppose that Don Carlos married Maria Theresa and France captured Lorraine in a war, then France could annex it while giving the Austrian Netherlands to Leopold/Francis.
items.original_question: What if Partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th Century? Hi, everyone. This is my second post sharing some lesser-known yet fascinating PoDs in European history. I stumbled upon a historical academic journal written by Frederik Dhondt, a history professor from the Ghent University in Belgium titled " So Great a Revolution’: Charles Townshend and the Partition of the Austrian Netherlands, September 1725 " (2012, Journal of Low Countries Studies). According to the article, Charles Townshend, the British Northern Secretary (equivalent to the Foreign Minister) and his predecessor James Stanhope (†. 1721) had proposed a partition of the Austrian Netherlands. The plan would see Austria surrendering its holdings in the Low Countries. The article summarised three possibilities. Some background before moving on. In the Nine Years' Year and the War of the Spanish Succession, Austria had allied with the Dutch Republic and Great Britain (or England-Scotland before 1707) to counter French ambitions in the Low Countries and the Rhineland. Towards the end of the Spanish Succession War, Britain became weary of increasing Austrian power. In 1716, it allied with France. The Austro-Spanish alliance confirmed by the Treaty of Vienna rang alarm bells in London. Not only did it reconcile the enmity between Emperor Charles XI and King Philip V, the combined power of Spain and Austria threatened the established balance of power. There were even talks to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos (future Charles III). Prime Minister Walpole and Townshend, therefore, desired to weaken the power of Austria. These plans were never made public, Townshend only discussed them with the ambassador in Paris, Horace Walpole. On page 56, Townshend suggested the partition plan could be implemented if the marriage between Maria Theresa and Don Carlos took place. James Stanhope first suggested that the Duke of Lorraine could receive Austria Netherlands. Alternatively, Stanhope suggested awarding it either to the Elector of Cologne or the Elector of Trier. The Electorate would be secularised. Townshend outright dismissed these ridiculous ideas, and offered his own solution. The Dutch will annex some territories including Antwerp. Ypres, Bruges, and Ostend would fall under joint Dutch-British control while the inland and southern portions of the Austrian Netherlands will go to France. What will be the geopolitical and diplomatic consequences of one of these plans was realised? Although I personally doubt the likelihood of this happening, nevertheless the ramifications will be interesting. You can access the article here through your university: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1179/0309656411Z.0000000002 .

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines the hypothesized partition of the Austrian Netherlands in its 18th-century diplomatic context, including who receives what and why the partition is attempted.

criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual with historically grounded territorial stakes such as Flanders, Brabant, Hainaut, Namur, Luxembourg, Dunkirk, or barrier fortresses, and explains why each actor would accept or resist the arrangement.

criteria.name: Dutch, British, and French Strategic Incentives
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer analyzes the likely positions of the Dutch Republic, Britain, and France, especially regarding balance of power, barrier security, trade, naval power, and fear of French expansion.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or seriously misrepresents the Dutch, British, or French interests.
criteria.3-4: Mentions their preferences but reduces them to simple land-grabbing or alliance loyalty.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that the Dutch would fear French gains and that Britain and France might hold leverage, but gives limited mechanism.
criteria.7-8: Explains Dutch security concerns, British balancing calculations, and French interest in pushing its frontier or weakening Austria.
criteria.9-10: Integrates the Barrier Treaty, Dutch decline, British finance/naval leverage, French strategic depth, trade concerns, and the possibility that Dutch participation would depend on compensation and fortified frontiers.

criteria.name: Austria, Spain, HRE, and Wider European Response
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of how Austria and its potential allies or rivals would react, including Spain, the Holy Roman Empire, German states, and possibly the Ottoman Empire.
criteria.1-2: Treats Austria as passive or ignores wider European reactions entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Austria resisting but gives little sense of allies, constraints, or diplomatic consequences.
criteria.5-6: Includes Austria, Spain, or the HRE but with shallow or one-sided analysis.
criteria.7-8: Considers Austria’s military limitations, possible Spanish expectations, divided German responses, and the diplomatic shock of partitioning Habsburg territory.
criteria.9-10: Shows nuanced interaction among Austrian vulnerability, Eugene’s aging military leadership, Spain’s uncertain alliance value, HRE mobilization limits, German state divisions, and possible Ottoman pressure on Austria’s eastern flank.

criteria.name: Military, Financial, and Logistical Causal Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer grounds its scenario in concrete 18th-century power mechanisms: armies, fortresses, finance, naval capacity, logistics, and alliance credibility.
criteria.1-2: Relies on unsupported assertions about who wins without mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions armies or money in generic terms without connecting them to outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some relevant factors such as British finance, French land power, Dutch forts, or Austrian weakness.
criteria.7-8: Connects military and financial capacities to likely bargaining, deterrence, campaign outcomes, and defensive lines in the Low Countries.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent mechanism-based assessment using naval supremacy, credit systems, fortress networks, supply lines, French land access, Dutch barrier defenses, and Austria’s multi-front constraints.

criteria.name: Long-Range Coherence, Uncertainty, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer develops plausible downstream consequences over decades while acknowledging uncertainty and avoiding internal contradictions or anachronism.
criteria.1-2: Gives an implausible or contradictory chain of events with little historical grounding.
criteria.3-4: Offers some consequences but they are abrupt, deterministic, or poorly linked to the premise.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible short-term outcome and some longer-term effects, but with gaps or overconfidence.
criteria.7-8: Traces coherent effects on the balance of power, Anglo-French relations, Dutch security, Austrian strategy, and later European conflicts while noting uncertainties.
criteria.9-10: Builds a disciplined long-range causal chain showing how the partition could reshape Franco-Dutch borders, Habsburg priorities, British continental alliances, HRE politics, and future wars, with careful caveats and no major contradictions.

items.model_answer:
If the Austrian Netherlands had been partitioned in the 18th century—most plausibly under a scheme like the 1757 Treaty of Versailles or a successful Bavarian exchange in the 1780s—the map and political trajectory of Western Europe would have been fundamentally altered. The Habsburg-ruled region, roughly modern Belgium, was a strategic crossroads and a recurring source of conflict. A division among France, the Dutch Republic, and Prussia would have removed the buffer state that later became a cockpit of revolution and war.

France gaining the French-speaking southern provinces (Hainaut, Namur, Luxemburg) and key fortresses like Ypres or Tournai would have pushed its frontier northward, securing its “natural borders” earlier and reducing the strategic vulnerability that drove much revolutionary expansion. The Dutch Republic, inheriting coastal Flanders and perhaps Antwerp, would have controlled the Scheldt estuary even more tightly, likely stifling the economic revival of that great port permanently and reinforcing Dutch commercial hegemony—though it might also have accelerated the Republic’s decline by adding a restless Catholic population. Prussia would have absorbed the eastern territories (Limburg, perhaps Guelders), linking its Rhenish possessions and gaining a firm foothold on the Meuse, which would have intensified its rivalry with France and made the later rise of a unified Germany more fraught.

No independent Belgian state would have emerged in 1830 because the territory would have been fragmented and assimilated into stronger neighbours over generations. The absence of a neutral Belgium would have transformed 19th-century diplomacy: there would be no treaty-guaranteed neutrality for a major power to violate, fundamentally reshaping the causes of both the First World War and Britain’s continental commitments. The region’s dense population and industrial potential would have been incorporated directly into the French, Dutch, or Prussian economies, accelerating their industrialization but also embedding deeper ethno-linguistic tensions within those states—a Flemish question inside the Netherlands, a Walloon question inside France, each potentially sharpening domestic conflicts. The French Revolution itself might have been delayed or deflected, since the Austrian Netherlands’ revolt in 1789–90 was a key early destabilizer; a partition would have removed the Habsburg grievance and altered the internal pressures that led to war in 1792. In short, the partition would have deleted a habitual theatre of war from the European map, but at the cost of storing up nationalist tensions inside the absorbers well into the modern era.

items.question: My Alternative History Scenario: What If Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799?
human_answers: It's very obscure and I couldn't track down the reference this morning, which I think came from some book on the First Serbian Uprising. The Turkish fortress on the island blocked easy communication between the Serbs and the Russian forces in Wallachia. Well, Russia sent an auxiliary force into Poland to aid Napoleon, as promised, and was rewarded with Tarnopol in the peace treaty. So it looks like a victory. But in reality as you say Russia did very little but go through the motions and Napoleon gave them the merest scrap of a reward. Despite the common view, I don't think Alexander ingratiated himself to Vienna by doing this and I don't think Austria would have been more active in 1812 had things been different in 1809. Fair enough. Austria was at least thought to be supplying weapons to the Sultan in 1829, though I don't know if that was confirmed to actually be true.

Why would Hapsburgs or Hohenzollerns circa 1803 care about the US? None of them had colonies in the Western hemisphere (or anywhere else) and, IIRC, at that time the former colonies were not ideologically, not to mention economically or militarily, of a any serious importance for the continental Europe. Which, putting aside Spain, leaves “certain trade arrangements” and the obvious question is what these arrangements would be? Would they hurt or benefit France? In OTL to a great degree the French bellicosity was supported by the strategic factor called “Bonaparte” who, besides military glory, provided looting (both on state and individual levels) on the “industrial” scale. It seems that ITTL French government behaves “Napoleonic” without Napoleon, which brings some obvious questions without clear answers to which episode with tearing the document looks as an act of imbecility. AFAIK, none of the OTL generals of that period were that good in both areas and without Bonaparte the war of 2nd coalition most probably would end due to the exhaustion of both sides without too much to show for it (in OTL in 1799 the French were kicked out of Italy and exercises on the Danube led to nowhere for either side so the only area of clear success was Switzerland). Which means that enthusiasm in France is unlikely and, in OTL the Directory was in almost permanent fiscal crisis. So, it would be quite interesting to find out in more details how the things were proceeding (including financial aspect) without Nappy? Were ITTL any indications of the Russian desire to conquer Hungary? Anyway, this was clearly not an consideration during the 2nd Coalition when Austria asked for the Russian help (at least in OTL). BTW, without Nappy, is Paul still on the throne? If yes, and if the 2nd Coalition ended along the OTL lines, the issue would be not Francis’ reluctance but Paul’s refusal to deal with a former ally who screwed him up. Alexander hated Napoleon on a personal level, which mostly defined his actions in the 3rd and 4th coalitions, but, while being pro-British, was not actively anti-French in general. Anyway, it does not look like he would be doing Francis’ bidding. Why not Greenland? The XVII - XVIII centuries coalition wars against the Ottomans demonstrated to the Russians that the Austrians are, at best, useless as the allies and impotent as the enemies. If Austria is at war with France, whoever is the Russian emperor, can start war with the OE without paying any attention to Vienna’s position. Besides, how would Russia simultaneously fight the French and the OE? Obviously, expecting that after the French war the Hapsburg emperor is going to honor his generous promise to grant Russia the Ottoman territories (how about the Ottoman consent?) assumes a rather unrealistic level of a naivety on the Russian side. Which is of no importance to Vienna and Berlin by the obvious reason: none of them has colonies in the Americas. Then, the US in the early 1800s as a serious military threat? In 1812 it had less than 10,000 troops when war started and its navy had 12 frigates. Yes, and the question is how an obvious idiot managed to become the head of the French government and how his actions got approval of the parliament?
items.original_question: My Alternative History Scenario: What if Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799? EPISODE THREE​ German Pact ​ ​ A sudden storm breaking out across Europe had created a massive shockwave. Austria, still struggling to recover from the economic and military wounds of the War of the Second Coalition, was deeply displeased by France’s abrupt rekindling of hostilities. Emperor Francis II had been expecting a long period of peace, one he intended to devote to revitalizing Germany. Unfortunately, history had once again disappointed him. His federalist ambitions had not yet completely faded, but this meant confronting French republicanism earlier than anticipated. Moreover, following the referendum held on 18 February 1803 and the subsequent election, the country transitioned into what was called a presidential system. As a result, Fourier—who came to power and was a prominent representative of socialist thought—began spreading his ideas more widely across Europe. This signified a gradual shift of the German peoples toward republicanism. Although the Kingdom of Prussia and the Habsburg Monarchy did not hold each other in high regard, they shared a common enemy: France and republicanism. Approximately one week had passed since the outbreak of the Franco-Spanish War. French armies advanced rapidly, exploiting the dire condition of the Spanish forces to seize Catalonia and push toward Eastern Aragon. The Basque region had also fallen. Emperor Francis convened his cabinet, and they debated at length what course of action should be taken. Johann Amadeus Franz, the Minister of Finance of the era, was firmly opposed to breaking the peace with France, as any potential war would further devastate Austria’s already fragile economy. József Alvinczi, the Chief of the General Staff, argued that this war represented an opportunity to eliminate both France and the spread of republican ideas on the European continent. He maintained that, as demonstrated in the previous conflict, the Austrian army was not in as poor a condition as believed and demanded that an open ultimatum be issued to France. However, the Emperor had a different plan in mind. Although there was no certainty it would succeed, he deemed it worth attempting. For this reason, he decided to send a delegate to the Kingdom of Prussia, carrying a note requesting a private meeting with the King. The delegation set out on 15 March 1803. Meanwhile, across Europe, no clear decision had yet emerged from the British Isles. Prime Minister Henry Addington had no desire to see Spain under French control, but he also believed that the British Army was not yet prepared. After lengthy discussions with other statesmen, he sent an envoy to the Kingdom of Portugal to further expand the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance and present several proposals. In the meantime, the delegation sent by Austria to Prussia returned two weeks later. The Emperor’s proposal to the King of Prussia was to intervene in the Franco-Spanish War by forming a German coalition. The Prussian King, eager to enhance his prestige among the German states, responded favorably and announced his acceptance. Thus, the German Pact was formed. Both sides began final preparations for their already mobilized armies, and within approximately two weeks, everything was ready. A note bearing the personal signatures of both the Emperor and the King was delivered to the French delegates by a joint Austro-Prussian mission. The note demanded that France sever its alliance with the United States, withdraw from Spain, and agree to certain trade arrangements. French President Charles Fourier tore the original document to pieces in parliament. This act provided the Habsburg Monarchy and the Kingdom of Prussia with sufficient legitimacy to launch a military intervention against France. Emperor Francis II was deeply uneasy about Russia’s ambiguous stance. He neither wanted Russia to emerge excessively strong nor excessively weak. Poland could be the first step, and the Russian flag might one day fly over Hungary or the borders of the Holy Roman Empire. Taking such a risk seemed irrational. Therefore, depending on the course of the war, he considered enticing Russia into joining their side by offering the Balkan territories of the already weakened Ottoman Empire—despite his preference for preserving the balance of power in the Balkans and Eastern Europe. The French threat, however, took precedence. Although the United States did not yet pose a direct threat to Europe, it continued to threaten the colonial powers in the Americas. While it had not yet entered the conflict, such an involvement was not impossible. On the other hand, the Emperor foresaw that the French government’s aggressive and overly idealistic actions would ultimately lead to its downfall. By initiating this war, France had effectively shot itself in the foot, and these events would pave the way for a rise in anti-French sentiment throughout Europe.

criteria.3-4: Names some coalition powers but gives simplistic outcomes, such as automatic French collapse or automatic French dominance.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that France was under pressure in Italy and Europe, but gives only partial causal links to coalition behavior.
criteria.7-8: Connects Napoleon’s absence to campaigns, coalition coordination problems, Austrian and Russian aims, British strategy, and peace prospects.
criteria.9-10: Balances French resilience with coalition limitations and gives a nuanced account of likely military stalemate, altered treaties, and divergent Austrian/Russian/British incentives.

criteria.name: Long-range European and global downstream effects

criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent medium- and long-term chain affecting France, Germany, Italy, Britain, Russia, Austria, Spain, and colonial affairs.
criteria.9-10: Shows sophisticated long-range reasoning across European institutions, nationalism, war finance, imperial reform, colonial policy, and Ottoman/Russian dynamics while preserving causal continuity.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, plausibility, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes; avoids contradictions with the premise and known constraints; and does not overstate obscure or unsupported claims.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, anachronisms, or confident claims that violate the premise or basic historical facts.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible ideas but also unsupported leaps, internal inconsistencies, or overconfident deterministic conclusions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent and plausible, with some uncertainty noted, but includes gaps or weakly justified assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly signals uncertainty, explains assumptions, avoids deterministic overreach, and maintains internal consistency across the timeline.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates high-probability consequences from speculative branches, flags evidentiary limits, and rigorously checks all claims against the 1799 counterfactual logic.

items.model_answer:
Without Napoleon’s return in 1799, the coup against the Directory would still likely have occurred, but it would have taken a very different shape. Sieyès, the political mastermind seeking a strong executive, had already lost his first choice—General Joubert—at Novi. Without Napoleon as his “sword,” Sieyès would have turned to a less charismatic general like Moreau, Jourdan, or perhaps Bernadotte. These men lacked Napoleon’s personal ambition and ruthless political instinct, so the resulting regime—probably still a Consulate—would have been more collegial and less authoritarian, with Sieyès as the dominant civilian figure.

Militarily, the absence of Napoleon’s genius would have been felt immediately. The War of the Second Coalition was not going well for France before Marengo; without that stunning victory, the Republic might have been forced into an earlier and less favorable peace, ceding Italy and the Rhine frontier. Internally, royalist forces would have been emboldened, and the fragile republic could have collapsed, leading either to a restored Bourbon monarchy by 1804–1805 or to prolonged instability and civil strife. Reforms such as the Civil Code, the Bank of France, and centralized administration were not solely Napoleon’s ideas—many were in the air—but their systematic implementation required his singular drive. Without him, France would have modernized more slowly and unevenly.

Europe would have been spared the Napoleonic Wars, but also the sweeping reform of legal systems, the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, and the spread of nationalism. The Concert of Europe might never have formed in the same way, and the revolutions of the 19th century would have unfolded against a more conservative, fragmented map. In short, removing Napoleon from 1799 changes not just French history but the entire trajectory of the modern world, likely delaying constitutionalism, national unification, and the rise of the modern state.

edus.text: Without Napoleon’s return in 1799, the coup against the Directory would still likely have occurred,
but it would have taken a very different shape.
Sieyès, the political mastermind seeking a strong executive, had already lost his first choice—General Joubert—at Novi.
Without Napoleon as his “sword,” Sieyès would have turned to a less charismatic general like Moreau, Jourdan, or perhaps Bernadotte.
These men lacked Napoleon’s personal ambition and ruthless political instinct,
so the resulting regime—probably still a Consulate—would have been more collegial and less authoritarian,
with Sieyès as the dominant civilian figure.
Militarily, the absence of Napoleon’s genius would have been felt immediately.
The War of the Second Coalition was not going well for France before Marengo;
without that stunning victory, the Republic might have been forced into an earlier and less favorable peace,
ceding Italy and the Rhine frontier.
Internally, royalist forces would have been emboldened,
and the fragile republic could have collapsed,
leading either to a restored Bourbon monarchy by 1804–1805
or to prolonged instability and civil strife.
Reforms such as the Civil Code, the Bank of France, and centralized administration were not solely Napoleon’s ideas—many were in the air—
but their systematic implementation required his singular drive.
Without him, France would have modernized more slowly and unevenly.
Europe would have been spared the Napoleonic Wars,
but also the sweeping reform of legal systems, the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, and the spread of nationalism.
The Concert of Europe might never have formed in the same way,
and the revolutions of the 19th century would have unfolded against a more conservative, fragmented map.
In short, removing Napoleon from 1799 changes not just French history but the entire trajectory of the modern world,
likely delaying constitutionalism, national unification, and the rise of the modern state.

items.question: What If the Greek 'Great Plan' had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire?
human_answers: A more decisive Ottoman defeat against Greece can give birth to the "Megali Idea" before 1844. In such a scenario, a larger independent Greek state can invited Louis-Philippe d’Orléans to become its king, before 1830 of course. This arrangement can be supported by both France and its Bourbon king, who might want to sideline a troublesome cousin, and by the United Kingdom. For the British, the presence of a Great European power south of the Straits, one aligned with neither Austria nor Russia can further divide the continental great powers and serve British strategic interests. With France satisfied in Greece and Austria compensated with territories along the Adriatic coast, Britain can focus on securing Egypt for itself. Even if the Suez Canal is not even a dream, control of Egypt is already strategically valuable for strengthening connections with India. By 1829, railway projects are already under consideration, making overland transit increasingly plausible and reinforcing Egypt’s geopolitical importance. And if its happen after 1830, Louis-Philippe has enough sons (6 minus one who died in 1828) to send one to Greece.

Considering their interest is not even religious (GB: Protestant, France: Catholic, Russia: Orthodox) and that really none of these Great Powers saw the Greek War of Independence with positive eyes (to them it was no different than the revolutions in Spain, Portugal and Naples; which, btw, they sent huge armies to crush). There was later a British change, but even the Metternich, Alexander and so on weren't super happy about it. Remember: at this point, the memory of Napoleon is far fresher than that of the Ottoman invasions into the Balkans, so the concern, far above Islam, is revolutionary sentiment. What I do see happening is them deliberating and taking too long to make a decision that the situation ends up devolving on its own (it took them like 3 years to agree to send an invasion to Spain). Then again, the French were sympathetic to Muhammad Ali while the British aided Ali Pasha plenty of times (through Maitland, specifically). They will always prefer a rotting corpse of the Ottoman empire maintaining power over the ambitious and reformist Albanian Pashas in power, this is why they went out of their way to put them out IRL, but when shit hits the fan, they have to re-examine their approach of course.

Agreed that the Great Powers, including even Russia under Alexander, don't want a full Ottoman collapse. That's not the same as saying they would intervene to stop it. It's hard to conceive of a situation in which Great Britain, France, or Russia would go to war to suppress Christian rebels fighting against the Sultan, particularly after the various atrocities committed at Chios and other places. There were also similar atrocities committed by the Greeks against Muslims, but this did not register in the European consciousness of the time and would not be a factor. It's also not a given that any intervention would be successful at stopping chaos and preserving the Empire, even if it did somehow occur. This would be a formidable job if the situation became so extreme that the Ottomans asked for such support. More likely the intervention would be directed towards managing the collapse and achieving a partition either formally or in terms of spheres of influence.
items.original_question: What if 'Great Plan' more or fully successful - Greek War of Independence causes early Ottoman collapse? There have been many threads about the Greek War of Independence here, but one what if I haven't seen anyone talk about might be one of the most crazy ones. Mark Mazower states the following in his book on the Greek War of Indepdendence: Of course, aside from the revolt in the Peloponnese, none of these plans ever came close to succeeding. These plans were modified or abandoned entirely when the focus of the revolt shifted from the Peloponnese to the Danubian Principalities. There was a letter sent to cause terror in Constantinople, but the letter never made it and plans were changing so often that no action was taken. Now this seems like an insane scheme which would be insanely hard to pull off, even if all the circumstances were right, but let's hypothetically ask, what if some, or all of them did? Would this cause the Ottoman Empire to collapse entirely, or enter a prolonged period of unrest? A torching of the fleet, coordinated with the assassination of Mahmud II, coupled with all the other issues the empire was facing in the early 1820's seem like they would be a complete headache, who would even be Sultan had this happened, considering Abdulmecid wasn't even born yet and Mahmud II had no sons? Edit: Turns out Mahmud II had a single surviving son by this point, Abdulhamid. But he died in 1825 IOTL, which, if it still happens, might actually make things even worse if the revolt didn't fizzle out by then.

items.model_answer:
If the Greek War of Independence had triggered the sudden, complete collapse of the Ottoman Empire in the 1820s—and an expansive “Great Plan” had immediately restored a Hellenic-dominated state stretching from the Peloponnese to Constantinople and western Anatolia—the European order would have been convulsed decades before the Crimean War and the Balkan crises that actually unfolded. No power was prepared for a rapid Ottoman vacuum, and the result would have been a chaotic, multilateral free-for-all rather than a clean Greek revival.

First, the very survival of a Greater Greece would have depended on the forbearance of the powers that had just crushed Napoleon. Russia, which saw itself as the Orthodox heir to Byzantium, would likely have invaded the Balkans under the pretext of protecting Christians but in reality to seize Constantinople and the Straits. A Russian occupation of the city would have triggered an immediate British and French naval intervention, risking a general European war far earlier than 1853. The Concert of Europe, still fragile in the 1820s, could have shattered, and the “Eastern Question” would have been answered not by decades of managed decline but by a partition crisis in which Austria, Britain, France, and Russia carved up Ottoman territories into spheres of influence.

Greece itself would have been too weak to hold its maximalist claims. The fledgling state had no navy capable of matching the Great Powers, no administrative machinery to govern a multi-ethnic empire, and a society riven by factional conflicts. Even if a Greek king (perhaps Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, who briefly accepted and then refused the Greek throne) had been installed in Constantinople, he would have faced immediate revolts from Muslims, Bulgarians, and other groups who had no desire to trade Ottoman rule for Greek domination. A “Byzantine” restoration would have been stillborn, quickly reduced to a rump state by foreign pressure or internal collapse.

Elsewhere, the early disintegration of the empire would have accelerated national movements not only in Serbia, Wallachia, and Moldavia but also in Bosnia, Albania, and among the Armenians and Kurds. Without the Ottoman framework, these groups would have fought each other and the encroaching empires, producing a patchwork of conflict early in the 19th century. The Middle East would have fractured: Egypt under Muhammad Ali had already demonstrated its autonomy; with the sultan gone, he would have openly seized Syria and the Hejaz, challenging the Greek claim to Jerusalem and setting off an Arab–Greek–Russian contest for the Holy Places. North Africa would have fallen under some combination of French, British, and local rule, with Algeria’s conquest perhaps accelerated.

In short, an early Ottoman collapse after a sweeping Greek success would not have meant a peaceful realization of the Megali Idea but an earlier and more violent version of the Eastern Question, with the Great Powers imposing a settlement that redrew borders far more radically than in 1832 or 1878. edus.text: If the Greek War of Independence had triggered the sudden, complete collapse of the Ottoman Empire in the 1820s
and an expansive “Great Plan” had immediately restored a Hellenic-dominated state stretching from the Peloponnese to Constantinople and western Anatolia
the European order would have been convulsed decades before the Crimean War and the Balkan crises that actually unfolded.
No power was prepared for a rapid Ottoman vacuum
and the result would have been a chaotic, multilateral free-for-all rather than a clean Greek revival.
First, the very survival of a Greater Greece would have depended on the forbearance of the powers that had just crushed Napoleon.
Russia, which saw itself as the Orthodox heir to Byzantium, would likely have invaded the Balkans under the pretext of protecting Christians
but in reality to seize Constantinople and the Straits.
A Russian occupation of the city would have triggered an immediate British and French naval intervention
risking a general European war far earlier than 1853.
The Concert of Europe, still fragile in the 1820s, could have shattered
and the “Eastern Question” would have been answered not by decades of managed decline but by a partition crisis
in which Austria, Britain, France, and Russia carved up Ottoman territories into spheres of influence.
Greece itself would have been too weak to hold its maximalist claims.
The fledgling state had no navy capable of matching the Great Powers
no administrative machinery to govern a multi-ethnic empire
and a society riven by factional conflicts.
Even if a Greek king (perhaps Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, who briefly accepted and then refused the Greek throne) had been installed in Constantinople
he would have faced immediate revolts from Muslims, Bulgarians, and other groups
who had no desire to trade Ottoman rule for Greek domination.
A “Byzantine” restoration would have been stillborn
quickly reduced to a rump state by foreign pressure or internal collapse.
Elsewhere, the early disintegration of the empire would have accelerated national movements not only in Serbia, Wallachia, and Moldavia but also in Bosnia, Albania, and among the Armenians and Kurds.
Without the Ottoman framework, these groups would have fought each other and the encroaching empires
producing a patchwork of conflict early in the 19th century.
The Middle East would have fractured:
Egypt under Muhammad Ali had already demonstrated its autonomy
with the sultan gone, he would have openly seized Syria and the Hejaz
challenging the Greek claim to Jerusalem
and setting off an Arab–Greek–Russian contest for the Holy Places.
North Africa would have fallen under some combination of French, British, and local rule
with Algeria’s conquest perhaps accelerated.
In short, an early Ottoman collapse after a sweeping Greek success would not have meant a peaceful realization of the Megali Idea
but an earlier and more violent version of the Eastern Question
with the Great Powers imposing a settlement that redrew borders far more radically than in 1832 or 1878.
Greece would have been left with a modest coastal enclave at most
while the bulk of the lost Ottoman domains would have been divided into protectorates or absorbed by Russia, Austria, and Britain.
The nationalist energies that the Greek cause inspired would have been channeled into rival movements
and the 19th-century Balkan powder keg would have begun exploding even before the term “Balkanization” existed.
