items.question: What If the French become one of the largest communities in the US
human_answers: Hordes of Catholics, even if not all that devout, descending on the US will cause some tension. On the flip side, though, France is one of the civilized nations, and they're seen as more desirable shade of white. Timing matters, too. Napoleonic era, when immigration is still low, is a whole lot different than the final decades of the 19th century, when millions is a drop in the bucket. Location matters, too. Are the French hordes joining into the crowded East, where they likely assimilate? Or are they carving out a big chunk of the midwest/west as largely French? Reason for the diaspora might matter. If we mess with the Napoleonic era, especially if we butterfly it (not killing off a generation or two of males would be a good start in having excess population to export), the state of the world could affect the state of the USA (maybe even the size if no Mex-Am War/Texas). With such a generic What if, we can only talk in generics. If we stipulate a recognizable world, more or less the same, except a massive French diaspora for some reason that hasn't caused OTL to derail.... I would guess the French would be like any other large group. There'll be tension, but everyone will adapt. It's an age of racism, and French are in the top class, so I suspect they'll have an easier time of it. (caveat edit: In no way am I saying French are better than any other nation, but reality is that skin color mattered. My understanding is that not all whites were considered equal)

I would assume rather than staying in the east, the French would largely settle in former Louisiana- centring probably on New Orleans. Texas and Florida as well are likely spots for French settlement. Of the 13 colonies, I would guess it’s the southern ones which would be most amenable to French settlement- though how that affects racial dynamics in the south, and how that affects potential north south tensions is difficult to say. It’s difficult as well to say what the economic impact of French settlement would be- I’d say as a community they’d probably be more educated and thus better off than the Irish or Italians, perhaps more comparable to German or Swedish immigrants. Perhaps the planter class ends up going fully bilingual. Depending on how the 19th century goes you could end up with an Alt-confederacy that stays independent because it has so many French speakers and Catholics that the north simply isn’t interested in reintegrating them.
items.original_question: What if the French become one of the largest communities in the US Let’s suppose that millions of French flocked to the US in the 19th century for one reason or another—for example, because harsher Napoleonic Wars and a more severe Congress of Vienna plunged France into a deep economic crisis, while the Irish and Italians would be less numerous in the US, for example because the Irish Great Famine never happened and the Italian peninsula unified and modernized earlier. No PoD before 1780. How would the French be treated in the US? Would they face xenophobia and form a distinct community like the Irish and Italians, or would they be assimilated among the WASPs within one or two generations like the Germans did IOTL? French culture was admired, but I’m not sure that the arrival of millions of French people (with a Latin culture and Catholic religion) would be particularly well received.

items.model_answer:
If the French had become one of the largest communities in the United States, the nation’s cultural, linguistic, and political landscape would likely be profoundly different, weaving a strong Francophone thread into the fabric of American identity. Such a scenario could have emerged from a more successful French colonial strategy, a massive wave of immigration from France or other Francophone regions (like Canada, Haiti, or West Africa) at a critical juncture, or even a different outcome of the Louisiana Purchase that preserved a vast French-speaking territory.

The most immediate and visible change would be linguistic. Instead of a largely monolingual English-speaking nation with a significant Spanish-speaking minority, the U.S. might function as a de facto bilingual country, with French enjoying widespread use in government, education, and daily life. Entire regions—beyond modern Louisiana and New England—could be Francophone strongholds, perhaps the Great Lakes, the Mississippi Valley, or the Pacific Northwest, where French place names already hint at another history. Public signage, official documents, and national media would routinely accommodate both languages, and the vitality of French might spark earlier and more robust bilingual education movements, softening the historic nativist resistance to multilingualism.

Culturally, a large French community would reshape America’s self-conception. The dominant Anglo-Protestant narrative would be balanced by a powerful Catholic and secular republican tradition rooted in the French Enlightenment. The tension between a puritanical work ethic and a more Mediterranean joie de vivre could lead to a different rhythm of life, with stronger protections for leisure, culinary culture, and the arts. Gastronomy, wine consumption, and café society would likely be more deeply entrenched across the country. In literature, philosophy, and political thought, French intellectual currents—from existentialism to postmodernism—might find a more direct and earlier purchase in American universities and public debate, potentially shifting the national penchant for pragmatism toward a greater embrace of abstract theory.

Politically, the presence of a large French community would introduce a distinct electoral bloc with its own historical preoccupations. Unlike the English colonial legacy of limited government and common law, the French tradition carries a strong centralizing, étatist impulse and a civil law system in its heartland. This could manifest in greater support for state-led social programs, universalism, and a more assertive foreign policy that at times aligns with—and at other times tugs against—Anglo-American hegemony. The community might serve as a bridge between the U.S. and the Francophone world, deepening ties with Canada (perhaps averting Quebec’s isolation), the Caribbean, Africa, and Europe, and making the U.S. a more active member of international bodies like La Francophonie. Religious dynamics would also shift: a large French population would swell the ranks of American Catholicism and possibly secularism, challenging the historical dominance of Protestant denominations and reframing debates on church-state separation, education, and morality.

Even the psychology of American exceptionalism might evolve. With a strong internal voice that remembers an alternative colonial experiment—one that produced a different revolution and a different notion of liberty—the American historical narrative would become more pluralistic. The foundational myth of the Pilgrims and the frontier would share space with the legacies of Champlain, Lafayette, and the Code Noir. This richer, more complicated past could foster a more self-critical and globally aware national identity, less tempted to view its path as uniquely ordained.

In essence, a French community of such magnitude would not merely add a new accent to the American chorus; it would fundamentally re-key the composition, infusing the United States with a deeper duality between Anglo-Saxon pragmatism and French humanist idealism, and blurring the lines between what the world considers “American” and “Francophone.”

edus.text: If the French had become one of the largest communities in the United States,
the nation’s cultural, linguistic, and political landscape would likely be profoundly different,
weaving a strong Francophone thread into the fabric of American identity.
Such a scenario could have emerged from a more successful French colonial strategy,
a massive wave of immigration from France or other Francophone regions (like Canada, Haiti, or West Africa) at a critical juncture,
or even a different outcome of the Louisiana Purchase that preserved a vast French-speaking territory.
The most immediate and visible change would be linguistic.
Instead of a largely monolingual English-speaking nation with a significant Spanish-speaking minority,
the U.S. might function as a de facto bilingual country,
with French enjoying widespread use in government, education, and daily life.
Entire regions—beyond modern Louisiana and New England—could be Francophone strongholds,
perhaps the Great Lakes, the Mississippi Valley, or the Pacific Northwest,
where French place names already hint at another history.
Public signage, official documents, and national media would routinely accommodate both languages,
and the vitality of French might spark earlier and more robust bilingual education movements,
softening the historic nativist resistance to multilingualism.
Culturally, a large French community would reshape America’s self-conception.
The dominant Anglo-Protestant narrative would be balanced by a powerful Catholic and secular republican tradition rooted in the French Enlightenment.
The tension between a puritanical work ethic and a more Mediterranean joie de vivre could lead to a different rhythm of life,
with stronger protections for leisure, culinary culture, and the arts.
Gastronomy, wine consumption, and café society would likely be more deeply entrenched across the country.
In literature, philosophy, and political thought, French intellectual currents—from existentialism to postmodernism—
might find a more direct and earlier purchase in American universities and public debate,
potentially shifting the national penchant for pragmatism toward a greater embrace of abstract theory.
Politically, the presence of a large French community would introduce a distinct electoral bloc with its own historical preoccupations.
Unlike the English colonial legacy of limited government and common law,
the French tradition carries a strong centralizing, étatist impulse and a civil law system in its heartland.
This could manifest in greater support for state-led social programs, universalism, and a more assertive foreign policy
that at times aligns with—and at other times tugs against—Anglo-American hegemony.
The community might serve as a bridge between the U.S. and the Francophone world,
deepening ties with Canada (perhaps averting Quebec’s isolation), the Caribbean, Africa, and Europe,
and making the U.S. a more active member of international bodies like La Francophonie.
Religious dynamics would also shift:
a large French population would swell the ranks of American Catholicism and possibly secularism,
challenging the historical dominance of Protestant denominations
and reframing debates on church-state separation, education, and morality.
Even the psychology of American exceptionalism might evolve.
With a strong internal voice that remembers an alternative colonial experiment—one that produced a different revolution and a different notion of liberty—
the American historical narrative would become more pluralistic.
The foundational myth of the Pilgrims and the frontier would share space with the legacies of Champlain, Lafayette, and the Code Noir.
This richer, more complicated past could foster a more self-critical and globally aware national identity,
less tempted to view its path as uniquely ordained.
In essence, a French community of such magnitude would not merely add a new accent to the American chorus;
it would fundamentally re-key the composition,
infusing the United States with a deeper duality between Anglo-Saxon pragmatism and French humanist idealism,
and blurring the lines between what the world considers “American” and “Francophone.”

human_answers: I wouldn't say that Philip is foolish, simply naive, since it is impossible for him to imagine that Ferdinand II and Catherine are plotting against him, to shape Joanna and especially the little Charles into a figure totally different from his own ( so that he may become the perfect archetype of a Christian Monarch ), but in any case I am certain that Queen Isabella would never do anything wrong in compromising her nephew's chances of inheriting his father's possessions ( Burgundy and Austria ) or preventing him from aspiring to the imperial throne, after all doing this risks it compromise to the international prestige of his family ( the Trastamaras ) let's say that the Catholic Monarchs only want to make sure that the future King of Castile and Aragon is not too accommodating to French wishes, it is realistic to think that Charles was initially educated at his mother's court, and then, when he was sure he could face a sea voyage, he was transferred to his grandfather Maximilian

Oh, please… the POD is interesting but the development is full of things that are blatantly false. OTL Isabella and Ferdinand were the ones that wanted Catalina’s remarriage to the future Henry VIII, and insisted that her marriage with Arthur was not consummated. Henry VII OTL was bullied in accepting the engagement of his second son to Catalina as he believed she was too old for his son. He would have zero troubles in giving back the half of her dowry he had already received (for all that getting back her dowry meant that Catherine had no right to any English money or lands) and send Catherine back at home as he had no use for her. Catalina’s aunt, the Dowager Queen of Naples would first try to marry her own daughter to the new Ferdinand III of Naples, as Giovanna was still in her mid-20s (or she would expect to see another match arranged for her daughter before agreeing to support Catalina as future Queen of Naples. Sea journeys at the time were extremely dangerous (I don’t remember if Catalina got lucky, but both Joanna and Margaret got close to die in their respective wedding journeys) reason for which Philip used his friendship with the French King for securing a land passage into France for going to receive the investitures. Eleanor and Charles at the time were too little for making safely the long journey, for not talking about baby Isabella, and Philip would never agree to bring them in Castile in any case. And if she had been so inclined Catalina, being the youngest of her sisters, could very well be allowed to take the veil. In 1502 Juana had three children and Maria one and both were likely to have soon more…

The year 1502 starts very rough for Catalina of Aragon. She and her husband, Arthur , Prince of Wales had both fallen ill at the end of March and when she recovered, she discovered that her husband had died. She could not believe it. She was a widow after only five months of marriage. She knew that she was not pregnant, as her marriage was unconsummated. One month after she was made a widow, Catalina was moved to Durham House in London and was visited by King Henry VII and his wife, Queen Elizabeth of York. Catalina told them that she had bled already and there was no hope for an heir from their late son, so his younger brother, Prince Henry, Duke of York, was officially declared as the heir. When the news to Catalina's parents, King Fernando II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile, they were disappointed that the alliance seemed to have fallen through and that their daughter was widowed at only sixteen years old. This began a struggle over Catalina. Queen Isabella was adamant that her youngest child be returned to her, since there was not a hope of an English grandchild to seal the alliance with Spain and England. King Henry VII, however, did not want to lose her or her dowry. He offered to marry her to his younger son and she could still be Queen of England one day. Queen Isabella made up her mind and told her husband that she wanted their daughter to be returned home. King Ferdinand sent an ambassador to tell King Henry that the Princess would be returned to Spain, either with her entourage or by force. When King Henry VII heard this, he was furious, but also terrified. He needed this alliance with Spain and he did not want to let his daughter-in-law go. Finally, an agreement was finally reached. The Infanta would return to her parents and half her dowry would be returned with her and she would retain her status of Dowager Princess of Wales and would still receive her marriage jointure for the remainder of her life. Her English attendants, like Margaret Pole, would remain in England. When she was told Princess Catalina had a mix of grief and relief. She was happy to return home to her parents, especially since her older sister, Juana, who was now Princess of Asturias, was back home as well. On August 1, 1502, Princess Catalina and her entourage arrived at Dover, preparing to board the ship that will cross the sea once again. Prince Henry, the young Prince of Wales accompanied her, just like he escorted her down the aisle to marry his late older brother. The eleven year old, who was talkative and social, was unusually quiet through the journey. Princess Catalina gave him a little kiss on his forehead and told him that she will never forget him or her time in England and she knew that one day, he will be the greatest King that England ever had, before she boarded the ship. Thankfully, this journey was much easier than her original one taking her to England. She and her entourage arrived in Laredo on the 15th of August. Princess Catalina found herself smiling, as she saw the familiar Castilian villages and knew she was home. However, she then was wondering what would happen to her and her future. Due to the deaths of her older brother, sister and nephew, she knew that taking holy vows was not an option, as he parents only had three surviving daughters. Would she just remain a spinster? Would she be married off again to a foreign Kingdom, even France? Her father was definitely ambitious and was a shrewd ruler, so she knew that she would not remain unmarried for long, but she was still looking forward to just feeling her mother's embrace once more.
items.original_question: Independent Naples: What if Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505? Hey all! This question has been on my mind a little too. What if instead of the long seven years in England in virtual poverty, Catherine of Aragon returns to her parents in the summer of 1502 and they arrange a marriage for the young King of Naples, which is still an independent Kingdom in this timeline? In this timeline, Henry VIII will instead marry Eleanor of Austria instead.

items.model_answer:
If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505, Naples would almost certainly have emerged as a fully independent kingdom ruled by a restored Trastámara line, permanently reshaping Italian and Mediterranean power dynamics.

The match was highly plausible in its own terms. After Queen Isabella’s death in 1504, Ferdinand II of Aragon needed to shore up his contested hold over Naples, which he had seized from France only a year earlier. Ferdinand of Calabria, the son of the last independent Neapolitan king, was his prisoner in Spain and a focal point for local discontent. Marrying his widowed daughter Catherine—stranded in England after Prince Arthur’s death and with her betrothal to the future Henry VIII mired in dowry disputes—to the legitimate heir would have been a masterstroke. By uniting the rival Trastámara claims, Ferdinand could present the new regime as a restoration rather than a conquest, while binding his daughter’s fate directly to Spanish dynastic interests.

The key difference from actual history is that this marriage would not have been intended as a viceroyalty. The couple would have been installed as sovereign rulers of an independent Naples, and Ferdinand of Aragon would have relinquished direct control in exchange for a permanent alliance, the return of his daughter to a throne, and the marginalization of French pretensions. In our world, Ferdinand of Calabria was kept in honorable captivity for decades and later married Germaine de Foix only after Ferdinand II’s death, receiving the viceroyalty of Valencia—a provincial consolation. But in this counterfactual scenario, Naples becomes a separate Trastámara kingdom from the moment of union.

The immediate consequences for Italy are dramatic. An independent but Spanish-allied Naples alters the balance of power: it removes the centerpiece of Spanish direct rule in Italy a century early, likely preventing the long, costly Spanish involvement in Italian wars that drained the treasury. The kingdom, now with a resident monarch and not a distant viceroy, would develop its own court, bureaucracy, and foreign policy. The local nobility, which repeatedly revolted against Spanish administrators, would instead be co-opted into a functioning Neapolitan government. Over time, Naples might have evolved into a significant regional power, acting as a buffer between Habsburg and Valois ambitions.

For the broader “what if” of Catherine’s life, she escapes the humiliating limbo in England and the eventual tragedy of her marriage to Henry VIII. As Queen of Naples, she would have wielded real influence, perhaps even becoming regent or co-ruler in the model of her mother Isabella. Her well-documented piety and education would have shaped the Neapolitan court, and her children would have inherited a stable crown—eliminating one of the deepest sources of instability that in our timeline led to the War of the Spanish Succession.

The English dimension is equally momentous. Without Catherine as his queen, Henry VIII likely marries a French princess or a domestic noblewoman far earlier, producing an heir with less marital strain. The entire chain of events that triggered the English Reformation—the search for a male heir, the annulment, the break with Rome—is averted or at least deeply delayed. Mary I is never born; the Tudor succession follows a wholly different path. In a single stroke, the marriage unburdens England of its most infamous marital tangle and gives Naples a royal house capable of surviving the storms of early modern Europe.

Thus, the marriage of Catherine and Ferdinand of Calabria in 1505 would have created a durable, independent Kingdom of Naples, prevented the long Spanish hegemony in southern Italy, and fundamentally altered the religious and political trajectory of England. It is one of those rare counterfactuals where a single changed match produces three centuries of divergent history.

edus.text: If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505,
Naples would almost certainly have emerged as a fully independent kingdom ruled by a restored Trastámara line,
permanently reshaping Italian and Mediterranean power dynamics.
The match was highly plausible in its own terms.
After Queen Isabella’s death in 1504,
Ferdinand II of Aragon needed to shore up his contested hold over Naples,
which he had seized from France only a year earlier.
Ferdinand of Calabria, the son of the last independent Neapolitan king, was his prisoner in Spain
and a focal point for local discontent.
Marrying his widowed daughter Catherine
stranded in England after Prince Arthur’s death
and with her betrothal to the future Henry VIII mired in dowry disputes
to the legitimate heir would have been a masterstroke.
By uniting the rival Trastámara claims,
Ferdinand could present the new regime as a restoration rather than a conquest,
while binding his daughter’s fate directly to Spanish dynastic interests.
The key difference from actual history is that this marriage would not have been intended as a viceroyalty.
The couple would have been installed as sovereign rulers of an independent Naples,
and Ferdinand of Aragon would have relinquished direct control
in exchange for a permanent alliance, the return of his daughter to a throne, and the marginalization of French pretensions.
In our world, Ferdinand of Calabria was kept in honorable captivity for decades
and later married Germaine de Foix only after Ferdinand II’s death,
receiving the viceroyalty of Valencia
a provincial consolation.
But in this counterfactual scenario, Naples becomes a separate Trastámara kingdom from the moment of union.
The immediate consequences for Italy are dramatic.
An independent but Spanish-allied Naples alters the balance of power:
it removes the centerpiece of Spanish direct rule in Italy a century early,
likely preventing the long, costly Spanish involvement in Italian wars
that drained the treasury.
The kingdom, now with a resident monarch and not a distant viceroy, would develop its own court, bureaucracy, and foreign policy.
The local nobility, which repeatedly revolted against Spanish administrators, would instead be co-opted into a functioning Neapolitan government.
Over time, Naples might have evolved into a significant regional power,
acting as a buffer between Habsburg and Valois ambitions.
For the broader “what if” of Catherine’s life,
she escapes the humiliating limbo in England
and the eventual tragedy of her marriage to Henry VIII.
As Queen of Naples, she would have wielded real influence,
perhaps even becoming regent or co-ruler
in the model of her mother Isabella.
Her well-documented piety and education would have shaped the Neapolitan court,
and her children would have inherited a stable crown
eliminating one of the deepest sources of instability
that in our timeline led to the War of the Spanish Succession.
The English dimension is equally momentous.
Without Catherine as his queen,
Henry VIII likely marries a French princess or a domestic noblewoman far earlier,
producing an heir with less marital strain.
The entire chain of events that triggered the English Reformation
the search for a male heir, the annulment, the break with Rome
is averted or at least deeply delayed.
Mary I is never born;
the Tudor succession follows a wholly different path.
In a single stroke, the marriage unburdens England of its most infamous marital tangle
and gives Naples a royal house capable of surviving the storms of early modern Europe.
Thus, the marriage of Catherine and Ferdinand of Calabria in 1505 would have created a durable, independent Kingdom of Naples,
prevented the long Spanish hegemony in southern Italy,
and fundamentally altered the religious and political trajectory of England.
It is one of those rare counterfactuals
where a single changed match produces three centuries of divergent history.

criterion_evaluations.reason: The answer shows some baseline knowledge, but it is overconfident and contains significant factual/control problems that weaken the scenario. It repeatedly states speculative outcomes as near certainties ('almost certainly,' 'would have created a durable, independent Kingdom of Naples') rather than separating fixed facts from plausible branches. More importantly, it makes notable factual errors or misleading claims: Naples was conquered by Ferdinand of Aragon in 1504, not 'only a year earlier' after Isabella's death in the way implied; Ferdinand of Calabria later became Duke of Calabria and Viceroy of Valencia, not holder of a mere 'provincial consolation'; and saying Spanish rule in Naples caused repeated revolts against 'Spanish administrators' is too broad for the early period and is used to support a deterministic claim about easy local acceptance. It also leaps from the marriage to Ferdinand of Aragon willingly creating a fully sovereign Naples, which is precisely the point needing the strongest justification, given his demonstrated preference for retaining control. Downstream claims about preventing Spanish hegemony in Italy, averting the English Reformation, and eliminating causes of the War of the Spanish Succession are presented with far too little uncertainty and mechanism. Overall this fits 3-4: some correct facts, but significant errors and major overstatement about Naples, dynastic politics, and later succession consequences.

items.question: What If Curb Global Warming after 1980
human_answers: India has only recently emerged as one of the world’s chief polluters; some two decades ago, Russia and Japan had a bigger mark, and in 1980 Canada was the bigger polluter. Depending on how decarbonized the economies of the First World are by 2000, India’s subsequent economic growth could be magnitudes cleaner than it was OTL. China you have a better point about, though first, their massive economic rise in the three decades after Mao’s death or so is pretty contingent, and second, they still only caught up to the already carbon stagnant EU in 2002. Imagine if the US was still comparable, as they were OTL until the mid 1980’s; now imagine, as China is getting ready to join the WTO in the late 90’s and early 2000’s, the west is also pushing a world climate treaty that (among other things) pushed these three major blocs (the US, Europe, and China) to curb their emissions going into the future. Even if India still sees their emissions rise, wouldn’t the fact that by far the largest producers are simultaneously cutting emissions lead to net reduction?

Well, is the point of your question, can we limit temperature rise by today , or in perpetuity? If the former, then greater adoption of nuclear energy in the West is probably a good enough answer; by the time Chinese and Indian energy use spikes, the resultant temperature spike won't come until after today. Maybe. But that seems like the wrong question, I interpret it as how to prevent such a spike from EVER occurring, rather than just occurring 10 years late. And for that, there's a big challenge. How do developing countries get off the ground? Hydrocarbons are great for that. If the big emitters of the 60s all switched to nuclear, that's fantastic--but China and India can't afford to START with nuclear, nobody can, which means a huge amount of hydrocarbons being burned when they start heavily industrializing. As a solution, perhaps their rise as industrial powers can be delayed a few decades? If they started industrializing in 2025 instead, they might use shale gas or solar, which are now the cheapest sources of power. But the production of those isn't domestic to China, which is a huge part of their use of coal--they don't have to import it. Tentatively, maybe the Soviet Union needs to have greater economic development and a softer landing when it falls? If they can be an industrial exporter while powered off domestic nuclear and natural gas, and remain so in the 1990s, then Chinese growth will be very different, and overall emissions will be lower. Cars and planes are obvious problems. I would also posit beef as a problem--methane is significantly more powerful than carbon in greenhouse effect, and is estimated as responsible for 20 to 30 percent of human-origin warming. Sixty percent of methane emissions are estimated as human-caused, with a big one being agriculture, and beef is responsible for a LOT of agriculture. So a poorer world, that eats less meat, would have lower methane emissions. So too would a world with fewer wetlands, so perhaps a little more paving of swamps would be good from the perspective of this question. Just thoughts. I'll be back for more, probably.

No, because they're already too anti-nuclear. The R&D and thus cost curves on silicon-based solar cell production, and on improved battery capacity, are both pushed pretty hard historically by electronics industry spinoffs. It's hard to see any sort of policy pushes for renewables accelerating those more than marginally, and dramatic acceleration is what you need to make them cost-viable decades ahead of schedule. On the other hand, nuclear was deliberately hobbled by US policy in the 1970s. People like to blame 1979's Three Mile Island, but (for a couple examples) the AEC to NRC switchover was passed by Congress and signed by Ford in 1974, while Carter's anti-reprocessing moratorium was in 1977. If you instead have the US adopt its own version of France's Messmer Plan in 1974 (which is tricky, because Messmer was able to simply ignore anti-nuclear sentiments due to government and economy structure in ways the US government couldn't), you get nuclear power economies of scale driven by the joint US-French demand that make it a more-attractive alternative throughout the rest of the industrialized world. Imagine Thatcher's government nuclearizing Britain in part to undercut the coal unions, for example. Then, if US electricity is something like 75% nuclear in 1990 (like France in 1990, instead of the historical 20%), with the UK fast-following? Now you have the necessary condition (it not hobbling the US) for international trade treaties and the like based on carbon emissions, after a decade of greenhouse effect publicity (since the 1979 NAS report), with the first IPCC report coming out. (Yes, sure, butterflies will scramble the details, but "coal is bad" science, if anything, will be better-funded if the US is transitioning from coal.) If Japan has (as is likely) lagged the US/France/UK in adoption of nuclear, this will be a particularly easy sell, since everybody in the West in 1990 is looking for an excuse to be protectionist against "Japan, Inc." And with that set up, you have the trick for going forward. If China (etc.) has to avoid coal power to export to Western markets, China either will figure out how to avoid coal, or it won't develop because it won't have markets to sell into.

I can give you two, PODs, One being no 3 Mile Island and the other being no John Sununu. So the real easy way to cut down on CO2 emissions is to cut down on coal use, and both PODs give easy ways to do just that. After the banning of CFCs in the late 80s, momentum existed for much harder caps on carbon than were discussed later. In particular, serious curtailment of coal as an energy source in the developed world was mooted. However, this momentum was handicapped with a lack of US Presidential support, with Bush Sr being advised against supporting these efforts by his Chief of Staff, John Sununu. Remove Sununu, and US support for carbon caps become more likely earlier. In addition with no 3MI incident, nuclear technology in the west could become less taboo, giving a viable alternative to coal fired power earlier. I could see a scenario where industry, much like CFCs, sees the financial opportunities in replacing coal with a nuclear/gas mix, and does not get in the way of any cuts to carbon emissions. A good book on the subject in your timeframe is Loosing Earth, by Nathanial Rich, which goes into detail about the drive to curtail emissions in the late 80s. would highly recommend giving it a read.
items.original_question:
AHC: Curb Global Warming after 1980

So you know how Global Surface Temperatures have increased 1.3°C over pre-industrial levels at present, and how a big part of the current Climate Movement is trying to limit further change as much as possible, 1.5°C being the best known* goal? Well, as recently as circa 1980, GST above PIL was only about 0.3°C, and had been hovering just below those levels for decades since the aftermath of WWII; in other words, a full degrees celsius of global warming only happened in the past 45 years alone. This is actually pretty astonishing when you realize how much of a turning point circa 1980 was to global carbon emissions -- both the biggest producers world-wide at the time, the US and Europe, initially saw their emissions peak, with Europe remaining controlled even as the US reversed course after a few years; Japan and Canada have a similar "false peaks" around the same time as the US; the USSR, of course, collapse circa 1990 and saw their emissions collapse thereafter, never to recover; and China was about to undergo a massive economic expansion that would see them become the world's largest emitters. So what I want to determine here is -- what is the latest PoD for avoiding this massive escalation of climate change, or of making it as small as possible? Could a PoD in the late 1970's (eg a continuation of Carter's energy policies in the US) have done the trick? If avoiding a full degrees celsius of warming wasn't seriously avertable by, say, 1975, how early do we need to go? 1960? The aftermath of WWII? In the event we can come to a consensus on the latest possible PoD and what would do the trick, we might also discuss how those changes to said countries' energy polices and to the global economy as a whole would have changed things overall. Thanks. *I'm really trying to avoid getting sidetracked in this discussion for the thread, so for anyone wanting to weigh in on whether its still feasible or how big of a deal missing that goal is, please take that to one of the Chat discussions -- much thanks!

rubrics.question_focus: What If Curb Global Warming after 1980

criteria.name: 1980 Baseline and Emissions Chronology Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately anchors the counterfactual in the post-1980 emissions landscape, including which countries/blocs mattered when, and avoids anachronistic assumptions about China, India, the USSR/Russia, Japan, Canada, the EU, and the US.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the 1980 baseline or treats present-day emitters as if they had the same role in 1980; little connection to historical emissions timing.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes some major emitters but gives a shallow or partially anachronistic chronology of who drove emissions after 1980.
criteria.5-6: Mostly accurate on broad emissions timing, distinguishing early Western dominance from later Chinese and Indian growth, with minor omissions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly tracks major emitter shifts across the 1980s, 1990s, 2000s, and later, using this chronology to shape the counterfactual.
criteria.9-10: Precisely integrates historical emissions sequencing, industrialization timing, and bloc-level comparisons to evaluate whether post-1980 warming could plausibly be curbed.

criteria.name: Decarbonization Mechanism Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the specificity and plausibility of proposed mechanisms for curbing warming after 1980, especially nuclear expansion, coal displacement, renewables cost curves, efficiency, carbon treaties, and fossil-fuel lock-in.
criteria.1-2: Offers vague claims such as 'use clean energy' without explaining feasible mechanisms or constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions plausible technologies or policies but ignores cost, deployment speed, political resistance, or energy-system inertia.
criteria.5-6: Provides one or two workable mechanisms, such as Western nuclear buildout or coal limits, with some attention to feasibility.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple mechanisms and constraints, including nuclear politics, renewable timing, grid deployment, coal dependence, and international policy leverage.
criteria.9-10: Builds a highly plausible decarbonization pathway with detailed technological, economic, political, and institutional mechanisms appropriate to the 1980 onward timeline.

criteria.name: Developing-World Industrialization and Trade Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles the central downstream issue: how China, India, and other developing economies industrialize if the West curbs emissions, and whether trade, technology transfer, delayed growth, or carbon standards change their trajectories.
criteria.1-2: Ignores China, India, and developing-country growth or assumes they simply copy Western decarbonization without constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions China or India but gives little explanation of energy affordability, domestic coal, export markets, or development incentives.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that developing-country industrialization is a major challenge and links it to coal, trade, or technology access.
criteria.7-8: Analyzes how Western decarbonization, carbon tariffs, WTO-era trade, Soviet/Russian alternatives, or technology transfer could alter Chinese and Indian emissions.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced account of developing-world growth paths, including affordability, domestic resources, export dependence, geopolitical contingencies, and whether global emissions fall despite later industrialization.

criteria.name: Climate Outcome Reasoning and Greenhouse-Gas Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how well the answer connects emissions changes to climate outcomes, including cumulative CO2, timing of warming, methane, land use, transport, agriculture, and the distinction between delaying warming and preventing it in the long run.
criteria.1-2: Conflates annual emissions with temperature outcomes or ignores cumulative emissions and climate lag.
criteria.3-4: Makes broad claims about reduced warming but gives little explanation of cumulative carbon, timing, or non-CO2 gases.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes that lower emissions reduce warming and includes some discussion of climate lag or non-CO2 sources.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes short-term delay from long-term prevention and covers major sectors such as electricity, transport, industry, agriculture, and methane.
criteria.9-10: Rigorously links sectoral emissions pathways to cumulative forcing and temperature outcomes, explicitly assessing whether warming is merely postponed or durably limited.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence, Uncertainty, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses the overall counterfactual chain from post-1980 interventions to late-20th and 21st-century outcomes, including internal consistency, handling of contingencies, and calibrated confidence.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims, deterministic assertions, or contradictions that break the counterfactual chain.
criteria.3-4: Has a recognizable scenario but weak causal links, unsupported leaps, or unacknowledged conflicts between assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly coherent chain with some uncertainty acknowledged, though parts remain underdeveloped or loosely connected.
criteria.7-8: Develops a consistent multi-decade causal pathway, flags key contingencies, and avoids major contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Provides a tightly reasoned long-range scenario with explicit causal dependencies, alternative branches, uncertainty calibration, and careful distinction between necessary and sufficient conditions.

items.model_answer:
If the world had taken decisive, coordinated action to curb global warming starting in 1980, the planet would be in a far less precarious climate state today. Global average temperatures would likely have risen by only about half of the observed 1.2°C above pre-industrial levels, avoiding much of the intensification of extreme weather that has already occurred. Arctic sea ice would be more stable, summer ice loss far less severe, and permafrost thaw would have been significantly slower, preserving more frozen carbon stores. Sea level rise would still be underway due to emissions already committed, but the rate would be noticeably lower, buying precious time for coastal communities to adapt. Coral reefs, though not unscathed, would show less frequent and severe bleaching, and ecosystems worldwide would be under less immediate stress from rapid climate shifts.

Economically, an early transition would have been disruptive but ultimately cheaper than the cost of inaction. The fossil fuel industry would have declined gradually rather than facing abrupt asset stranding, and clean energy technologies—solar, wind, nuclear, and storage—would have matured sooner, driving down costs through decades of sustained investment and learning. Energy independence would be more advanced, and geopolitical conflicts over oil and gas would be less acute. Air quality improvements from phasing out coal and oil would have saved millions of lives prematurely lost to pollution, reducing healthcare burdens and boosting productivity.

Socially, the generational burden would be lighter. Today’s youth would not face the same level of climate anxiety, and vulnerable nations—many in the Global South—would have experienced fewer climate-driven disasters, preserving livelihoods and reducing migration pressure. The political polarization around climate science and policy, while not eliminated, would be less entrenched, as early action would have built broad, bipartisan consensus before the issue became a culture war flashpoint. Instead of scrambling to meet distant net-zero targets against a ticking clock, the world would be in a managed, steadily decarbonizing state, with a fighting chance to stabilize the climate near 1.5°C and avoid the most catastrophic tipping points. The transformation would stand as one of the great cooperative achievements of the 20th century, a pivot from a collision course with nature to a sustainable path, proving that foresight and collective will can reshape the future.

edus.text: If the world had taken decisive, coordinated action to curb global warming starting in 1980,
the planet would be in a far less precarious climate state today.
Global average temperatures would likely have risen by only about half of the observed 1.2°C above pre-industrial levels,
avoiding much of the intensification of extreme weather that has already occurred.
Arctic sea ice would be more stable,
summer ice loss far less severe,
and permafrost thaw would have been significantly slower,
preserving more frozen carbon stores.
Sea level rise would still be underway due to emissions already committed,
but the rate would be noticeably lower,
buying precious time for coastal communities to adapt.
Coral reefs, though not unscathed, would show less frequent and severe bleaching,
and ecosystems worldwide would be under less immediate stress from rapid climate shifts.
Economically, an early transition would have been disruptive but ultimately cheaper than the cost of inaction.
The fossil fuel industry would have declined gradually rather than facing abrupt asset stranding,
and clean energy technologies—solar, wind, nuclear, and storage—would have matured sooner,
driving down costs through decades of sustained investment and learning.
Energy independence would be more advanced,
and geopolitical conflicts over oil and gas would be less acute.
Air quality improvements from phasing out coal and oil would have saved millions of lives prematurely lost to pollution,
reducing healthcare burdens and boosting productivity.
Socially, the generational burden would be lighter.
Today’s youth would not face the same level of climate anxiety,
and vulnerable nations—many in the Global South—would have experienced fewer climate-driven disasters,
preserving livelihoods and reducing migration pressure.
The political polarization around climate science and policy, while not eliminated, would be less entrenched,
as early action would have built broad, bipartisan consensus
before the issue became a culture war flashpoint.
Instead of scrambling to meet distant net-zero targets against a ticking clock,
the world would be in a managed, steadily decarbonizing state,
with a fighting chance to stabilize the climate near 1.5°C
and avoid the most catastrophic tipping points.
The transformation would stand as one of the great cooperative achievements of the 20th century,
a pivot from a collision course with nature to a sustainable path,
proving that foresight and collective will can reshape the future.

items.original_question: What if No Seven Bishops' Death in 1558? Everyone knows about the death of Cardinal Pole, Archbishop of Canterbury shortly after Queen Mary in 1558. But less known- as in, not even listed when you google them- is that there were six other bishops who died around the same time (including Maurice Griffith, Bishop of Rochester). This led to the opening of several vacancies in the English Catholic Church at the start of Elizabeth I's reign. To the seven bishops who died, can be added Bishop Oglethorpe of Carlisle (who, while he crowned Elizabeth, was no fan of hers after she stormed out of his celebration of Christmas Mass in 1558 because he defied her) and Nicolas Heath, the archbishop of York, who, as the highest ranked cleric in England should've crowned Elizabeth, but declined the "honour". He lost his see in 1559. What would've happened to the Elizabethan Settlement if those seven (or nine) sees had not fallen vacant at exactly the same time (many remaining vacant until 1561). How much opposition would there be to Elizabeth TTL? And how would Elizabeth have dealt with the situation TTL? @BlueFlowwer @isabella @RedKing @HortenseMancini

items.model_answer:
There is no historical event in 1558 involving the death of seven bishops. You may be thinking of two separate moments in English history. One possibility is the Marian Persecutions (1553–1558), during which several Protestant bishops were burned at the stake—most famously Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer, Nicholas Ridley, John Hooper, and Robert Ferrar. Mary I’s death in November 1558 ended the burnings. The other is the trial of the Seven Bishops in 1688, a landmark event that led to the Glorious Revolution, but those bishops were acquitted and did not die.

Assuming you mean **“What if the key bishops executed under Mary I had not died?”**, the counterfactual alters the English Reformation profoundly. If Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley, and others survived into Elizabeth I’s reign, the Elizabethan Religious Settlement (1559) might have faced a stronger, more unified Protestant leadership with direct links to earlier reform. Cranmer’s martyrdom had made him a powerful symbol; his survival could have sharpened theological disputes rather than allowing Elizabeth to steer a moderate via media. The memory of the martyrs also fueled John Foxe’s _Acts and Monuments_, which cemented anti-Catholicism in English identity. Without their deaths, popular Protestant mythology would be weaker, possibly softening the long-term antagonism between England and Catholic Europe.

If instead you mean **“What if the Seven Bishops had been executed in 1688 instead of acquitted?”**, the consequences would be even more dramatic. James II’s attempt to re-Catholicize England would have backfired sooner and more violently. The execution of seven respected Anglican prelates would have triggered widespread outrage, likely sparking an earlier, bloodier revolution. The invitation to William of Orange might have been replaced by open rebellion, possibly resulting in a more radical political settlement—perhaps a republic or a stricter constitutional monarchy. The public memory of such a judicial murder would have poisoned Catholic-Protestant relations for generations and made later toleration far more difficult.

In either case, the survival or death of such prominent churchmen was not a minor detail: it shaped the myths, politics, and religious direction of the nation for centuries.

edus.text: There is no historical event in 1558 involving the death of seven bishops.
You may be thinking of two separate moments in English history.
One possibility is the Marian Persecutions (1553–1558),
during which several Protestant bishops were burned at the stake
most famously Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer, Nicholas Ridley, John Hooper, and Robert Ferrar.
Mary I’s death in November 1558 ended the burnings.
The other is the trial of the Seven Bishops in 1688,
a landmark event that led to the Glorious Revolution,
but those bishops were acquitted
and did not die.
Assuming you mean “What if the key bishops executed under Mary I had not died?”,
the counterfactual alters the English Reformation profoundly.
If Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley, and others survived into Elizabeth I’s reign,
the Elizabethan Religious Settlement (1559) might have faced a stronger, more unified Protestant leadership
with direct links to earlier reform.
Cranmer’s martyrdom had made him a powerful symbol;
his survival could have sharpened theological disputes
rather than allowing Elizabeth to steer a moderate via media.
The memory of the martyrs also fueled John Foxe’s Acts and Monuments,
which cemented anti-Catholicism in English identity.
Without their deaths,
popular Protestant mythology would be weaker,
possibly softening the long-term antagonism between England and Catholic Europe.
If instead you mean “What if the Seven Bishops had been executed in 1688 instead of acquitted?”,
the consequences would be even more dramatic.
James II’s attempt to re-Catholicize England would have backfired sooner and more violently.
The execution of seven respected Anglican prelates would have triggered widespread outrage,
likely sparking an earlier, bloodier revolution.
The invitation to William of Orange might have been replaced by open rebellion,
possibly resulting in a more radical political settlement
perhaps a republic or a stricter constitutional monarchy.
The public memory of such a judicial murder would have poisoned Catholic-Protestant relations for generations
and made later toleration far more difficult.
In either case,
the survival or death of such prominent churchmen was not a minor detail:
it shaped the myths, politics, and religious direction of the nation for centuries.
