items.question: What If the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed?
human_answers: Define failed - do you just mean the fighter planes are sitting armed in their revetments, the AA guns (both fleet and land based) are manned, the ships are at condition ZED, the radar stations are manned, and the Air Information Center has been set up (probably not fully manned but at least some minimal level of staffing). This gets you raid warning, fighters get into the air in time to meet the raid, and the ships in port and ready to take the punch. That is not done due any specific intelligence about an attack it is simply done as a response to the war warnings of late November. Between fighter defenses and AA fire and planes not making it back to the carriers the Japanese lose somewhere between 1/3 and 1/2 of their attacking aircraft. Damage to the Pacific Fleet is a lot less because the ships are buttoned up and a lot less planes are destroyed on the ground because they are either in the air or in protected revetments or at least dispersed. Losses to fighter pilots are higher because of more guys getting shot down but they also take their measure of the Japanese. That constitutes failure for the Japanese, particularly given the losses in trained air crews. What it means going forward I'm not sure but it sure is an ugly start. Or, do you mean by failure the US does all of the above but also has knowledge a Japanese carrier task force is going to attack Oahu during the morning of 7 December from a position between 200-250 miles north of Oahu. This means every available attack aircraft on Oahu is bombed up and ready to go (6 B-17s, 21 B-18s, 5 A-20s, 23 SBDs, 8 SB2Us) and Kimmel is able to position Enterprise and Lexington 150 miles to the southwest of where the KB is expected to be operating as well as sending the small number of submarines he has in port to the north as well. By the way, Kimmel also has a moment of profound insight and realizes the safest place for his fat slow battleships is sitting in port at Condition ZED. That scenario has the US forces on island ready to take the punch and the US has about 180 attack aircraft of various types ready to throw at the KB to include roughly the equivalent of seven squadrons of US Navy and US Marine Corps dive bombers the most effective weapon in the US arsenal. Scenario One is quite realistic and only needs some fairly minor PODs to make it work. Scenario Two is a lot less realistic but if you squint hard enough you can probably come up with some PODs that still make it work. Scenario One the attacking aircraft get butchered but the KB likely gets away clean. Scenario Two the attacking aircraft get butchered and Nagumo loses at least two carrier maybe as many as four depending on the breaks.

I do not disagree with the analysis above, but I would take a different path in logical application from the same starting point. Define failure. What if the Japanese failed to attack Pearl Harbor at all. What if on the morning of 7 December the seas were unexpectedly, and unseasonably rough enough to preclude any launch of aircraft. The invasion of Malaya started four hour earlier, and it is too late to cancel attacks on US possession in the western Pacific. Conditions are not much better on the eighth. Kido Butai trundles back home to Japan, undetected by US aircraft.. This may seem like a "what if Japan declared war, and did not attack Pearl Harbor" scenario but it is not. The key difference is, what if Japan launched surprise attacks all over Asia without declaring war, and its most powerful naval assets were non-combat effective for the first 25 days of the war? Comments?

I'm not too familiar either with how much intelligence the US had on Japan pre-Pearl Harbor, but I do know that a Japanese submarine was sunk by the US just hours before Pearl Harbor, and the message either was ignored or received too late to mobilize the dock. I could totally see an early warning, through this incident, cause Pearl Harbor to mobilize and allow for Japanese pilots to lose the element of surprise. Assuming the Japanese ships aren't found and only the planes are destroyed, this would make Japan more cautious against the US, since the Pacific Fleet wouldn't be as weak as it was after Pearl Harbor in our timeline. Additionally, because of the warning, there might be less civilian causalities and so, in the United States, there is anger at being attacked, there wouldn't be the rallying cry of "OMG THEY MURDERED A BUNCH ON INNOCENT AMERICANS!" But, overall, Pearl Harbor not being totally destroyed is definitely an interesting and plausible scenario that would have an impact on WWII.
items.original_question: What if the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed? This was something that popped into my head. What if the USA has gained early warning of Pearl Harbor and had managed to defeat the attack? I am not too familiar with the intelligence background of it but I do believe I heard that there were some potential early signs before the attack that were ignored. If say the USA had received information a few days in advance and was able to crush the japanise attack and keep many of their best ships in a strong position in Hawaii now much would it change the pacific campaign? Would America be able to defeat Japan early maybe before the Nazis even fall?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise definition and plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines what 'the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed' means and grounds that point of divergence in plausible December 1941 conditions.
criteria.1-2: Leaves 'failed' undefined or assumes an incoherent premise, such as Japan never being at war while still discussing Pearl Harbor effects.
criteria.3-4: Gives a vague failure premise, e.g. 'the U.S. was ready,' with little explanation of warning, weather, intelligence, or defensive readiness.
criteria.5-6: Defines a recognizable failure scenario, such as effective U.S. warning or poor Japanese launch conditions, but with limited support for plausibility.
criteria.7-8: Specifies a plausible point of divergence, such as radar response, submarine warning, war-warning readiness, or bad seas, and explains why it could occur.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes multiple plausible meanings of failure, such as failed surprise versus carrier losses versus aborted strike, and evaluates their different implications.

criteria.name: Military-mechanism fidelity in the immediate battle
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately reasons through the operational consequences at Oahu and for Kido Butai, including aircraft, ships, radar, AA readiness, and carrier vulnerability.
criteria.1-2: Makes major military errors, such as treating battleships as able to chase Japanese carriers immediately or ignoring carrier aviation entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions reduced damage or more Japanese losses but gives little operational mechanism for how this happens.
criteria.5-6: Covers some key mechanisms, such as U.S. fighters getting airborne, AA guns manned, ships buttoned up, or aircraft dispersed.
criteria.7-8: Explains several interacting mechanisms, including warning time, U.S. air response, Japanese aircrew losses, harbor damage reduction, and likely Japanese withdrawal.
criteria.9-10: Provides a detailed and balanced operational analysis, including distinctions between losing attacking aircraft and losing Japanese carriers, realistic U.S. strike capacity, and uncertainty in outcomes.

criteria.name: Pacific War downstream consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer coherently traces how a failed Pearl Harbor attack affects Japan's early-war operations, U.S. naval power, and the broader Pacific campaign.
criteria.1-2: Jumps to sweeping conclusions, such as instant Japanese defeat or no U.S. entry, without causal support.
criteria.3-4: Identifies one downstream effect, such as a stronger U.S. Pacific Fleet, but does not connect it to later campaigns.
criteria.5-6: Discusses plausible medium-term effects, such as less battleship damage, preserved aircraft, Japanese caution, or altered timing in the Pacific.
criteria.7-8: Connects immediate survival of U.S. assets and Japanese aircrew losses to early-war operations in the Philippines, Dutch East Indies, Coral Sea, Midway, or carrier strategy.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent long-range chain across 1941-1943, accounting for Japan's simultaneous offensives, logistics, carrier attrition, U.S. mobilization, and possible changes to major battles.

criteria.name: Political and strategic effects on U.S., Japan, and Allies
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles the diplomatic, public-opinion, alliance, and grand-strategic consequences of a failed or blunted Pearl Harbor attack.
criteria.1-2: Ignores political effects or claims the U.S. would not enter the war despite Japanese attacks on U.S. or Allied possessions.
criteria.3-4: Mentions U.S. anger or morale but treats public reaction as the only strategic consequence.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that the U.S. likely still enters the war if Japan attacks U.S./Allied territories, though public shock and propaganda may differ.
criteria.7-8: Explains how a failed Pearl Harbor affects U.S. mobilization, Roosevelt's political position, Japanese strategic confidence, and Allied coordination.
criteria.9-10: Nuances political consequences by separating scenarios: aborted attack, failed surprise, heavy Japanese losses, or carrier defeat, and explains how each changes U.S. resolve and Japanese decision-making.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains internal consistency, avoids overclaiming, and signals uncertainty where the counterfactual branches depend on contested assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Contains contradictions, impossible sequences, or deterministic claims unsupported by the premise.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible points but mixes incompatible scenarios or overstates outcomes without caveats.
criteria.5-6: Generally coherent and acknowledges at least one uncertainty, but leaves some causal leaps or scenario ambiguity unresolved.
criteria.7-8: Separates assumptions clearly, uses conditional language, and avoids conflating a failed air raid with destruction of the Japanese carrier force.
criteria.9-10: Consistently tracks branches, probabilities, and dependencies, explicitly noting where outcomes hinge on warning time, U.S. strike effectiveness, Japanese carrier losses, or wider Japanese operations.

items.model_answer:
If the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor had been a complete failure—with U.S. defenses fully alert, Japanese aircraft shot down in droves, and no significant damage to ships or facilities—it would have fundamentally reshaped the Pacific War without necessarily preventing America’s entry into World War II. The key shift would be strategic, not diplomatic.

Even a failed surprise attack would still have been an act of war on U.S. territory, making a declaration of war by Congress virtually certain. President Roosevelt’s “date which will live in infamy” speech would have carried a tone of righteous defiance rather than shock and mourning, but the outcome of the vote would have been little changed. The attack’s failure might, however, have complicated Japan’s immediate operational plans. The Pearl Harbor strike was intended to cripple the U.S. Pacific Fleet so Japan could seize resource-rich Southeast Asia unopposed. With the fleet intact and battle-ready, the U.S. could have contested Japan’s expansion from day one. A swift U.S. response—perhaps an early carrier strike against the Japanese invasion forces bound for Malaya or the Philippines—would have disrupted Japan’s timetable. The Japanese carriers that historically rampaged across the Pacific would have been severely depleted or sunk in the failed attack, blunting the main instrument of Japan’s naval power.

In this scenario, the Pacific War likely would have been shorter. An undamaged U.S. Navy, its carriers still numerous and its battleship line ready, could have moved aggressively to relieve the Philippines and cut off Japan’s oil supply from the Dutch East Indies. The Doolittle Raid might have been replaced by a larger, more damaging strike as early as spring 1942. Japan’s perimeter would have contracted quickly, and the attrition that historically bled U.S. forces would have been far more lopsided in America’s favor. The “Germany first” grand strategy might still have held, but the Pacific theater would have demanded fewer resources, potentially accelerating the buildup for the invasion of North Africa and later France.

The failure might also have ripple effects on Allied morale and Axis calculations. Britain and the Soviet Union would see immediate proof of American resolve and capability, while Germany might delay its own declaration of war on the U.S.—though given Hitler’s undervaluing of American power, that delay would likely be short. A faster American victory in the Pacific could free up forces for the European theater earlier, possibly altering the postwar map by bringing the war to a close before the Soviet Union occupied as much of Eastern Europe.

In the end, a failed attack at Pearl Harbor would not have kept America out of the war, but it would have saved thousands of lives, preserved the Pacific Fleet’s pre-war strength, and dramatically compressed the timeline of Japan’s defeat, with far-reaching consequences for the entire conflict.

edus.text: If the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor had been a complete failure
with U.S. defenses fully alert, Japanese aircraft shot down in droves, and no significant damage to ships or facilities
it would have fundamentally reshaped the Pacific War
without necessarily preventing America’s entry into World War II
The key shift would be strategic, not diplomatic.
Even a failed surprise attack would still have been an act of war on U.S. territory
making a declaration of war by Congress virtually certain.
President Roosevelt’s “date which will live in infamy” speech would have carried a tone of righteous defiance rather than shock and mourning
but the outcome of the vote would have been little changed.
The attack’s failure might, however, have complicated Japan’s immediate operational plans.
The Pearl Harbor strike was intended to cripple the U.S. Pacific Fleet
so Japan could seize resource-rich Southeast Asia unopposed.
With the fleet intact and battle-ready
the U.S. could have contested Japan’s expansion from day one.
A swift U.S. response
perhaps an early carrier strike against the Japanese invasion forces bound for Malaya or the Philippines
would have disrupted Japan’s timetable.
The Japanese carriers that historically rampaged across the Pacific would have been severely depleted or sunk in the failed attack
blunting the main instrument of Japan’s naval power.
In this scenario, the Pacific War likely would have been shorter.
An undamaged U.S. Navy, its carriers still numerous and its battleship line ready
could have moved aggressively to relieve the Philippines and cut off Japan’s oil supply from the Dutch East Indies.
The Doolittle Raid might have been replaced by a larger, more damaging strike as early as spring 1942.
Japan’s perimeter would have contracted quickly
and the attrition that historically bled U.S. forces would have been far more lopsided in America’s favor.
The “Germany first” grand strategy might still have held
but the Pacific theater would have demanded fewer resources
potentially accelerating the buildup for the invasion of North Africa and later France.
The failure might also have ripple effects on Allied morale and Axis calculations.
Britain and the Soviet Union would see immediate proof of American resolve and capability
while Germany might delay its own declaration of war on the U.S.
though given Hitler’s undervaluing of American power, that delay would likely be short.
A faster American victory in the Pacific could free up forces for the European theater earlier
possibly altering the postwar map
by bringing the war to a close before the Soviet Union occupied as much of Eastern Europe.
In the end, a failed attack at Pearl Harbor would not have kept America out of the war
but it would have saved thousands of lives, preserved the Pacific Fleet’s pre-war strength, and dramatically compressed the timeline of Japan’s defeat
with far-reaching consequences for the entire conflict.

items.question: The Highest Patriotism: What If George McGovern became President in 1968
human_answers: The one thing that keeps coming to me is Nixon would have the greatest meltdown in political history, screaming bloody murder then the Eastern Establishment has screw him for a third and final time. Even in OTL 68 a lot of the GOP had in fact become very weary over backing Nixon over his defeats in 1960, and 1962 in California. Now this last minute scandal, Nixon messing with the peace talks, cost him and the Republicans the election for a third time. At the very best, Tricky Dick might become a Secretary of State under a future Republican president and a Statesman, but the White House is forever gone. GOP swings back to the Rockefeller Republicans like George Romney and Nelson Rockefeller himself, but could also swing to Reagan. McGovern quickly makes a peace deal for Vietnam and pulls out. The South eventually falls. But we wash our hands of that conflict. items.original_question: The Highest Patriotism: What if George McGovern became President in 1968 ​ The initial frontrunner for the Democratic nomination in 1968 was President Johnson of course, but an insurgent primary challenge from one Senator Eugene McCarthy set off a spark that would blow open a wide power vacuum in the Democratic party following Johnson's withdrawal from consideration. Johnson had endorsed Hubert Humphrey, his ambitious VP, but he chose not to run in the primaries, instead gaining support through backroom deals with delegates to win at the convention. This led to a bitter primary fight between McCarthy and Robert F. Kennedy, who had jumped into the race shortly before Johnson's withdrawal. As the primaries carried on, this fight would all come to a head with the hotly-contested California primary. Both campaigns put valiant efforts and loads of funding into this contest, but in the end, McCarthy would narrowly prevail, winning 45% to Kennedy's 42% and taking all of California's delegates. Kennedy would immediately announce his withdrawal from the nomination after the loss, but refused to make an endorsement. When it came to the convention, however, most of Kennedy's delegates coalesced around McCarthy, leading to a deadlocked convention between him and Humphrey. Kennedy had only privately backed McCarthy, even though he hated the man. With the convention at an impasse, Kennedy looked for an alternate who could emerge as a compromise candidate, despite his own ego making him hurt that no matter what, it wasn't going to be him. That man was none other than Senator from South Dakota George Stanley McGovern. McGovern was a Kennedy ally who had served as his brother's director for Food for Peace and an ambassador to the Peace Corps his brother founded. However, he was also firmly of the anti-war wing of the party and was more amenable to McCarthy and his delegates than Kennedy, whom McCarthy deeply despised. McCarthy vowed to stay in, but as more and more Kennedy-turned-McCarthy delegates flipped to McGovern, he saw the writing on the wall. After six more ballots, McCarthy would release his delegates, with all but a few holdouts voting for McGovern on the next ballot. However, the race was not over yet. There still was not an agreed upon consensus, and it would take more backroom dealing to put McGovern over the hump. To that, Kennedy looked to the Texas delegation, which was backing Humphrey, led by the old friend of his brother's, Governor John Connally. Kennedy aimed to make a deal with Connally to give his delegates over to McGovern in exchange for major concessions. Initially resistant, and more and more concessions being offered, Connally would finally accept the offer on one singular condition; he would be made VP. With the two coming to an agreement, Texas would announce the switch of its delegates to McGovern, putting him over the line to win the nomination after 10 ballots, and Connally was selected as McGovern's running mate. Republican nominee Richard Nixon had a strong lead in early polls, and it looked as if the McGovern/Connally ticket was heading for a demolishment. Some polls even had McGovern losing Texas despite Connally's presence on the ticket. But slowly McGovern chipped at Nixon. Nixon was seen as a crooked insider and someone who would do anything to win, while McGovern appeared to be more honest in his approach. However, the race still remained in Nixon's favor weeks before the election, despite McGovern's best efforts. Then, a bombshell emerged. Johnson, who had only tacitly supported McGovern, if only for his buddy Connally becoming VP if they won, had leaked to the press that Nixon attempted to sabotage the peace talks occurring in Vietnam. McGovern didn't wish to make the campaign dirty, but he still called the reports "troubling" and placed serious question into his opponent's integrity while not outright placing guilt, which helped his honest image even further, and painted an even greater contrast between the two men . In the end, it was close, but... McGovern/Connally (Democratic) - 279 electoral votes, 42.62% Nixon/Agnew (Republican) - 182 electoral votes, 41.04% Wallace/LeMay (American Independent) - 77 electoral votes, 16.01% ​ ...the last second scandal proved to be just enough for McGovern to win this election by the slimmest of margins. If he had lost any of the states of California, Illinois, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Texas, or Wisconsin, with Texas being decided by just 1.04% for him and only winning 39.74% of the vote there, this election would have been thrown to the House of Representatives, and all of them, decided by only a few points each, had flipped, than Nixon would have won an outright majority himself. George McGovern was never meant to win this election, but through a deadlocked convention, backroom deals, and scandals, it was the honest prairie man that triumphed over them all.

items.model_answer:
If George McGovern had become president in 1968, the United States would have taken a radically different path—one that likely accelerated the end of the Vietnam War, deepened social democratic reforms at home, and reshaped America’s global role, though not without fierce backlash. McGovern, a liberal senator from South Dakota and an outspoken anti-war critic, would have entered the White House on a mandate of moral clarity, reversing the trajectory of escalation and cynicism that defined the Nixon years.

The most immediate change would have been in Vietnam. McGovern would have sought a swift and complete withdrawal of U.S. troops, framing the war not as a noble cause but as a catastrophic mistake. He likely would have halted the bombing campaigns, refused to widen the war into Cambodia or Laos, and prioritized humanitarian aid and political asylum for South Vietnamese allies. The fall of Saigon would have come sooner—perhaps by 1970—and without the years of additional bloodshed, draft calls, and domestic trauma. While critics would decry him as “soft on communism,” McGovern’s stance might have spared tens of thousands of American and Vietnamese lives, and the ensuing national reckoning might have been less corrosive than the prolonged agony that actually occurred.

Domestically, a McGovern presidency would have embraced the social ferment of the late 1960s. The “highest patriotism,” in his view, meant expanding democracy and lifting up the marginalized. He would have pushed aggressively for a guaranteed minimum income, universal health insurance, and major investments in education and public housing. The Equal Rights Amendment would have received full-throated support, and civil rights enforcement would have been strengthened. However, such an ambitious progressive agenda would have collided with a Congress dominated by conservative Democrats and Republicans, leading to legislative gridlock. McGovern’s outsider, moralistic style might have struggled to build the bipartisan coalitions necessary to pass his sweeping reforms, leaving many promises unfulfilled and fueling disillusionment on the left.

The cultural and political backlash would have been intense. Without Nixon’s “silent majority” rhetoric to channel it, conservative anger might have erupted more chaotically—perhaps in third-party movements or intensified street-level conflict. McGovern’s very identity (a prairie preacher’s son turned dove) would have been caricatured as weak and un-American by a furious right wing. The 1972 election, instead of a Nixon landslide, might have seen a conservative revolt that could have ended McGovern’s presidency after one term, but not before the political center was permanently realigned.

On the world stage, a McGovern administration would have dramatically altered the Cold War dynamic. Détente would have been pursued less through Kissingerian realpolitik and more through a principled emphasis on human rights and arms reduction. Relations with the Soviet Union and China might have been cooler initially, but McGovern’s willingness to slash defense spending and forgo interventionism could have set a precedent for a humbler foreign policy. America’s image abroad, tarnished by war, might have been partially restored—though allies in Europe and Asia would have questioned U.S. reliability.

Ultimately, McGovern in 1968 would have been a prophet armed with power, attempting to translate moral clarity into governance. The result would have been a nation more honest about its limits, more generous in its domestic ambitions, but perhaps no less divided. His greatest legacy might have been proving that the “highest patriotism” required not military might but the courage to admit failure, heal wounds, and pursue justice at home. Whether that vision could have held under the weight of reactionary forces is the tragic tension of this counterfactual—a presidency that would have asked Americans to rethink what it means to love their country.

edus.text: If George McGovern had become president in 1968,
the United States would have taken a radically different path
one that likely accelerated the end of the Vietnam War,
deepened social democratic reforms at home,
and reshaped America’s global role,
though not without fierce backlash.
McGovern, a liberal senator from South Dakota and an outspoken anti-war critic,
would have entered the White House on a mandate of moral clarity,
reversing the trajectory of escalation and cynicism that defined the Nixon years.
The most immediate change would have been in Vietnam.
McGovern would have sought a swift and complete withdrawal of U.S. troops,
framing the war not as a noble cause but as a catastrophic mistake.
He likely would have halted the bombing campaigns,
refused to widen the war into Cambodia or Laos,
and prioritized humanitarian aid and political asylum for South Vietnamese allies.
The fall of Saigon would have come sooner—perhaps by 1970—
and without the years of additional bloodshed, draft calls, and domestic trauma.
While critics would decry him as “soft on communism,”
McGovern’s stance might have spared tens of thousands of American and Vietnamese lives,
and the ensuing national reckoning might have been less corrosive than the prolonged agony that actually occurred.
Domestically, a McGovern presidency would have embraced the social ferment of the late 1960s.
The “highest patriotism,” in his view,
meant expanding democracy and lifting up the marginalized.
He would have pushed aggressively for a guaranteed minimum income, universal health insurance, and major investments in education and public housing.
The Equal Rights Amendment would have received full-throated support,
and civil rights enforcement would have been strengthened.
However, such an ambitious progressive agenda would have collided with a Congress dominated by conservative Democrats and Republicans,
leading to legislative gridlock.
McGovern’s outsider, moralistic style might have struggled to build the bipartisan coalitions necessary to pass his sweeping reforms,
leaving many promises unfulfilled and fueling disillusionment on the left.
The cultural and political backlash would have been intense.
Without Nixon’s “silent majority” rhetoric to channel it,
conservative anger might have erupted more chaotically—
perhaps in third-party movements or intensified street-level conflict.
McGovern’s very identity (a prairie preacher’s son turned dove)
would have been caricatured as weak and un-American by a furious right wing.
The 1972 election, instead of a Nixon landslide,
might have seen a conservative revolt
that could have ended McGovern’s presidency after one term,
but not before the political center was permanently realigned.
On the world stage, a McGovern administration would have dramatically altered the Cold War dynamic.
Détente would have been pursued less through Kissingerian realpolitik
and more through a principled emphasis on human rights and arms reduction.
Relations with the Soviet Union and China might have been cooler initially,
but McGovern’s willingness to slash defense spending and forgo interventionism could have set a precedent for a humbler foreign policy.
America’s image abroad, tarnished by war, might have been partially restored—
though allies in Europe and Asia would have questioned U.S. reliability.
Ultimately, McGovern in 1968 would have been a prophet armed with power,
attempting to translate moral clarity into governance.
The result would have been a nation more honest about its limits,
more generous in its domestic ambitions,
but perhaps no less divided.
His greatest legacy might have been proving
that the “highest patriotism” required not military might
but the courage to admit failure, heal wounds, and pursue justice at home.
Whether that vision could have held under the weight of reactionary forces
is the tragic tension of this counterfactual—
a presidency that would have asked Americans to rethink what it means to love their country.

items.question: What If A drastically better Russian history in the 20th century (2026 ed)
human_answers: The problem is that everything becomes possible with enough wankium, hence the implied 'it would be best achieved by starting very early on, as per the other thread'; otherwise it's not a Challenge, an exploration of history and factors, rather an exercise in taking OTL and changing it all to successful/lucky/positive events while applying a large butterfly net. No assassination of AII; so he gets scared and Stolypin's reforms are implemented earlier and more decisively; but then, Japan still lucks out in War and so people are angry; WWI however you like, except with less Russian losses; Revolution happens later so Russia wins or at least doesn't lose as much, so the Mensheviks come into power and start building a social democracy in Russia; a couple decades of luck preventing any bad luck until the Nazis go West, while Russia prepares herself for being attacked; so when they come they are pushed back faster and with less losses, leading to a well-integrated post-WWII Russia that can enjoy a few decades of growth, has larger borders, and as a result reaches 300M by 2000 as you asked. But somehow, I don't think that's really what you are after, are you?

I do think early PoDs (which naturally make our world unrecognisable and certainly butterfly the birth of Lenin) are more plausible if you want Russia thoroughly similar to Scandinavia. But the 20th century is a good time for catching up, for radical jumps, for deep transformations, as OTL has also shown, only not in the way the OP desires. Steering a course between Bolshevik tyranny of OTL and its most likely counterpart, continuation of a relatively autocratic tsardom, is not impossible. Neither are the population numbers. A solid multi-party democracy, well, if it works in India, why not in Russia. But you could call what is required for it a good run of sixes, or a healthy dose of wankium. I've dabbled in that in Feeble Constitution , so I'll not dwell on the path of February 1917 consolidating with different policies after the April Days. Instead, I can see both earlier and later PoDs. For a good planning thread on a later PoD (basically SR victory in the Civil War), you could have a look at @galileo-034 's Century of the Common Man . Though this may not entirely fulfill your OP challenge - Lenin would not be an obscure footnote here, and instead die in 1918. So maybe let's go with the one big earlier opportunity - a successful revolution of 1905. @Powdermonkey started a TL on this last year. I'd be thrilled to see where this could go. One could argue that the path towards what the OP describes is still stony and uphill. How one would tackle the Great War problem is still up in the air, among other things. But still probably one path worth exploring more here since it hasn't been done often, I think.
items.original_question:
AHC: A drastically better Russian history in the 20th century (2026 ed)

The goal is simple - we want to have a 20th century in which Russia avoids the interlocked chain of events leading to a century of trumas as IOTL. In this world, Russia becomes a vibrant multi party democracy, heavily integrated with the rest of Europe and with its intellectual and cultural elites intact. It follows an economic model analogous to the Social Market Economy of post ww2 Germany or even the Nordic Model if things go very positively. Its population is over 300 mln people by 1991 (the year the USSR collapsed IOTL). In this world, Vladimir Lenin is still born (despite the butterfly effect) and still becomes a revolutionary but he dies as an obscure, disillusioned theoretician. His last work, Delusions of the Proletariat , is a scathing critique of the supposed naivety of the working class, lured into capitalism through voting rights and social safety nets. It sells less than 500 copies. When the internet era arrives (either sooner or later than IOTL), Lenin is included in various "10 Failed Radicals You Have Never Heard of" type of articles on various history-related websited but is otherwise a forgotten figure.

rubrics.question_focus: What If A drastically better Russian history in the 20th century (2026 ed)

criteria.name: Plausible point of divergence and counterfactual discipline
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer chooses a believable divergence capable of producing a drastically better 20th-century Russia without relying on arbitrary good luck, excessive 'wankium,' or implausible suppression of butterflies.
criteria.1-2: Uses vague wish-fulfillment or many unexplained positive changes with no credible point of divergence.
criteria.3-4: Names a divergence, but it is too late, too weak, or requires repeated lucky overrides to work.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible divergence such as altered 1905, Alexander II surviving, or different 1917 dynamics, but with limited justification.
criteria.7-8: Selects a strong divergence and explains why it could plausibly redirect Russian institutions and later crises.
criteria.9-10: Clearly frames the divergence, its limits, butterfly effects, and why it is one of the few credible routes to a much better Russian century.

criteria.name: Domestic political and institutional mechanism depth
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains Russia's transition away from autocracy, Bolshevik dictatorship, or failed liberalism toward a stable and comparatively humane political order.
criteria.1-2: Simply asserts Russia becomes democratic or prosperous without explaining institutions or social forces.
criteria.3-4: Mentions reforms or democracy but ignores resistance from the Tsar, elites, radicals, peasants, army, or national minorities.
criteria.5-6: Sketches a reformist path involving Duma power, 1905 success, Stolypin-style reforms, Menshevik/SR victory, or February consolidation.
criteria.7-8: Explains party politics, land reform, constitutional constraints, military loyalty, labor unrest, and minority management in a coherent sequence.
criteria.9-10: Shows a robust institutional pathway balancing monarchy/republic, socialism/liberalism, federalism, land hunger, and mass politics without assuming automatic Scandinavianization.

criteria.name: Handling of major wars and geopolitical shocks
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer coherently addresses the Russo-Japanese War, World War I, revolution/civil war risks, the rise of Nazi Germany, World War II, and Russia's postwar position.
criteria.1-2: Ignores major wars or assumes Russia effortlessly avoids or wins them.
criteria.3-4: Mentions wars but treats them as background events with little causal impact.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that Japan, WWI, revolution, and WWII are key stress tests, though outcomes are only partly explained.
criteria.7-8: Gives plausible military, diplomatic, and domestic consequences for each major conflict and avoids easy total victories.
criteria.9-10: Integrates wars as central causal bottlenecks, explaining how a better Russia survives them with realistic tradeoffs, losses, alliances, and postwar borders.

criteria.name: Long-range socioeconomic and demographic plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly connects reforms and avoided catastrophes to higher living standards, industrialization, public health, migration, fertility, and possible population targets such as roughly 300 million by 2000.
criteria.1-2: States Russia becomes rich or populous without mechanisms or numbers.
criteria.3-4: Provides optimistic outcomes but ignores famine, repression, war deaths, urbanization, or demographic transition.
criteria.5-6: Links reduced civil war, famine, terror, and WWII losses to better population and development, but only broadly.
criteria.7-8: Explains industrial growth, agrarian reform, education, health, infrastructure, and demographic effects over decades.
criteria.9-10: Quantitatively and causally grounds the improved outcome, showing which deaths are avoided, how growth compounds, and what limits remain.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, tradeoffs, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer acknowledges uncertainty, avoids internal contradictions, and distinguishes plausible causal chains from speculative or authorially forced outcomes.
criteria.1-2: Presents a deterministic fantasy timeline with contradictions or impossible coexistence of events.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of difficulty but still stacks convenient outcomes or contradicts known constraints.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges that the scenario requires luck and identifies some fragile links.
criteria.7-8: Clearly marks uncertain junctures, offers alternatives, and explains why the selected path is plausible but not guaranteed.
criteria.9-10: Maintains tight causal consistency across decades, openly flags low-probability assumptions, and avoids both excessive optimism and cynical inevitability.

items.model_answer:
If the February Revolution of 1917 had consolidated into a stable democratic republic, Russia’s 20th century would be unrecognisably brighter. The key turn is that the Provisional Government manages to take Russia out of the Great War by mid-1917 through a separate peace, accepting modest territorial concessions but retaining its industrial core and army intact. Without the war’s momentum fuelling Bolshevik radicalism, the Constituent Assembly meets in late 1917, freely elected, and produces a federal, parliamentary system with broad land reform and minority rights. Lenin remains a marginal exile; the Cheka, Red Terror, and one-party state never emerge.

Through the 1920s, democratic Russia leverages its vast resources and educated workforce to become the world’s principal grain exporter and a magnet for European investment. It industrialises organically, without collectivisation, so it avoids the Holodomor and the destruction of the peasantry’s knowledge. By the early 1930s, Russia’s per capita income is closing in on France’s. Its military, though substantially reduced, is professional and well-equipped. This Russia faces a revisionist Germany with confidence but no paranoia: when Hitler reoccupies the Rhineland, Russia joins France and Britain in a firm tripartite alliance. The Nazi-Soviet Pact never materialises, and in 1938 the threat of a two-front war deters the Munich sell-out. War, if it comes, is fought on German soil with Western Allies, preventing the Wehrmacht from ever reaching Moscow or Leningrad. The post-war order is agreed at a table where Russia is a co-equal democracy, not an exhausted totalitarian power that needs a cordon sanitaire.

Domestically, artistic and scientific life thrive without ideological controls. A Russian might win the Nobel Prize in economics or biology in the 1930s, while the space programme develops as a civilian endeavour, putting the first satellite into orbit in the late 1950s as part of an international consortium. The internet, once it arrives, is woven into a society that never knew samizdat or censorship. Prosperity, rule of law, and civic engagement make Russia a model of a successful multi-ethnic federation, acting as a keystone for a loosely integrated Eurasia. The Cold War’s nuclear arms race is stillborn, freeing trillions of dollars globally. By the century’s end, without the trauma of Stalinism, the humiliation of Crimea’s transfer, or the collapse of a dys-functional Soviet economy, Russia faces no 1990s “lost decade”. Instead, it follows a steady arc from constitutional monarchy to advanced social democracy, setting global standards for literature, science, and conflict mediation while hosting permanent peace congresses at its Baltic resorts.

nodes.text: If the February Revolution of 1917 had consolidated into a stable democratic republic,
Russia’s 20th century would be unrecognisably brighter.
The key turn is that the Provisional Government manages to take Russia out of the Great War by mid-1917 through a separate peace,
accepting modest territorial concessions
but retaining its industrial core and army intact.
Without the war’s momentum fuelling Bolshevik radicalism,
the Constituent Assembly meets in late 1917, freely elected,
and produces a federal, parliamentary system with broad land reform and minority rights.
Lenin remains a marginal exile;
the Cheka, Red Terror, and one-party state never emerge.
Through the 1920s, democratic Russia leverages its vast resources and educated workforce
to become the world’s principal grain exporter and a magnet for European investment.
It industrialises organically, without collectivisation,
so it avoids the Holodomor and the destruction of the peasantry’s knowledge.
By the early 1930s, Russia’s per capita income is closing in on France’s.
Its military, though substantially reduced, is professional and well-equipped.
This Russia faces a revisionist Germany with confidence but no paranoia:
when Hitler reoccupies the Rhineland,
Russia joins France and Britain in a firm tripartite alliance.
The Nazi-Soviet Pact never materialises,
and in 1938 the threat of a two-front war deters the Munich sell-out.
War, if it comes, is fought on German soil with Western Allies,
preventing the Wehrmacht from ever reaching Moscow or Leningrad.
The post-war order is agreed at a table
where Russia is a co-equal democracy,
not an exhausted totalitarian power that needs a cordon sanitaire.
Domestically, artistic and scientific life thrive without ideological controls.
A Russian might win the Nobel Prize in economics or biology in the 1930s,
while the space programme develops as a civilian endeavour,
putting the first satellite into orbit in the late 1950s as part of an international consortium.
The internet, once it arrives, is woven into a society
that never knew samizdat or censorship.
Prosperity, rule of law, and civic engagement make Russia a model of a successful multi-ethnic federation,
acting as a keystone for a loosely integrated Eurasia.
The Cold War’s nuclear arms race is stillborn,
freeing trillions of dollars globally.
By the century’s end, without the trauma of Stalinism, the humiliation of Crimea’s transfer, or the collapse of a dys-functional Soviet economy,
Russia faces no 1990s “lost decade”.
Instead, it follows a steady arc from constitutional monarchy to advanced social democracy,
setting global standards for literature, science, and conflict mediation
while hosting permanent peace congresses at its Baltic resorts.

criterion_evaluations.reason: The answer does choose a recognizable and potentially strong divergence—February 1917 stabilizing via a mid-1917 separate peace—and links it to major avoided disasters like Bolshevik seizure of power, civil war, and Stalinism. That is enough to clear the basic plausibility threshold. But the counterfactual discipline is weak. It does not explain how the Provisional Government overcomes the severe political and military constraints that made separate peace, regime stability, and army cohesion so difficult, nor does it address likely butterfly effects of territorial concessions, elite fragmentation, nationalist secessions, or German leverage. After the initial premise, the answer becomes a cascade of highly favorable outcomes with little constraint or uncertainty: near-French income by the early 1930s, deterrence of Munich, war on German soil, no Cold War, smooth advanced social democracy, etc. Those are mostly asserted rather than carefully derived. So this fits a plausible divergence with limited justification, not a strongly disciplined or expert-level counterfactual.

items.question: What If the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up?
human_answers: I agree with most of what you said but that’s not quite what happened to Hua - he was backed by Ye Jianying, an ‘elder’, and implemented reforms while publicly proclaiming his support of Mao Zedong Thought. It was Hua who saw the reintroduction of "material incentives". However Hua relied on collective leadership and as Ye's health decline Hua was outflanked by Deng, who took a much harsher stance of de-Maoification despite being economically similar to Hua. I’m going to go on a bit of a tangent to explain why I agree with the rest of what you said and think some equivalent to reform and opening was the most likely outcome - Deng spent the 80s balancing the other “elders” and younger officials. As @Georg von Frundsberg said, other elders were more 'conservative' but generally embraced reform - while younger officials like Hu and Zhao were aggressively reformist. Deng himself was a lot closer to the centre than is remembered - on agriculture for example Zhao Shukai had a good article about how Deng was slow to embrace reform and one of his signature reforms, "household production" (allowing households to dictate production instead of communes) was only adopted by central diktat in 1982 after years of discussion. However throughout the tumultuous 80s political instability remained, culminating in 1989, the removal of Zhao Ziyang and the introduction of martial. Deng was ont he defence for three years until 1992, at which point he returned to power by coordinating “reformist” officials through the southern tour. Deng enjoyed is last five years at his relative peak of influence and admiration since he had outlived everyone else. I mention this to show though that Reform and Opening up was somewhat inevitable. There was a large chunk of the elders that were open to reform and an even larger pool of younger officials. Someone sometime was going to remove the Gang of Four and the only real question left was how much reform and when. To return to OP’s question, the only real alternative to reform and opening up was a coup. People were tired of the stagnant economy and the damage done by the cultural revolution was significant - in certain periods it was closer to a civil war, as PLA and militia fought in the streets. If the government tried to stick with central planning it would be removed by the majority of officials, and if not by them then a popular uprising.

Without reform and opening up in 1978 I think the only alternative would be to chug along with five year plans and central planning. This was attempted immediately after Mao's death, but it failed because everyone believed that continuing that way was a dead end, so it's plausible but unlikely that the Communist Party goes down that path. There's reason to believe that the Cultural Revolution was launched in part as a reaction to the bureaucracy and corruption of the Stalinist party-state, as a way to try and find an alternative to it, which was eventually put to bed in 1968 when Mao sent in the PLA. Broadly, you can characterise the initial years of the Cultural Revolution as the 'left-wing' attempt to find an alternative to the Soviet model, and Reform and Opening up as the 'right-wing' attempt to find an alternative in the wake of the GPCR's failure. Maybe they could've made it work, compared to the post-war Soviet communist party, the Chinese communist party was far more afraid of stagnancy and was far more willing to put themselves behind ambitious economic programmes (this is probably the main the reason they carried out Reform and Opening up and the USSR didn't), and maybe that allows them to pull through and create a creating a working planned economy that marches proudly into the 21st century, avoiding concessions to market economics. Most people will probably dismiss this possibility. It is perhaps more likely that the whole thing ossifies and stagnates at some point, prompting the party to do something like reform and opening up at a later date. If the party has reached Soviet levels of complacency and don't do anything, the system will begin to rot, the black market will explode and you'll get something like North Korea. I don't think Chinese citizens would be as poor as North Koreans are though, considering the collapse of North Korea's living standards was largely caused by the disappearance of Soviet economic aid, something China stopped receiving long before then, but I'm not wholly sure on that one. EDIT: I can't believe I forgot to mention this, but people associated with China's New Left movement often look favourably upon Belarus' Market Socialism as an alternative to what happened in China, with all the social chaos it caused. I am not entirely familiar with how Market Socialism works in Belarus, but in a journal article by Chinese economists praising the Belarusian model they take a liking to the dominance of state-owned companies, central planning, strong leadership and stronger social security and welfare than what exists in China and the rest of the ex-USSR. I don't really know much about how things actually work in practice in Belarus and if it's at all feasible China could copy this economic model, but it gives some pointers.

He was weak. At the time, the Chinese Communist Party was filled with veteran figures who had followed Mao since its early days. In such a situation, Hua Guofeng was merely a novice. As the elders pushed for reform, the young Hua Guofeng could not hold his ground. The Gang of Four, who had driven the Cultural Revolution, were not elders either; they relied on Mao’s personal trust. Hua Guofeng found himself caught between the Gang of Four and the veteran elders. While suppressing the Gang of Four, he also had to confront the elders who were advocating reform. Faced with such an overwhelming burden, Hua Guofeng was simply too young and lacked the political influence to manage it. Unlike the Soviet Communist Party, the Chinese Communist Party had a much stronger tendency to pursue “a today different from yesterday” rather than “a today the same as yesterday.” Even if the result turned out to be disastrous, they were still more inclined to act proactively and at least try to do something. Is this what you mean? If that is true, then it seems that for the PRC, it was ultimately a matter of timing—it would have carried out reform and opening up sooner or later. Then, in your view, is a scenario in which the PRC becomes like North Korea impossible? I mean a situation in which a particular vested elite seizes control of the bureaucracy and the military, crushes all resistance, and pushes for isolation in order to preserve its own power even at the cost of weakening the state’s capabilities. Certainly, the politics of the PRC and North Korea were different. In the PRC, even after Mao had secured absolute power, figures like Deng Xiaoping at least managed to survive by keeping a low profile. As a result, change became possible after Mao’s death. By contrast, in North Korea, Kim Il Sung had already eliminated all alternative forces by the 1960s, and from the 1970s onward he was able to prepare to pass power on to his son.
items.original_question: What if the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up? Unlike in OTL, assume that a POD occurred in the succession struggle after Mao Zedong’s death. Or, if you prefer, assume that the Cultural Revolution itself unfolded differently. In any case, because of this change, Deng Xiaoping either never came to power or was removed partway through. Reform and Opening Up did not take place in the 1980s. Post in thread 'What if succession had occurred in China after Mao's death?' Feb 5, 2025 And I could see Lin being not really into the idea of Mao Anying succeeding Mao lead to a more serious involvement by Lin Biao in Project 571 or an equivalent plot, as opposed to IOTL where his son was the main driving force behind it. Whiteshore (For example, something like this.) What do you think would have happened if the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up? Would the PRC have eventually collapsed under economic crisis, or would it have endured like North Korea? Would the CCP have fallen because its claim to rule lost credibility? Or, like the Kim family and the North Korean ruling elite, could it have remained in power as a poor and isolated dictatorship by maintaining control over the military and political system while eliminating opposition?

rubrics.question_focus: What If the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise discipline and historical anchoring
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the premise that the PRC never undertakes Reform and Opening Up, while accurately grounding the divergence in late-1970s CCP politics after Mao, including Hua Guofeng, Deng Xiaoping, party elders, the Gang of Four, and the legacy of the Cultural Revolution.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or treats Reform and Opening Up as still occurring normally; contains major historical errors about post-Mao leadership.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges the premise but relies on vague or inaccurate history; key actors such as Hua, Deng, elders, or the Gang of Four are missing or misrepresented.
criteria.5-6: Provides a basically accurate post-Mao setup and identifies a plausible point of divergence, but with limited detail or some inconsistencies.
criteria.7-8: Accurately situates the counterfactual in CCP succession politics and explains why avoiding reform would require specific political changes or blockages.
criteria.9-10: Maintains strict premise discipline and uses precise historical anchoring to show what institutional, factional, and ideological conditions would have had to differ for reform never to occur.

criteria.name: Causal mechanism coverage inside the CCP
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains the political mechanisms that could prevent, delay, or replace reform, including elite bargaining, elder authority, bureaucratic incentives, military support, ideological legitimacy, and possible coups or purges.
criteria.1-2: Offers only broad claims such as 'China would be poor' without explaining how the CCP avoids reform.
criteria.3-4: Mentions leadership conflict or ideology but gives little causal detail about how anti-reform forces prevail or why reformist forces fail.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some relevant mechanisms, such as conservative dominance, Hua retaining power, Deng losing influence, or stronger Maoist control, but underdevelops their interaction.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple interacting mechanisms, including elite coalitions, PLA or elder support, bureaucratic resistance, and legitimacy pressures.
criteria.9-10: Provides a robust causal account of how a non-reform path is sustained over decades despite strong pro-reform pressures within the CCP and society.

criteria.name: Economic and social trajectory plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer develops plausible long-run economic and social outcomes for a China without Reform and Opening Up, including central planning, agricultural organization, industrial productivity, living standards, black markets, urban-rural dynamics, and comparisons to the USSR, North Korea, Belarus, or other socialist models where appropriate.
criteria.1-2: Makes implausible or unsupported economic claims, such as instant superpower status or total collapse without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Gives a simplistic outcome, such as 'China becomes North Korea' or 'China stays poor,' with little attention to scale, resources, or institutional differences.
criteria.5-6: Discusses stagnation, planning, poverty, or black markets in a plausible way but omits important sectors such as agriculture, industry, or trade.
criteria.7-8: Traces credible economic and social effects across sectors and decades, distinguishing China from Soviet, North Korean, or Belarusian analogues.
criteria.9-10: Presents a nuanced economic-social trajectory with clear mechanisms linking non-reform policies to productivity, state capacity, welfare, inequality, unrest, and informal markets over the long run.

criteria.name: Long-range geopolitical and institutional consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer coherently follows downstream effects beyond the 1980s, including China's global trade position, relations with the US and USSR/Russia, East Asian production networks, Hong Kong/Taiwan dynamics, military modernization, state capacity, and the survival or transformation of CCP rule.
criteria.1-2: Ignores long-term consequences or jumps directly to a final outcome without intervening reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few downstream effects but treats them as disconnected or inevitable.
criteria.5-6: Covers some long-range consequences, such as slower growth, weaker global influence, or possible instability, but with limited causal linkage.
criteria.7-8: Connects domestic non-reform choices to international trade, diplomacy, military capacity, and regime durability across several decades.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent multi-decade chain showing how no Reform and Opening Up reshapes China's domestic institutions, global economic integration, regional politics, and CCP survival prospects.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, plausible, and unlikely scenarios; avoids overconfident determinism; handles alternative paths such as delayed reform, neo-Maoist isolation, Soviet-style stagnation, market socialism, coup, or popular upheaval; and avoids internal contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Presents a single dogmatic outcome with major contradictions or no acknowledgement of uncertainty.
criteria.3-4: Allows for uncertainty only superficially and contains tension between claims, such as saying reform was impossible while also assuming reform-like outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes more than one possible path but does not clearly rank probabilities or resolve tensions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates likely from less likely scenarios and explains why some alternatives, such as North Korea-style isolation or delayed reform, are more or less plausible.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, compares competing scenarios, states assumptions, and preserves logical consistency throughout the counterfactual chain.

items.model_answer: If the People's Republic of China had never embarked on Reform and Opening Up, the country would likely have remained a poor, isolated, and economically stagnant nation, trapped in the inefficiencies of a centrally planned system. Living standards would have stayed at pre-1978 levels, with widespread poverty and scarcity, while technological and industrial progress would have fallen far behind the rest of the world. Internationally, China would have remained a peripheral player, cut off from global trade and investment, and its geopolitical influence would be minimal. The post-Mao leadership might have faced mounting internal pressures—economic discontent, ideological rigidity, and potential political instability—as the survival of the system would have been increasingly untenable without the legitimacy derived from tangible improvements in people's lives. In short, the absence of Reform and Opening Up would have deprived China of its historic transformation into a major global power and perpetuated a cycle of backwardness and isolation.

edus.text: If the People's Republic of China had never embarked on Reform and Opening Up,
the country would likely have remained a poor, isolated, and economically stagnant nation,
trapped in the inefficiencies of a centrally planned system.
Living standards would have stayed at pre-1978 levels,
with widespread poverty and scarcity,
while technological and industrial progress would have fallen far behind the rest of the world.
Internationally, China would have remained a peripheral player,
cut off from global trade and investment,
and its geopolitical influence would be minimal.
The post-Mao leadership might have faced mounting internal pressures—economic discontent, ideological rigidity, and potential political instability—
as the survival of the system would have been increasingly untenable
without the legitimacy derived from tangible improvements in people's lives.
In short, the absence of Reform and Opening Up would have deprived China of its historic transformation into a major global power
and perpetuated a cycle of backwardness and isolation.

items.question: What If the Vickers Wellington had been produced with a stressed-skin airframe instead of its geodetic fabric-covered structure?
human_answers: Picked this up from John Dell, whose site is quite often mentioned here, a long time ago. Geodetic structures only show advantages for big aircraft - e.g. a small geodetic fighter would be a non-starter. The advantages of Geodetic aircraft are better the bigger the aircraft - From this point of view it is a shame the Warwick + Windsor were so late. The main Geodetic structures (fuselage + wings) are built as whole units - So it is harder to break up the structure into subassemblies for distributed manufacture. Advantages of Geodetic over steel-tube, wooden formers and fabric covering are... Much greater strength, including ability to absorb greater battle damage, and more g force. No internal bracing - so unobstructed space within for passengers, fuel tanks + other equipment. The potential for cheaper construction if planned + implemented properly and a very large production run with no changes in the primary structure - It may take more people to construct a geodetic aircraft but many more of them will be low-skilled, lower-waged workers. Drag difference between the two types is probably not much. Advantages of Steel tube, wooden formers and fabric covering over Geodetic are... Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Much more cost-effective for short production runs. Advantages of Geodetic over all wood stressed structures (i.e. Mosquito) Potentially greater strength, including ability to absorb greater battle damage. Again, if produced in great numbers the potential for cheaper production (Wood-workers are some of the most skilled factory workers around and therefore have higher wages and take longer to train) - In actual fact during WWII this was not such a great problem, because so many wood-working companies (i.e. furniture makers) were closed there was a relative glut of wood workers available. Not susceptible to woodworm or termites - a real danger in tropical climates. Advantages of Wooden stressed structures over Geodetic The wooden aircraft should have a lower drag, because of its smooth finish. Wood was more readily available, whereas aviation alloys were in short supply. Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Easier to make a profit out of a short production run. Advantages of Geodetic over Fully-stressed skin metal aircraft Ability to absorb more battle damage + keep flying (but not necessarily protect the crew) Again, if produced in great numbers the potential for cheaper production - not actually realised by Vickers. Uses less metal, a particular advantage if aviation alloys are scarce. Advantages of fully stressed metal skin over geodetic Lower drag (smoother skin). More suitable for cabin pressurisation. Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Easier to make profit out of smaller production run (but still nowhere near that possible with wooden + steel tube structures). Maybe more crew protection. Possibilities for weight saving by integrating structures (eg a fuel tank or firewall could be an integral part of the main structure rather than being something added after the main structure is built - this becomes increasingly important).

Specification B.1/35 was effectively a replacement for the Hampden and Wellington which were designed to meet Specification B.9/32. What became the Halifax began as the HP.55 with 2 Hercules class engines to Spec B.1/35, then the HP.56 with 2 Vultures to Spec. P.13/36, then the HP.57, 59 & 63 with 4 Merlins and the HP.61 with 4 Hercules engines. Handley Page delivered its 500th and last Hampden in July 1940 and its first production Halifax in August 1940. English Electric built 770 Hampdens which were delivered from March 1940 to March 1942. English Electric's Hampden production overlapped with its Halifax production because the first one was delivered in October 1941. The Halifax was also built by Fairey, the London Aircraft Production Group and Rootes. The Warwick was designed to meet Spec. B.1/35 with 2 Hercules class engines too, which was changed to 2 Vulture class engines, but still to B.1/35 rather than the later B.12/36 or P.13/36. If its development had proceeded as smoothly as the Halifax it's likely that this would have happened. Weybridge would have switched from the Wellington to the Warwick in the summer of 1940. Chester may have swiched in August 1940 too, after delivering the 200 Wellingtons ordered 1937-38. The next batch of Wellingtons ordered IOTL (550 in May 1939) would have been the first batch of Warwicks. Blackpool didn't get its first Wellington contract until December 1939 and commenced deliveries in August 1940. Based on the above a contract for 500 Warwicks would have been let instead. 750 Wellingtons were ordered from the Castle Bromwich factory in December 1939 IOTL. It was cancelled before any were built, I don't know when and why, but it was probably so it could concentrate on building Spitfires. The factory also received orders for 650 Lancasters and Lincolns from September 1941 to June 1944 of which 300 were delivered from December 1943 to August 1945. Although the Warwick was only built at Weybridge (first delivery June 1942) it was also ordered from the Blackpool and Chester factories. So contradicting what I wrote in Message 8, if the stressed-skin Warwick is allowed to evolve in the same way that the Halifax did, we may see it built by the thousand at the Vickers factories at Blackpool, Chester and Weybridge instead of most of the OTL Wellingtons and all the OTL Warwicks. Depending upon how the TTL version compares to the Lancaster it might be built at Castle Bromwich too instead of the Lancasters it built IOTL.

items.model_answer:
If the Vickers Wellington had been built with a conventional stressed-skin metal airframe instead of Barnes Wallis’s geodetic lattice and fabric covering, it would have been a markedly different aircraft—gaining in some areas but losing the very quality that made it legendary.

**Production and development**  
The geodetic structure was labor-intensive, requiring skilled workers to assemble thousands of light alloy channel sections into a complex three-dimensional web. Switching to a stressed-skin design—where the metal skin itself bears much of the load—would have lent itself far better to mass production, especially using semi-skilled labor and American-style flow-line methods. This could have increased output beyond the 11,400 actually built, or at least eased the strain on factory capacity. However, if the change had come during the original design phase in the mid-1930s, it might have delayed the Wellington’s entry into service. The Air Ministry had already seen the promise of the geodetic Wellesley and was counting on a rapid follow-on; a conventional redesign might have meant fewer bombers in the early war years.

**Performance and survivability**  
In the air, a stressed-skin Wellington would almost certainly have been faster. A flush-riveted aluminum skin produces less drag than doped fabric over a geodesic framework, potentially adding 10–15 mph to its top speed—no small matter for a night bomber trying to evade flak and night fighters. It would also have eliminated the serious fire hazard of the fabric covering, which could be ignited by incendiary bullets. Maintenance would have been simpler, with no need to regularly re-dope or repair torn fabric, and the airframe would have coped better with jungle humidity or desert sun.

Yet the geodetic Wellington’s greatest strength was its ability to absorb battle damage that would have destroyed any stressed-skin design. Because loads were carried through a redundant lattice, the loss of multiple members—and even large sections of fabric—still left a viable airframe. A stressed-skin aircraft relies on the integrity of its skin panels; a large hole or a torn skin can spread stress and cause catastrophic failure. Swapping to stressed-skin would therefore have cost the Wellington its near-mythical ruggedness, and likely its reputation for bringing crews home in staggering states of disrepair.

**Operational impact**  
A heavier stressed structure might also have nibbled into the Wellington’s bomb load or range, especially in early marks with modest engine power. Conversely, the cleaner airframe could have offset some of that weight penalty. Tactically, fewer crew would have survived severe flak or fighter damage, but a slightly higher speed and less flammable covering might have reduced total losses. The net effect on loss rates is debatable, but the qualitative difference is clear: bomber crews valued the geodetic Wellington’s “get-you-home” resilience above almost anything else.

**Legacy and follow-on development**  
Geodetic construction was a technological dead end, never used on a major production aircraft after the war. Vickers itself abandoned it for later projects, and the Wellington’s successor, the Warwick, eventually adopted a stressed-skin design after initial geodetic versions faltered. Had the Wellington been conventional from the start, the RAF would have gained earlier experience with the type of airframe that would dominate bomber design, potentially smoothing the transition to more advanced aircraft. But it would have lost the unique machine that sustained Bomber Command through the first half of the war, and the boost to morale that came from flying a bomber that refused to fall apart.

In short, a stressed-skin Wellington would have been a more modern-looking bomber on paper—faster, less flammable, and easier to build—but at the cost of the exceptional structural toughness that made the real Wellington an outstanding combat survivor when it was needed most.

edus.text: If the Vickers Wellington had been built with a conventional stressed-skin metal airframe instead of Barnes Wallis’s geodetic lattice and fabric covering,
it would have been a markedly different aircraft—gaining in some areas but losing the very quality that made it legendary.
The geodetic structure was labor-intensive,
requiring skilled workers to assemble thousands of light alloy channel sections into a complex three-dimensional web.
Switching to a stressed-skin design—where the metal skin itself bears much of the load—
would have lent itself far better to mass production,
especially using semi-skilled labor and American-style flow-line methods.
This could have increased output beyond the 11,400 actually built,
or at least eased the strain on factory capacity.
However, if the change had come during the original design phase in the mid-1930s,
it might have delayed the Wellington’s entry into service.
The Air Ministry had already seen the promise of the geodetic Wellesley
and was counting on a rapid follow-on;
a conventional redesign might have meant fewer bombers in the early war years.
In the air, a stressed-skin Wellington would almost certainly have been faster.
A flush-riveted aluminum skin produces less drag than doped fabric over a geodesic framework,
potentially adding 10–15 mph to its top speed—
no small matter for a night bomber trying to evade flak and night fighters.
It would also have eliminated the serious fire hazard of the fabric covering,
which could be ignited by incendiary bullets.
Maintenance would have been simpler,
with no need to regularly re-dope or repair torn fabric,
and the airframe would have coped better with jungle humidity or desert sun.
Yet the geodetic Wellington’s greatest strength was its ability to absorb battle damage
that would have destroyed any stressed-skin design.
Because loads were carried through a redundant lattice,
the loss of multiple members—and even large sections of fabric—
still left a viable airframe.
A stressed-skin aircraft relies on the integrity of its skin panels;
a large hole or a torn skin can spread stress and cause catastrophic failure.
Swapping to stressed-skin would therefore have cost the Wellington its near-mythical ruggedness,
and likely its reputation for bringing crews home in staggering states of disrepair.
A heavier stressed structure might also have nibbled into the Wellington’s bomb load or range,
especially in early marks with modest engine power.
Conversely, the cleaner airframe could have offset some of that weight penalty.
Tactically, fewer crew would have survived severe flak or fighter damage,
but a slightly higher speed and less flammable covering might have reduced total losses.
The net effect on loss rates is debatable,
but the qualitative difference is clear:
bomber crews valued the geodetic Wellington’s “get-you-home” resilience above almost anything else.
Geodetic construction was a technological dead end,
never used on a major production aircraft after the war.
Vickers itself abandoned it for later projects,
and the Wellington’s successor, the Warwick, eventually adopted a stressed-skin design
after initial geodetic versions faltered.
Had the Wellington been conventional from the start,
the RAF would have gained earlier experience with the type of airframe that would dominate bomber design,
potentially smoothing the transition to more advanced aircraft.
But it would have lost the unique machine that sustained Bomber Command through the first half of the war,
and the boost to morale that came from flying a bomber that refused to fall apart.
In short, a stressed-skin Wellington would have been a more modern-looking bomber on paper—
faster, less flammable, and easier to build—
but at the cost of the exceptional structural toughness
that made the real Wellington an outstanding combat survivor
when it was needed most.
