items.question: What If a Modern Programmer with a Laptop Entered World War II?
human_answers:
The biggest advantage I see being given here is simply processing power. You have a machine that can run calculations at a speed that would beggar imagination for someone living in that era.

In relation to the Artillery mentioned in another answer. Generally, an artillerist would consult his range tables to determine how to aim his cannon...rather than running all the math on the fly. You could easily generate more granular artillery tables to pass out.

The number crunching part of code breaking would be massively accelerated. Especially if you built an Enigma machine on the computer, gave it access to a German Dictionary (can be installed with many programs), and just told it to brute force code attempts until it started spitting out actual words.

Hell, give the physicists access to the Microsoft Calculator in Scientific mode, and they are likely to name their first born after you. Then write programs to run common mathematical formulas, and the Manhattan project would happen a whole lot faster. Seriously? Something that can calculate the cubic root of a 20 digit number, accurate to a dozen decimal places? In a matter of milliseconds!? GIMME!

All in all, the best thing he could do (sadly, this isn't very exciting) is to go to all the scientists and ask them for any number crunching that they need to do repeatedly...or any complicated calculations they needed to make, and either write programs to do it for them, or just run the numbers in MS Calculator.

Alternately, install a localized version of Candy Crush, lock out all other features of the computer, and give it to the Furher. Then, when he's so addicted to the game that he isn't paying attention anymore...you win! (kidding, of course)

Note to time travelers: Beware of unintended consequences! Here's one rather significant problem that might occur:

Modern cryptography enables the Allies to crush the Germans much more quickly. Suddenly, they have a lot more resources to devote to taking down Japan.

The Japanese Empire crumbles beneath the onslaught. There is no need to use the atomic bomb on them to force them to surrender.

The Manhattan Project was still there, though, and was probably helped along quite a bit by this computing technology. (See other answers to this question.) Now we have atomic bombs, but have never used them on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

The USSR continues to rise. After a while, war breaks out in Korea. General McArthur wants to use the atomic bomb on the North Koreans and/or the Russians and/or the Chinese. (See: actual history.)

Because it never got used (very sparingly) to end a war, after which there was an interim period of a few decades during which we learned about the horrific after-effects of nuclear weapons, President Truman doesn't force him to resign over this, and The Bomb is now used (enthusiastically) at the start of the next war. Great horrors ensue.

At the risk of offending some, I think several of the answers on this thread are overestimating the skills of the average, fresh out of school, programmer. 

Being in the field, and having interviewed more recent graduates than I want to count in the past few years, I would estimate that somewhere over 80% of the people getting software degrees are doing so because they have heard there is high demand, and the money is good (both statements are true btw). The result is that many of them do not have the natural aptitude and personality traits that make one a good programmer. They got through school, and can be helpful in an established team with experienced people to coach them along, but they can't produce effectively if thrown out on their own with only vague directions from people that don't understand the code any better than they do.

If our time traveler is such a person, then the laptop is primarily going to be useful as a calculator. The programmer just doesn't have enough experience or understanding to do anything else effectively. At best the programmer will be able to implement the algorithms designed by the mathematicians of the era once they gain an understanding of the computer's strengths and weaknesses.

However, if the programmer falls into the group that does have some level of aptitude, then there are numerous possibilities. Stick them in a room with some theoretical scientist and they will be able to generate the algorithms that help to test their theories. Give them a dataset (and people to do the data entry for it), and they will be able to design a database and pattern analysis algorithms to predict future probabilities. Basic cypher algorithms are definitely possible without any deep knowledge of cryptography, but you need a computer on the other end to decrypt them if it is anything more complicated than you could already do by hand. Brute forcing existing cyphers and generating one time pads are probably among the most useful tasks they could do in the realm of cryptography. Creating drafting and 3D modeling tools would help speed the process developing useful prototypes. 

The catch is that the average laptop is still relatively limited in terms of space and processing power. While several orders of magnitude greater than what was available at the time, it will only be able to do a finite number of things before you have to start getting rid of the old stuff to make room for new items. As someone else noted, the only functioning interfaces are the built in ones that people interact with directly (screen, keyboard, speakers, etc.). There is no way to batch information in or out of it, no printers, & no storage media. If you delete something it is gone. The laptop also becomes a single point of failure. If too much relies on what it can do then what happens when it crashes? Eventually something in there is going to fail, and there is no way to recover it.

Others have discussed code-breaking or code-making, which would certainly be useful, but my first thought was more direct:

Artillery

One of the early projects in computing had a goal of pre-calculating shell trajectories to support targeting in the field. This is the ENIAC project. 
I expect a modern laptop could generate the firing tables needed by artillery operators in a fairly short period, giving our side a massive advantage in being able to target artillery quickly in the field.
Even if our protagonist knows nothing but basic programming, he should be able to go to the mathematicians working on these tables and coordinate to crunch all the numbers at a speed that would seem like magic to them.

Your every-man wouldn't have to do it all himself. I mean, if he had a interest in WW2 cryptography then he probably could do it all himself. Here's an enigma machine made with Javascript . Likewise, he could know German. But he doesn't need to do either of those things. 

I think that a modern laptop in WW2 would be the most useful if you got it to the people who ended up breaking enigma. If you showed up at Bletchley Park and said "I have a computer and the knowledge of how to program it, help me with the math" You'd speed up the cracking speed exponentially, which would probably have shortened WW2 by a lot, having that knowledge earlier than they did.

Other effects

Breaking enigma is great, but he could also help develop better ciphers for the allies that would have stumped the Germans. 

Having a little foreknowledge of WW2 events would have helped the allies too. To say "the Germans are going to go around the French Maginot Line though Belgium, attacking from the low countries and forests. Please warn them."

Without France surrendering Germany would have been weakened. 

You wouldn't have even needed to know that much history. Just saying "yeah, that plan to assassinate Hitler in his bunker that you're working on, it fails. try something else."

With some science and physics background, he probably could help give a boost to a lot of the science with better gun design. Jet turbine theory, etc.

Even without knowing exactly how to do something, just giving the raw ideas would do a lot. "I see you are doing it that way. Have you ever though about switching it around?"

A lot of our ideas seem obvious, but they weren't until they were.

rubrics.question_focus: What If a Modern Programmer with a Laptop Entered World War II?

criteria.name: Premise Grounding and Technological Constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer faithfully reasons from the exact counterfactual: a modern programmer with a single laptop entering World War II, including realistic limits on power, storage, durability, interfaces, software, knowledge, and reproducibility.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the premise or treats the laptop/programmer as magical, unlimited, or equivalent to modern infrastructure.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a laptop or programmer but overlooks key constraints such as power, maintenance, data entry, printing, networking, or hardware failure.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes some practical limits while still overstating what one person and one laptop could reliably accomplish.
criteria.7-8: Grounds most claims in realistic constraints, including limited interfaces, single-point failure, human data entry, and dependence on wartime institutions.
criteria.9-10: Consistently models the laptop as a powerful but fragile, isolated artifact and the programmer as a bounded actor embedded in WWII logistics, secrecy, and institutions.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage for Wartime Applications
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses depth and plausibility of concrete mechanisms by which the programmer and laptop could affect WWII, such as codebreaking, ballistics, logistics, scientific computation, cryptography, data analysis, drafting, or weapons research.
criteria.1-2: Provides vague claims of winning the war faster without explaining usable mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Lists possible applications but gives little explanation of how they would work or why they matter in WWII conditions.
criteria.5-6: Explains several relevant uses, such as faster calculations or codebreaking, but omits important implementation bottlenecks.
criteria.7-8: Covers multiple high-impact applications with plausible workflows, including collaboration with mathematicians, physicists, artillery staff, or intelligence teams.
criteria.9-10: Gives a rich, balanced account of major applications and bottlenecks, distinguishing feasible computation aids from infeasible modern-style software or communications systems.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether downstream consequences are traced coherently beyond immediate tactical benefits, including effects on the timing of Allied victory, the Manhattan Project, Japan, the USSR, Korea, nuclear norms, and postwar geopolitics where relevant.
criteria.1-2: Stops at immediate effects or jumps to unsupported outcomes such as instant Allied victory.
criteria.3-4: Includes downstream effects but relies on large causal leaps or ignores intervening military and political factors.
criteria.5-6: Presents a plausible medium-range chain, such as faster codebreaking or weapons research, but has limited treatment of second-order consequences.
criteria.7-8: Connects near-term computational advantages to broader military and geopolitical shifts with mostly clear intermediate steps.
criteria.9-10: Develops coherent long-range pathways, including unintended consequences and branching outcomes, while preserving historical constraints and institutional decision points.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Human Factors
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer appropriately calibrates uncertainty about the programmer's skill, knowledge, credibility, access, language, security clearance, and ability to influence WWII actors.
criteria.1-2: Assumes perfect competence, trust, access, and adoption with no uncertainty or resistance.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges uncertainty superficially but still treats cooperation and implementation as automatic.
criteria.5-6: Discusses some human factors, such as programmer ability or convincing authorities, but does not integrate them into outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Calibrates outcomes based on programmer skill, institutional placement, trust, and collaboration with experts.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly distinguishes scenarios by programmer competence, side joined, access level, credibility, and institutional uptake, using uncertainty to bound conclusions.

criteria.name: Contradiction Control and Historical Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses avoidance of internal contradictions, anachronistic assumptions, and historically implausible claims about WWII technology, cryptography, computing, nuclear development, or military operations.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or false assumptions that undermine the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Has several historical or technical inaccuracies, such as assuming internet access, easy mass replication of chips, or automatic decryption of all codes.
criteria.5-6: Mostly plausible but includes some overstatements or minor inconsistencies about WWII systems or modern computing limits.
criteria.7-8: Maintains internal consistency and generally accurate historical framing, with only minor simplifications.
criteria.9-10: Carefully avoids contradictions and anachronisms, accurately distinguishing what the laptop can compute from what WWII industry, intelligence, and command structures can actually exploit.

items.model_answer:
A modern programmer arriving in the early 1940s with a fully charged laptop would find themselves in a world that is simultaneously awed and utterly unprepared for their device. The laptop would be a near-magical artifact—a self-contained calculating engine millions of times faster than the electromechanical computers just being conceived, with a high-resolution color display and storage capacity beyond the wildest dreams of wartime scientists. But the immediate impact would be sharply limited by two brutal constraints: power and the absence of any modern network infrastructure. Once the battery died after a few hours, the machine would become a useless slab of exotic materials unless the programmer could jury-rig a charging solution—a non-trivial task given that the laptop expects clean, regulated DC power and 1940s grids (where they existed) delivered often-fluctuating AC. Even with a custom-built transformer and rectifier, the risk of frying the device would be high.

Assuming the laptop could be kept running, the software on it would initially be less useful than one might imagine. A typical developer’s machine contains a compiler or interpreter, a vast collection of libraries, and possibly offline documentation or full Wikipedia dumps. The programmer could use it to perform cryptanalysis on Enigma-like ciphers in seconds, but the Allies already had human and electromechanical Bombe machines doing that work effectively; the laptop would simply shorten the time from intercept to decryption, perhaps accelerating the war’s end by weeks or months. Far more disruptive would be the programmer’s modern *knowledge*—of code-breaking techniques, of the critical strategic errors the Axis would make, of the exact specifications of the V-2 rocket and the atomic bomb. That information, if trusted, could reshape the entire Manhattan Project, skipping the dead ends and slashing development time. But the laptop itself might play only a supporting role here: as a text repository for that knowledge, or as a simulation engine for physics calculations if the right software was installed.

The machine’s hardware would become a target of intense reverse-engineering. Engineers at Bletchley Park or Bell Labs would carefully examine the processor, memory chips, and solid-state storage, likely setting off a microelectronics revolution decades ahead of schedule. However, without a semiconductor industry to manufacture the components, they’d be like paleontologists studying a starship—they could admire the architecture but could not reproduce it. The biggest practical gift might be the laptop’s battery: lithium-ion chemistry was utterly unknown, and its analysis could jump-start advanced battery research, though the safety hurdles would be immense.

On the ground, the programmer would need to adapt personally. With no internet, no Stack Overflow, and no peers who understand their trade, they’d be the sole guardian of an entire technological priesthood. Their ability to write machine code for a 1940s computer (like the Harvard Mark I or ENIAC) would be limited unless they had that specific emulation or documentation. But the programmer’s problem-solving mindset—algorithmic thinking, debugging logic, modular design—might prove more valuable than the laptop itself. They could teach methods that would transform early computing, helping avoid the spaghetti-code patchwork that plagued first-generation machines. In the end, the laptop would be a fleeting wonder, but the programmer’s mind, and the intelligence they carried about the future, would be the true weapon—one that could alter the course of the war and the shape of the world that followed, for better or worse.

edus.text: A modern programmer arriving in the early 1940s with a fully charged laptop would find themselves in a world that is simultaneously awed and utterly unprepared for their device.
The laptop would be a near-magical artifact
a self-contained calculating engine millions of times faster than the electromechanical computers just being conceived
with a high-resolution color display and storage capacity beyond the wildest dreams of wartime scientists.
But the immediate impact would be sharply limited by two brutal constraints:
power
and the absence of any modern network infrastructure.
Once the battery died after a few hours,
the machine would become a useless slab of exotic materials
unless the programmer could jury-rig a charging solution
a non-trivial task
given that the laptop expects clean, regulated DC power
and 1940s grids (where they existed) delivered often-fluctuating AC.
Even with a custom-built transformer and rectifier,
the risk of frying the device would be high.
Assuming the laptop could be kept running,
the software on it would initially be less useful than one might imagine.
A typical developer’s machine contains a compiler or interpreter, a vast collection of libraries, and possibly offline documentation or full Wikipedia dumps.
The programmer could use it to perform cryptanalysis on Enigma-like ciphers in seconds,
but the Allies already had human and electromechanical Bombe machines doing that work effectively;
the laptop would simply shorten the time from intercept to decryption,
perhaps accelerating the war’s end by weeks or months.
Far more disruptive would be the programmer’s modern knowledge
of code-breaking techniques,
of the critical strategic errors the Axis would make,
of the exact specifications of the V-2 rocket and the atomic bomb.
That information, if trusted, could reshape the entire Manhattan Project,
skipping the dead ends and slashing development time.
But the laptop itself might play only a supporting role here:
as a text repository for that knowledge,
or as a simulation engine for physics calculations
if the right software was installed.
The machine’s hardware would become a target of intense reverse-engineering.
Engineers at Bletchley Park or Bell Labs would carefully examine the processor, memory chips, and solid-state storage,
likely setting off a microelectronics revolution decades ahead of schedule.
However, without a semiconductor industry to manufacture the components,
they’d be like paleontologists studying a starship
they could admire the architecture
but could not reproduce it.
The biggest practical gift might be the laptop’s battery:
lithium-ion chemistry was utterly unknown,
and its analysis could jump-start advanced battery research,
though the safety hurdles would be immense.
On the ground, the programmer would need to adapt personally.
With no internet, no Stack Overflow, and no peers who understand their trade,
they’d be the sole guardian of an entire technological priesthood.
Their ability to write machine code for a 1940s computer (like the Harvard Mark I or ENIAC) would be limited
unless they had that specific emulation or documentation.
But the programmer’s problem-solving mindset
algorithmic thinking, debugging logic, modular design
might prove more valuable than the laptop itself.
They could teach methods
that would transform early computing,
helping avoid the spaghetti-code patchwork
that plagued first-generation machines.
In the end, the laptop would be a fleeting wonder,
but the programmer’s mind, and the intelligence they carried about the future, would be the true weapon
one that could alter the course of the war and the shape of the world that followed,
for better or worse.

items.question: What If My Printer Could Really Print Money?
human_answers: In today’s article, I give shorter answers to several reader questions. (Previous installment here (http://what-if.xkcd.com/14/).) You can fit four bills on an 8.5”x11” sheet of paper: [Image: image] If your printer can manage one page (front and back) of full-color high-quality printing per minute, that’s $200 million dollars a year. [Image: image] This is enough to make you very rich, but not enough to put any kind of dent in the world economy. Since there are 7.8 billion (http://www.federalreserve.gov/paymentsystems/coin_currcircvolume.htm) \$100 bills in circulation, and the lifetime of a \$100 bill is about 90 months, that means there are about a billion produced each year. Your extra two million bills a year would barely be enough to notice. This question gets submitted a lot. It turns out the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration—the agency which runs the National Hurricane Center—gets it a lot, too. In fact, they’re asked about it so often that they’ve published a response (http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/tcfaq/C5c.html). I recommend you read the whole thing, but I think the last sentence of the first paragraph says it all: “Needless to say, this is not a good idea.” It makes me happy that an arm of the US government has, in some official capacity, issued an opinion on the subject of firing nuclear missiles into hurricanes. [Image: image] A house in a very rainy place, like the Alaska panhandle, might receive close to four meters of rain per year. Water turbines can be pretty efficient. If the house has a footprint of 1,500 square feet and gutters five meters off the ground, it would generate an average of less than a watt of power from rainfall, and the maximum electricity savings would be: \[1500\text{ft}^2 \times 4\tfrac{\text{ meters}}{\text{year}}\times1\tfrac{\text{kg}}{\text{liter}} \times9.81\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}\times5\text{ meters}\times15\tfrac{\text{cents}}{\text{kWh}}=\frac{$1.14}{\text{year}}\] The rainiest hour on record occurred in 1947 in Holt, Missouri, where about 30 centimeters of rain fell in 42 minutes. For those 42 minutes, our hypothetical house could generate up to 800 watts of electricity, which might be enough to power everything inside it. For the rest of the year, it wouldn’t come close. If the generator rig cost $100, residents of the rainiest place in the US—Ketchikan, Alaska—could potentially offset the cost in under a century. There are about 300,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 stars in the universe. If you make a word pronounceable by alternating vowels and consonants (there are better ways to make pronounceable words, but this will do for an approximation), then every pair of letters you add lets you name 105 times as many stars (21 consonants times 5 vowels). 105 possibilities per two characters is about the same information density that numbers have, which suggests the name will end up being about as long as the total number of stars written out: [Image: image] I like doing math that involves measuring the lengths of numbers written out on the page—which is really just a way of loosely estimating log~10~x. It works, but it feels so wrong. Reentering spacecraft heat up because they’re compressing the air in front of them (not, as is commonly believed, because of air friction). According to this calculator (http://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/BGH/stagtmp.html), to increase the temperature of the air layer in front of your body by twenty degrees Celsius (enough to go from freezing to room temperature), you would need to be biking at 200 m/s. The fastest human-powered vehicles at sea levels are recumbent bicycles enclosed in streamlined aerodynamic shells. These vehicles have an upper speed limit near 40 m/s. This is the speed at which the human can just barely produce enough thrust to balance the drag force from the air. Since drag increases with the square of the speed, this limit would be pretty hard to push any further. Biking at 200 m/s would require at least 25 times the power output needed to go 40 m/s. At those speeds, you don’t really have to worry about the heating from the air—a quick back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that if your body were doing that much work, your core temperature would reach fatal levels in a matter of seconds. There are a lot of ways to estimate the amount of information stored on the internet, but we can put an interesting upper bound on the number just by looking at how much storage space we (as a species) have purchased. The storage industry produces in the neighborhood of 650 million hard drives per year. If most of them are 3.5” drives, then that’s eight liters (two gallons) of hard drive per second. This means the last few years of hard drive production—which, thanks to increasing size, represent a large chunk of global storage capacity—would just about fill an oil tanker. So, by that measure, the internet is smaller than an oil tanker. [Image: image] Aerodynamics aside, I’m curious what tactical advantage you’re expecting to gain by having the high explosive fly back at you if it misses the target.

criteria.name: Quantitative grounding of the money-printing premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer anchors the counterfactual in realistic order-of-magnitude calculations for a home printer producing usable currency.
criteria.1-2: Provides no meaningful calculation or gives wildly implausible amounts without basis.
criteria.3-4: Attempts arithmetic but misses key factors such as bills per page, duplex printing, print speed, or yearly output.
criteria.5-6: Estimates output in the right broad range but with incomplete assumptions or unclear unit handling.
criteria.7-8: Correctly uses plausible assumptions, such as four $100 bills per sheet and about one duplex page per minute, to estimate hundreds of millions per year.
criteria.9-10: Gives a clear, checked order-of-magnitude calculation and distinguishes bills, face value, print rate, operating time, and annual total.

criteria.name: Macroeconomic scale and inflation reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer compares the printer's output to existing money supply, currency circulation, and economic scale rather than assuming instant economic collapse.
criteria.1-2: Claims global hyperinflation or economic destruction from one printer with no scale comparison.
criteria.3-4: Mentions inflation or money supply but treats the effect qualitatively and exaggeratedly.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that one printer makes the owner rich but likely has limited macroeconomic impact, with weak quantitative support.
criteria.7-8: Compares the output to circulation or annual production of high-denomination bills and concludes the macro effect is small.
criteria.9-10: Accurately separates personal wealth effects from aggregate effects, noting that a few million extra $100 bills per year is tiny relative to existing currency and broader money supply.

criteria.name: Causal chain from physical printing to spendable wealth
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the mechanisms that determine whether printed money actually functions as money, including authenticity, detection, laundering, banking, and spending constraints.
criteria.1-2: Assumes printed pages automatically become usable wealth without considering authentication or circulation.
criteria.3-4: Briefly notes legality or counterfeiting but does not analyze how the bills enter the economy.
criteria.5-6: Discusses some practical constraints such as serial numbers, security features, suspicious deposits, or spending limits.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent chain from printing to attempted use, including counterfeit detection, banking scrutiny, law enforcement, and transaction bottlenecks.
criteria.9-10: Thoroughly explains how physical realism, legal status, traceability, laundering difficulty, and behavioral responses govern the actual outcome under the premise.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects and institutional response
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces plausible longer-term consequences beyond the immediate windfall, including government, financial, and social responses.
criteria.1-2: Stops at 'you get rich' or 'the economy collapses' with no downstream reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few consequences but as disconnected guesses.
criteria.5-6: Covers likely personal, legal, and economic consequences, though with limited causal depth.
criteria.7-8: Explains escalating effects such as spending patterns, audits, seizure, Secret Service involvement, changes to bill designs, or containment of the anomaly.
criteria.9-10: Presents a coherent long-range scenario showing how institutions detect, investigate, adapt to, and likely neutralize or exploit the money-printing capability.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles the ambiguous counterfactual consistently and flags uncertainties without undermining its own assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise or makes mutually incompatible claims without acknowledgment.
criteria.3-4: Uses inconsistent assumptions about whether the money is real, counterfeit, magical, or legally valid.
criteria.5-6: Mostly maintains a consistent interpretation but leaves important ambiguities unresolved.
criteria.7-8: Clearly states assumptions, such as whether the bills pass authentication or merely look real, and keeps conclusions aligned with them.
criteria.9-10: Separates multiple plausible interpretations, calibrates confidence in each, and avoids overclaiming while preserving causal consistency throughout.

items.model_answer:
If your printer could actually produce legal tender indistinguishable from genuine currency, the immediate result would be a catastrophic collapse of the monetary system. Modern fiat money derives its value from scarcity and trust; if an ordinary person could create unlimited perfect copies, that scarcity vanishes. Hyperinflation would follow—prices would spiral as the supply of money exploded, making each bill worthless. Your newfound wealth would be fleeting: the moment the duplication became known, confidence would evaporate, and the economy would likely revert to barter or a rapid shift to alternative stores of value like gold or cryptocurrencies.

On a technical level, such a printer would have to bypass every anti-counterfeiting measure—specific paper composition, color-shifting inks, watermarks, microprinting, security threads, and machine-readable features. Pulling that off would mean you’ve essentially reinvented a perfect matter replicator that can spoof complex physical authentication, a breakthrough with far broader implications than just money. Legally, you’d be guilty of counterfeiting, but enforcement would become impossible at scale, prompting governments to immediately invalidate the current currency and hunt you as a systemic threat. Fundamentally, the concept of physical cash would die overnight.

items.question: What If You Tried to Launch a Real Rocket Using Only Model Rocket Engines?
human_answers: About 65,000, give or take a few. You’d have to arrange them like this: [Image: image] The rocket would weigh about as much as a tow truck. There wouldn’t be room for anything except the engines, aerodynamic shell, and minimal staging equipment. Each rocket motor would burn for about three seconds. The layer cake arrangement means that every three seconds, the bottom layer of spent rockets would detaches and the next stage would kick in. It would go through between 25 and 30 of these stages, burning for a total of a minute and a half, after which it would coast upward and just barely brush the edge of space. (For this design, I’m assuming something akin to Estes E9-4 engines, which are on the large end of the common model rocket engines. There are larger ones—the classes go all the way up to O and beyond—but at a certain point, they stop being model rocket engines, and just become rocket engines.) A 30-stage rocket is, to put it lightly, an engineering nightmare. This design assumes the non-engine portion of the vehicle is limited to the weight of a person (60 kg). In effect, the spaceship would be a solid block of rocket engines. They’d need to be insulated from each other so the upper stages didn’t ignite prematurely, and the staging and aerodynamics would both be a challenge. The stack of engines narrows as you go from bottom to top. By the time the top stages are firing, the rocket will have shed most of its mass, so it won’t need as much thrust to get the same acceleration. The reason the engine stack bulges in the middle is so that the acceleration profile will look like this: [Image: image] Rockets work best when their thrust is several times greater than the force of gravity. But you don’t want to accelerate too quickly while you’re low down. Air drag increases with the square of your speed, and if you accelerate too quickly, you’ll find yourself wasting all your fuel just to maintain your speed. You want to accelerate slowly at first, then ramp it up as the air starts getting thinner. [Image: image] Now, as you may have noticed, this rocket will get you into space (for a few seconds, at least), but not orbit. Can you use model rocket engines to dock with the ISS? No. Taking into account atmospheric drag, to get into space, you need a rocket capable of accelerating (in a vacuum) to about 2 kilometers per second. To get to orbit, you need a rocket capable of accelerating to about 10 kilometers per second. If you try to produce an orbital rocket using the same design math we used for the suborbital rocket, it spits out a description of a pancake-shaped mountain of model rocket engines over a mile wide. It would taper to a 10-meter-high spire in the center and would weigh about as much as the Great Pyramid. [Image: image] Not only would this vehicle never get out of the atmosphere, it would probably not stand up under its own weight. Frankly, the word “vehicle” is a bit misleading. Essentially, what you’ve created is an unstable pile of gunpowder the size of Central Park. If it went up in flames—which it would—it would break the record for the largest manmade non-nuclear explosion in history. (Interestingly, the current holder of that dubious record is also a rocket that exploded during launch (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m79UO4HOQmc).) The bottom line is that it would be very difficult, but perhaps not impossible, to launch something up to the edge of space using model rocket engines. However, if you try to build a ship capable of getting to orbit, you will not go to space today.

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Tried to Launch a Real Rocket Using Only Model Rocket Engines?

criteria.name: Quantitative Scaling Under Model-Engine Constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer uses plausible order-of-magnitude reasoning for how many model rocket engines, how much mass, burn duration, staging count, and velocity capability would result from trying to launch a real rocket with engines such as large Estes-class motors.
criteria.1-2: Gives no meaningful numbers or relies on wildly impossible claims such as a few engines launching a person to orbit.
criteria.3-4: Includes some quantities but they are mostly unsupported, off by many orders of magnitude, or ignore mass and thrust scaling.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that tens of thousands of engines and many stages are needed, but gives limited or partially inconsistent quantitative support.
criteria.7-8: Provides credible estimates for engine count, short burn times, staging, mass, and suborbital velocity needs with minor gaps.
criteria.9-10: Closely captures the scale: roughly 65,000 large model engines, tow-truck-like mass, 25-30 short stages, about 90 seconds burn, and only marginal space-reaching performance.

criteria.name: Propulsion, Staging, and Acceleration Mechanism Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the causal mechanism by which clustered model engines might work: layered staging, dropping spent motors, thrust-to-weight changes, acceleration shaping, and atmospheric drag effects.
criteria.1-2: Treats the engines as if they simply add together without explaining staging, thrust, drag, or mass loss.
criteria.3-4: Mentions clustering or staging but misses why spent engines must be discarded and how drag or acceleration matters.
criteria.5-6: Explains basic staging and thrust-to-weight issues but omits important effects such as drag losses or changing acceleration as mass falls.
criteria.7-8: Covers layered stages, short burns, shedding mass, changing thrust needs, and why acceleration should be moderated in dense air.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent mechanism including layer-cake staging, narrowing/bulging engine stack, gravity and drag tradeoffs, and rising acceleration as atmosphere thins.

criteria.name: Suborbital Space vs Orbit Endpoint Distinction
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly distinguishes briefly reaching the edge of space from achieving orbit or docking with the ISS, including the much larger delta-v requirement for orbit.
criteria.1-2: Confuses reaching space with orbit or claims ISS docking is feasible with model engines.
criteria.3-4: States orbit is harder but gives no clear physical reason or implies the same design could scale straightforwardly.
criteria.5-6: Correctly says suborbital flight might be possible and orbit is not, but gives only vague velocity or energy reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Clearly contrasts about 2 km/s effective suborbital need with about 10 km/s orbital need, and rejects ISS docking.
criteria.9-10: Precisely explains that the model-engine stack might barely brush space briefly but cannot reach orbit; scaling to orbit produces an absurd, atmosphere-bound, structurally untenable mega-pile.

criteria.name: Engineering Failure Modes and Practical Constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream engineering consequences specific to a rocket made almost entirely of model motors, including packaging, insulation, aerodynamics, ignition control, structural integrity, and explosion risk.
criteria.1-2: Ignores practical engineering constraints or assumes the design is straightforward once enough engines are added.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger or complexity but does not identify concrete failure modes.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several issues such as staging complexity, mass, or premature ignition, but misses major structural or aerodynamic consequences.
criteria.7-8: Covers most key constraints: minimal payload room, insulation, ignition sequencing, aerodynamics, structural load, and high explosion risk.
criteria.9-10: Shows how the counterfactual cascades into a near-solid block of motors, severe staging/aero/thermal control problems, structural collapse for orbital scaling, and possible record-scale non-nuclear explosion.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Discipline, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer stays within the premise of using model rocket engines, states assumptions and uncertainty appropriately, and avoids contradictions with rocket physics or its own causal chain.
criteria.1-2: Breaks the premise, invokes non-model engines or magic technology, or contains major internal contradictions.
criteria.3-4: Mostly follows the premise but makes unsupported leaps, overconfident claims, or inconsistent statements about feasibility.
criteria.5-6: Maintains the premise and basic physics, with some uncertainty acknowledged, but has minor contradictions or vague assumptions.
criteria.7-8: States reasonable assumptions about engine class, payload, and idealization; calibrates feasibility as difficult but not impossible for suborbital and impossible for orbit.
criteria.9-10: Consistently reasons from explicit assumptions, separates idealized math from real engineering risk, uses qualified estimates, and avoids conflicting claims about thrust, mass, staging, or orbital feasibility.

items.model_answer:
If you tried to launch a real rocket—meaning something capable of reaching space or orbit—using only standard model rocket engines, you’d fail dramatically. The problem isn’t just that the engines are small; it’s a brutal combination of physics and numbers that no amount of clustering can overcome.

First, consider thrust. A typical Estes C6 engine produces about 10 N of thrust for roughly 1.8 seconds, making its total impulse just 10 N·s. To even lift a small, useful payload (say, a 1 kg microsatellite) off the ground, you need at least 10 N of continuous thrust just to counteract gravity. But a single C6 weighs about 25 grams itself, and if you cluster thousands of them to build up thrust, the combined mass of the engines becomes enormous. The thrust-to-weight ratio quickly falls below 1, meaning your rocket would sit on the pad firing impotently, unable to lift its own engines.

Even if you could build an impossibly lightweight structure and stage them perfectly, the rocket equation dooms you. To reach low Earth orbit, you need a total velocity change (Δv) of roughly 9.4 km/s. Model rocket engines have an effective exhaust velocity of around 800 m/s (specific impulse ~80 s). Plug those into the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation: the required mass ratio (initial mass/final mass) is \( e^{9400 / 800} \approx e^{11.75} \approx 127,000 \). That means for every 1 kg of payload and structure that reaches orbit, you need over 127,000 kg of propellant—and in this case, that propellant comes inside heavy metal casings. The casings alone guarantee you can never get anywhere near that mass ratio, because each engine’s spent casing is dead weight that doesn’t go away after burnout. A model rocket engine’s structural mass fraction is terrible—often over 50% of its initial mass is non-propellant. With staging you can drop some casings, but you’d still need an astronomically large number of stages, each consisting of thousands of clustered motors, and the dry mass of the interstages and clustering hardware would eat up any theoretical gain.

In practice, you might be able to build a small multi-stage model rocket that could reach a few thousand feet, but calling it a “real rocket” that carries a significant payload is out of the question. The fundamental limitation is that model rocket engines are designed for recreation, not for achieving high Δv with usable payload fractions. They trade efficiency for simplicity, safety, and low cost, making them utterly inadequate for a serious launch vehicle. You’d have better luck with a firework skyrocket—and even that wouldn’t get close to space.

items.question: What If Humanity Sped Up Earth's Rotation to Eliminate Leap Seconds?
human_answers: The Earth’s spin is slowing down. This is annoying. One reason that it’s annoying is that it makes time standards more difficult. We already have way too many time standards (http://tycho.usno.navy.mil/systime.html), including: TAI, time based on an atomic clock, which ignores all motion of the Earth UT0 and UT1, time based on precise measurement of the Earth’s rotation GPS, the time standard used by GPS satellites UTC, the standard used in computing, which is like TAI but with leap seconds to keep it in sync with Earth TDT, TBT, TCB, and TCG, which are all even worse This leads to all kinds of little headaches, particularly for programmers. For example, the clock in your smartphone’s GPS is 16 seconds out of sync with the phone’s system clock. This is because the system clock uses Coordinated Universal Time (which has leap seconds), but GPS time doesn’t. They were in sync in January of 1980 and probably never will be again. Half a billion years ago (when the Earth was 4 billion years old, instead of 4.5), each day was 22 hours long instead of 24. The day has gotten longer because of tidal forces from the Moon. Loosely speaking, here’s how tidal drag works: The Moon’s tides raise bulges in the Earth, but the Earth’s rotation moves those bulges out of line with the Moon. The Moon’s gravity tries to tug the bulges back into line, which exerts a twisting force on the Earth, slowing it down: [Image: image] Strangely, the Earth is actually not slowing down as much as you’d expect from tidal drag. The biggest reason for the discrepancy is that during the last ice age, the continents were pushed down by the weight of the glaciers, and they’re still springing back into place. This has the effect of shifting mass toward the poles, closer to the axis of rotation: [Image: image] This makes us spin faster—or, at least, keeps us from slowing down as quickly. At the moment, each day is about 0.8 milliseconds longer than the 86,400 seconds it needs to be to avoid adding leap seconds. [Image: image] This difference fluctuates over time based on weather and other effects (it’s actually shortened a bit since the early 1990s), although in the long run, it will definitely get larger as the Earth slows. If we wanted to get rid of leap seconds, we’d need to keep the Earth spinning at a more constant rate. This means speeding up the Earth and shortening each day by about 0.8 milliseconds. This is a tough problem. Here are a few things that won’t work: Spinning counterclockwise (http://xkcd.com/162/) in a chair. It temporarily alters the Earth’s rate of rotation, but not enough to matter. Putting rocket engines on the Equator. This won’t work because the exhaust would go into the atmosphere, which transmits the force back to the ground as wind drag—it’d be like making a bike go forward by pushing on the handlebars. If the engines were somehow mounted above the atmosphere, they’d be able to slow the Earth, but not by enough to accomplish our goal. Triggering big earthquakes. This can alter the length of the day (http://www.nasa.gov/topics/earth/features/japanquake/earth20110314.html), but even those aren’t big enough to make a difference. In the end, there’s only one solution: Hitting the Earth with asteroids. Given enough time, we could send a spaceship (captained by an anti-Bruce Willis) to perform repeated flybys of a comet. Over time, the gravitational perturbation could steer the comet into a collision course with Earth. By hitting the Earth at the right angle, we would give it a push: [Image: image] Even if the comet burns up in the atmosphere, its momentum is transmitted to the surface by wind drag (taking a matter of days). It takes about a decade (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/227650235_Topographic_CoreMantle_Coupling_and_Polar_Motion_On_Decadal_TimeScales) for the core to sync up with the crust, so we’d have to plan the impact schedule carefully to avoid overshooting. Here’s the bad news: To get enough spin, we have to hit the Earth with on the order of a billion liters of rock per second (several times the volumetric discharge rate of the Amazon). This adds up to about one six-mile dinosaur-killing asteroid every couple days. Humanity—and life—wouldn’t survive the bombardment long. What about a steady stream of smaller asteroids? [Image: image] If asteroid B-612 in The Little Prince is four meters across and made of rock, we’d need an average of around fifty thousand of them to enter the atmosphere each second to keep up the pressure. [Image: image] Unfortunately, the steady high-altitude meteor shower would deliver just as much energy to the atmosphere that daily giant impacts would, and the eventual death toll would be the same: Seven billion humans, plus four billion Little Princes per day. But at least we could stop worrying about leap seconds.

items.model_answer:
If humanity somehow accelerated Earth’s rotation to make the mean solar day exactly 86,400 SI seconds—thereby eliminating the need for leap seconds—the immediate physical consequences would be barely perceptible, but the engineering demands and long-term maintenance would be staggering and ultimately self-defeating.

Leap seconds exist because Earth’s rotation is irregular and, on average, about 2 milliseconds longer than the atomic-day standard. Spinning the planet up by the required fraction (roughly one part in 40 million) would add roughly 10²² joules of rotational kinetic energy—more than a decade’s worth of humanity’s total current energy consumption. If that energy were delivered quickly, the torque needed would far exceed the strength of rock, triggering continent-shattering earthquakes, global tsunamis, and likely a mass extinction. Even if the process were spread over centuries, the cumulative strain on tectonic plates and the mantle would still pose unacceptable risks.

Once the new, faster rotation was achieved, the direct geophysical changes would be extremely subtle. A 2 ms shortening of the day alters centrifugal force by less than one part in 20 million, so equatorial sea level might drop by a few microns, and the Coriolis parameter would shift by a similarly tiny amount, with no meaningful impact on weather or ocean currents. However, the Earth does not rotate in isolation. Tidal friction from the Moon and Sun continuously transfers angular momentum away from Earth, lengthening the day by about 2.3 ms per century. To keep the day locked at exactly 86,400 seconds, we would need to perpetually counter that natural braking—an ongoing project of pumping immense energy into the planet’s spin. Failing to do so would simply allow leap seconds to return within a few decades.

In the end, speeding up Earth is a violently disproportionate solution to a timetabling inconvenience. The tiny change itself would harm nothing, but the act of applying that change—and the endless effort to maintain it against tidal evolution—makes the idea a non‑starter. A far simpler approach already under discussion is to decouple civil time from Earth’s rotation entirely, or to redefine the second itself. That would achieve the same leap‑second‑free future without having to physically spin an entire planet.

edus.text: If humanity somehow accelerated Earth’s rotation to make the mean solar day exactly 86,400 SI seconds
thereby eliminating the need for leap seconds
the immediate physical consequences would be barely perceptible
but the engineering demands and long-term maintenance would be staggering and ultimately self-defeating
Leap seconds exist because Earth’s rotation is irregular and, on average, about 2 milliseconds longer than the atomic-day standard
Spinning the planet up by the required fraction (roughly one part in 40 million) would add roughly 10²² joules of rotational kinetic energy
more than a decade’s worth of humanity’s total current energy consumption
If that energy were delivered quickly
the torque needed would far exceed the strength of rock
triggering continent-shattering earthquakes, global tsunamis, and likely a mass extinction
Even if the process were spread over centuries
the cumulative strain on tectonic plates and the mantle would still pose unacceptable risks
Once the new, faster rotation was achieved
the direct geophysical changes would be extremely subtle
A 2 ms shortening of the day alters centrifugal force by less than one part in 20 million
so equatorial sea level might drop by a few microns
and the Coriolis parameter would shift by a similarly tiny amount
with no meaningful impact on weather or ocean currents
However, the Earth does not rotate in isolation
Tidal friction from the Moon and Sun continuously transfers angular momentum away from Earth
lengthening the day by about 2.3 ms per century
To keep the day locked at exactly 86,400 seconds
we would need to perpetually counter that natural braking
an ongoing project of pumping immense energy into the planet’s spin
Failing to do so
would simply allow leap seconds to return within a few decades
In the end, speeding up Earth is a violently disproportionate solution to a timetabling inconvenience
The tiny change itself would harm nothing
but the act of applying that change—and the endless effort to maintain it against tidal evolution—makes the idea a non-starter
A far simpler approach already under discussion is to decouple civil time from Earth’s rotation entirely
or to redefine the second itself
That would achieve the same leap-second-free future
without having to physically spin an entire planet

items.question: What If One Extra Person Died Randomly Every Second?
human_answers: Every second, 1.8 humans die and 4.2 humans are born. Under Mr. Petzall’s plan, the number of deaths would increase to 2.8. This randomized culling would obviously be a big deal—it would be responsible for over a third of all deaths—but, at least for a while, our population would continue to grow. At one death per second, any given person currently has a 0.464% chance of being chosen each year. Put another way, the scenario would result in 4.64 deaths per 1,000 people (or 464 per 100,000). [Image: image] There are about twenty countries with death rates below 4.64 per 1,000. It’s an odd bunch (https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/rankorder/2066rank.html), including the Dominican Republic, Brunei, Singapore, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the Maldives, and Paraguay. These are the countries where Guy’s program would be responsible for the majority of all deaths. The death rate in all of these countries is going to go up. It has to, because of math. It seems intuitively obvious that death rates below 10 per 1,000 are unsustainable. If fewer than one person out of every hundred dies each year (and enough are born to sustain the population) then the average person must have to wait over a hundred years to die—which is clearly not compatible with our current lifespans. In those countries with low single-digit death rates, the rates are guaranteed to rise in the future. This includes the United States, whose death rate is 8.40 per 1,000—a number which will go up substantially as the Baby Boomers age. A rate of one death per second isn’t enough to reverse population growth at present, but it would have been until recently. In 1950, the world’s population was only 2.52 billion. One death per second would mean 12.5 annual deaths per 1,000 people, almost triple the number in 2013. At the start of the early 20th century, this would have been enough to reverse population growth, and within a handful of decades—as population levels off—it will be again. Of course, if people die faster, this in turn has an effect on birth rates—as people change their behavior in response to the change in mortality—so the actual result would be more complicated. [Image: image] In the United States, Guy Petzall would be the leading cause of death for females between the ages of 1 and 55 and for males between the ages of 1 and 48. Currently, about 96% of infants survive to age 40, but in Guy’s scenario, only 80% would. When would these deaths happen? Given the numbers of aircraft in the air at any given time, it’s certain that some pilots would die while flying. This wouldn’t be a disaster, though, since large commercial airliners have multiple crew members who can take over. Cars would be a different story. Since about 10 million Americans are driving (http://what-if.xkcd.com/5/) at any given time, 127 will die behind the wheel each day (plus a smaller but still significant number of passengers, pedestrians, and other drivers). Interestingly, this is only a little larger than the number of Americans who die in car accidents every day already. (This number has been declining, as a percentage of population, since the 1960s, and as a percentage of miles traveled since at at least the 1920s (http://www.saferoads.org/federal/2004/TrafficFatalities1899-2003.pdf).) About 50 million (http://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhsr/nhsr011.pdf) outpatient surgery procedures are performed each year. If they’re primarily performed by one surgeon and each last an average of half an hour, then about 13 surgeons per year will unexpectedly die mid-surgery (as will 13 extra patients). This is a scary thought. But to put it in perspective, that’s about the number of surgeons who will operate on the wrong body part or wrong patient every two days (http://www.cnn.com/2011/HEALTH/04/28/ep.wrong.side.surgery/index.html). It’s not that the scenario isn’t scary. It’s just that reality is far more terrifying. Lastly, what about our leaders? Members of Congress die in office at a rate of two or three per year, or about five per Congress. This used to be much higher, as explained in this strangely florid paper (http://home.gwu.edu/~forrest/fmdeathincongressps.pdf). 29 members of Congress died during 1939 and 1940, the two years the 76th Congress was in session. In Guy’s scenario, the current rate would double, leading to a loss of 10 per Congress. This would certainly be tragic, but it would be no higher than the levels seen as recently as the 1960s. All in all, the losses would be dramatic, but not devastating to our species as a whole. And really, in the end, the global death rate is 100%—everyone dies. [Image: image] … or do they? Strictly speaking, the observed death rate for the human condition is something like 93%—that is, around 93% of all humans have died. This means the death rate among humans who were not members of The Beatles is significantly higher than the 50% death rate among humans who were. rubrics.question_focus: What If One Extra Person Died Randomly Every Second?

criteria.name: Quantitative grounding of the extra-death premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly translates 'one extra random person dies every second' into annual deaths, individual risk, and effects on global population growth over time.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or gives wildly incorrect magnitudes, such as claiming immediate extinction or no meaningful added deaths.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes that deaths increase substantially but uses vague or mostly incorrect numbers and population-growth implications.
criteria.5-6: Gives approximately correct scale, such as about 31.5 million extra deaths per year, but only partially relates it to births, baseline deaths, or population growth.
criteria.7-8: Correctly compares extra deaths with current global births and deaths and explains that population would likely keep growing initially but more slowly.
criteria.9-10: Accurately quantifies annual deaths, per-person risk, share of total deaths, and explains how effects depend on population size, fertility, mortality trends, and future demographic transition.

criteria.name: Random-selection mechanics and demographic implications
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer respects the randomness of victim selection and derives realistic consequences across ages, countries, occupations, and risk groups.
criteria.1-2: Treats the deaths as targeted, disease-like, or concentrated without justification, contradicting the random premise.
criteria.3-4: Mentions randomness but fails to apply it consistently to age, location, or activity-based consequences.
criteria.5-6: Explains that everyone has roughly equal additional risk and notes some demographic effects, but with limited specificity.
criteria.7-8: Applies random risk to meaningful groups, such as children, working-age adults, low-mortality countries, leaders, pilots, drivers, or surgeons.
criteria.9-10: Shows nuanced demographic reasoning: equal per-person hazard changes relative mortality most for low-risk groups and young ages, while absolute deaths follow population distribution and time spent in activities.

criteria.name: Coverage of downstream physical and social hazards
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explores major secondary consequences caused by people dying suddenly during critical activities.
criteria.1-2: Ignores downstream effects or asserts civilization collapses without mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few sensational examples but does not estimate frequency or distinguish minor from severe effects.
criteria.5-6: Covers some plausible hazards, such as driving, aviation, surgery, childcare, or industrial operations, with limited causal detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains why some hazards would be manageable and others serious, using rough exposure reasoning or comparisons to existing accident rates.
criteria.9-10: Systematically analyzes cascading risks across transportation, medicine, infrastructure, governance, households, and workplaces while keeping consequences proportional to the added random mortality.

criteria.name: Long-range feedbacks and adaptation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reasons beyond the immediate death toll to behavioral, institutional, demographic, and technological adaptation over years to decades.
criteria.1-2: Only describes the first moments or gives a static conclusion with no longer-term causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Mentions long-term effects vaguely, such as fear or lower population, without tracing mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some adaptations, such as safety automation, redundancy, insurance changes, or fertility responses, but does not connect them deeply.
criteria.7-8: Develops coherent medium- and long-term chains involving fertility, life expectancy, labor markets, public health, political stability, and risk management.
criteria.9-10: Balances demographic transition, psychological normalization, institutional redesign, economic effects, and possible fertility/mortality feedbacks, distinguishing transient disruption from equilibrium outcomes.

criteria.name: Plausibility, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer remains internally consistent, avoids overclaiming, and clearly separates robust implications from speculative ones under the counterfactual.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible claims, or confident conclusions unsupported by the premise.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible points but mixes incompatible assumptions or exaggerates outcomes without acknowledging uncertainty.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent and plausible, with occasional unsupported leaps or weak distinction between certain and speculative effects.
criteria.7-8: Clearly flags uncertainty, avoids deterministic collapse/extinction claims, and keeps conclusions consistent with the stated random one-per-second mechanism.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous causal consistency throughout, quantifies uncertainty where possible, presents alternative plausible trajectories, and avoids both alarmist and dismissive distortions.

items.model_answer:
If one extra person died randomly every second, the global death rate would increase by 86,400 deaths per day, or about 31.5 million additional deaths per year. Currently, around 56 million people die annually (roughly 1.8 deaths per second), so this would nearly double the baseline mortality.

Because the extra deaths occur randomly across the entire population, the risk would be uniformly distributed: each person would face an additional annual death probability of about 0.4% (31.5 million / 8 billion). This is comparable to the existing overall death rate of roughly 0.7% per year. Life expectancy would drop significantly—from around 73 years to perhaps the mid-40s, depending on how the age distribution is affected.

Global population growth would not immediately reverse, since births still outnumber deaths. The current birth rate is about 4.3 per second, yielding a net increase of roughly 2.5 people per second today. With the extra death, net growth would fall to about 1.5 per second, slowing but not halting population rise. However, sustained random removal of individuals would disrupt societies: sudden losses of key workers, parents, and decision-makers would strain economies, healthcare, and governance. The psychological toll of unpredictable, constant mortality would be profound, possibly altering risk-taking behavior and long-term planning. In purely statistical terms, the human population would keep growing, but the quality and stability of life would degrade sharply.

items.question: How Far Would You Have to Drop a Steak to Cook It?
human_answers: I hope you like your steaks Pittsburgh Rare. And you may need to defrost it after you pick it up. Things get really hot when they come back from space. This isn’t because of air friction, strictly speaking—it’s because of air compression. The air can’t move out of the way fast enough, and gets squished in front of the spaceship/meteor/steak. Compressing air heats it up. As a rule of thumb, you start to notice compressive heating above about Mach 2 (which is why the Concorde had heat-resistant material on the leading edge of its wings). A few months ago, skydiver Felix Baumgartner jumped from 39 kilometers, and hit Mach 1 around 30 kilometers. This was enough to heat the air by a few degrees, but the air was so far below freezing that it didn’t make a difference. (Early in his jump, it was about minus 40 degrees, which is that magical point where you don’t have to clarify whether you mean Fahrenheit or Celsius—it’s the same in both.) As far as I know, this steak question originally came up in a lengthy 4chan thread (http://m.chanarchive.org/4chan/sci/63224/5209640#p5209833), which quickly disintegrated into poorly-informed physics tirades intermixed with homophobic slurs. There was no clear conclusion. To try to get a better answer, I decided to run a series of simulations of a steak falling from various heights. This involved a lot of research. I used Mathematica models of atmospheric density to generate a set of descent profiles for the plummeting steak. For a nice tutorial on how to do this, see the Wolfram Blog’s analysis of Felix Baumgartner’s jump (http://blog.wolfram.com/2012/10/24/falling-faster-than-the-speed-of-sound/). An 8 oz. steak is about the size and shape of a hockey puck, so I based my steak’s drag coefficients on those given on page 74 of The Physics of Hockey (which author Alain Haché actually measured personally using some lab equipment). A steak isn’t a hockey puck, but the precise drag coefficient turned out not to make a big difference in the result. I used a handy NASA compressive heating calculator (http://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/BGH/stagtmp.html) to determine the temperature of the shock layer in front of the steak. Since this blog tends to wind up looking at unusual objects in extreme physical circumstances, often the only relevant research I can find is US military studies from the Cold War era. (Apparently, the US government was shoveling tons of money at anything even loosely related to weapons research.) To get an idea of how the air would heat the steak, I looked at research papers on the heating of ICBM nose cones as they reenter the atmosphere. Two of the most useful were Predictions of Aerodynamic Heating on Tactical Missile Domes (http://www.dtic.mil/cgi-bin/GetTRDoc?AD=ADA073217) and Calculation of Reentry-Vehicle Temperature History (http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a231552.pdf). Lastly, I had to figure out exactly how quickly heat spreads through a steak. I started by looking at some papers from industrial food production which simulated heat flow through various pieces of meat. It took me a while to realize there was a much easier way to learn what combinations of time and temperature will effectively heat the various layers of a steak: Check a cookbook. Jeff Potter’s excellent book Cooking for Geeks (http://www.amazon.com/Cooking-Geeks-Science-Great-Hacks/dp/0596805888) provides a great introduction to the science of cooking meat, and explains what ranges of heat produce what effects in steak and why. Cook’s The Science of Good Cooking (http://www.amazon.com/Science-Cooking-Cooks-Illustrated-Cookbooks/dp/1933615982) was also helpful. Putting it all together, I found that the steak will accelerate quickly until it reaches about an altitude of about 30-50 kilometers, at which point the air gets thick enough to start slowing it back down. The falling steak’s speed drops steadily as the air gets thicker. No matter how fast it’s going when it reaches the lower layers of the atmosphere, it quickly slows down to terminal velocity. It always takes six or seven minutes to drop from 25 kilometers to the ground. For much of those 25 kilometers, the air temperature is below freezing—which means the steak will spend six or seven minutes subjected to a relentless blast of subzero, hurricane-force winds. Even if it is cooked by the fall, you’ll probably have to defrost it when it lands. When the steak does finally hit the ground, no matter the initial height, it will be traveling at about 30 meters per second. To get an idea of what this means, imagine a steak flung at the ground by a major-league pitcher. If the steak is even partially frozen, it could easily shatter. However, if it lands in the water, mud, or leaves, it will probably be fine. (Not clean, but intact.) A steak dropped from 39 kilometers will, unlike Felix, probably not break the sound barrier. It also won’t be appreciably heated. This makes sense—after all, Felix’s suit wasn’t scorched when he landed. [Image: image] Steaks can probably survive breaking the sound barrier. In addition to Felix, pilots have ejected at supersonic speeds (http://www.ejectionsite.com/insaddle/insaddle.htm) and lived to tell about it. To break the sound barrier, you’ll need to drop the steak from about 50 kilometers. But this isn’t enough to cook it. We need to go higher. If dropped from 70 kilometers, the steak will go fast enough to be briefly blasted by 350°F air. Unfortunately, this blast of thin, wispy air barely lasts a minute—and anyone with some basic kitchen experience can tell you that a steak placed in the oven at 350 for 60 seconds isn’t going to be cooked. From 100 kilometers—the formally defined edge of space—the picture’s not much better. The steak spends a minute and a half over Mach 2, and the outer surface will likely be singed, but the heat is too quickly replaced by the icy stratospheric blast for it to actually be cooked. [Image: image] At supersonic and hypersonic speeds, a shockwave forms around the steak which helps protect it from the faster and faster winds. The exact characteristics of this shock front—and thus the mechanical stress on the steak—depend on how an uncooked 8 oz. filet tumbles at hypersonic speeds. I searched the literature, but was unable to find anything to help me estimate this. For the sake of this simulation, I assume that at lower speeds some type of vortex shedding creates a flipping tumble, while at hypersonic speeds it’s squished into a semi-stable spheroid shape. However, this is little more than a wild guess. If anyone puts a steak in a hypersonic wind tunnel to get better data on this, please, send me the video. If you drop the steak from 250 kilometers, things start to heat up. 250 kilometers puts us in the range of low earth orbit. However, the steak, since it’s dropped from a standstill, isn’t moving nearly as fast as an object re-entering from orbit. [Image: image] The steak reaches a top speed of Mach 6, and the outer surface may even get pleasantly seared. The inside, unfortunately, is still uncooked. Unless, that is, it goes into a hypersonic tumble and explodes into chunks. From higher altitudes, the heat starts to get really substantial. The shockwave in front of the steak reaches thousands of degrees (Fahrenheit or Celsius; it’s true in both). The problem with these levels of heat is that it burns the surface layer completely, converting it to little more than carbon. That is, it becomes charred. Charring is a normal consequence of dropping meat in the fire. The problem with charring meat at hypersonic speeds is that the charred layer doesn’t have much structural integrity, and is blasted off by the wind—exposing a new layer to be charred. (If the heat is high enough, it will simply blast the surface layer off as it flash-cooks it. This is referred to in the ICBM papers as the “ablation zone”) Even from those heights, the steak stilldoesn’t spend enough time in the heat to get cooked all the way through. (I know what some of you are probably thinking, and the answer is no—it doesn’t spend enough time in the Van Allen belts to be sterilized by radiation). We can try higher and higher speeds, and we might lengthen the exposure time via dropping it at an angle, from orbit. But if the temperature is high enough or the burn time long enough, the steak will slowly disintegrate as the outer layer is repeatedly charred and blasted off. If most of the steak makes it to the ground, the inside will still be raw. Which is why we should drop the steak over Pittsburgh. As the probably-apocryphal story goes, steel workers in Pittsburgh would cook steaks by slapping them on the glowing metal surfaces coming out of the foundry, searing the outside while leaving the inside raw. This is, supposedly, the origin of the term Pittsburgh Rare (http://www.livestrong.com/article/436635-how-to-cook-pittsburgh-style-steaks/). So drop your steak from a suborbital rocket, send out a collection team to recover it, brush it off, reheat it, cut away any badly charred sections, and dig in. Just watch out for salmonella. And the Andromeda Strain. [Image: image]
