items.question: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?
human_answers: [Image: image] Google almost certainly has more data storage capacity than any other organization on Earth. Google is very secretive about its operations, so it's hard to say for sure. There are only a handful of organizations who might plausibly have more storage capacity or a larger server infrastructure. Here's my short list of the top contenders: NSA (http://www.nsa.gov/) NRO (http://www.nro.gov/) NGIP (https://www1.nga.mil/Pages/default.aspx) CIA (https://www.cia.gov/index.html) Schlumberger (http://www.slb.com/) Tencent (http://www.tencent.com/en-us/index.shtml) Chevron (http://www.chevron.com/) Honorable mentions: Amazon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River) (They're huge, but probably not as big as Google.) Facebook (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_book) (They're on the right scale and growing fast, but still playing catch-up.) Microsoft (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Bob) (They have a million servers,[1]Data Center Knowledge: [Ballmer: Microsoft has 1 Million Servers although no one seems sure why.) Let's take a closer look at Google's computing platform. Follow the money We'll start by following the money. Google's aggregate capital expenditures–spending on building stuff[2]I'm excluding the cost of an extremely expensive building they bought in New York.—adds up to somewhere over $12 billion dollars.[3]Data Center Knowledge: Google’s Data Center Building Boom Continues: $1.6 Billion Investment in 3 Months (http://www.datacenterknowledge.com/archives/2013/07/19/google-data-center-spending-continues-to-soar-1-6-billion-in-3-months/) Their biggest data centers cost half a billion to a billion dollars, so they can't have more than 20 or so of those. On their website,[4]Data center locations (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/inside/locations/index.html) Google acknowledges that they have datacenters in the following locations: Berkeley County, South Carolina Council Bluffs, Iowa Atlanta, Georgia Mayes County, Oklahoma Lenoir, North Carolina The Dalles, Oregon Hong Kong Singapore Taiwan Hamina, Finland St Ghislain, Belgium Dublin, Ireland Quilicura, Chile In addition, they appear to operate a number of other large datacenters (sometimes through subsidiary corporations), including: Eemshaven, Netherlands Groningen, Netherlands Budapest, Hungary Wrocław, Poland Reston, Virginia Additional sites near Atlanta, Georgia They also operate equipment at dozens to hundreds of smaller locations around the world. Follow the power To figure out how many servers Google is running, we can look at their electricity consumption. Unfortunately, we can't just sneak up to a datacenter and read the meter.[5]Actually, wait, can we? Somebody should try that. Instead, we have to do some digging. The company disclosed that in 2010 they consumed an average of 258 megawatts of power.[6]Google used 2,259,998 MWh of electricity in 2010 (http://www.environmentalleader.com/2011/09/09/google-reveals-electricity-use-breaking-its-silence/), which translates to an average of 258 megawatts. How many computers can they run with that? We know that their datacenters are quite efficient, only spending 10-20% of their power on cooling and other overhead.[7]Google: Efficiency: How we do it (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/efficiency/internal/) To get an idea of how much power each server uses, we can look at their "container data center" concept from 2005. It's not clear whether they actually use these containers in practice—it may just have been a now-outdated experiment—but it gives an idea of what they consider(ed) reasonable power consumption. The answer: 215 watts per server. Judging from that number, in 2010, they were operating around a million servers. They've grown a lot since then. By the end of 2013, the total amount of money they've pumped into their datacenters will be three or four times what it was as of 2010. They've contracted to buy over three hundred megawatts of power at just three sites,[8]Google: Purchasing clean energy (http://www.google.com/green/energy/use/#purchasing) which is more than they used for all their operations in 2010. Based on datacenter power usage and spending estimates, my guess would be that Google is currently running—or will soon be running—between 1.8 and 2.4 million servers. But what do these "servers" actually represent? Google could be experimenting in all kinds of wild ways, running boards with 100 cores or 100 attached disks. If we assume that each server has a couple[9]Anywhere from 2 to 5 (http://xkcd.com/1070/) of 2 TB disks attached, we come up with close to 10 exabytes[10]As a refresher, the order is: kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta, exa, zetta, yotta. An exabyte is a million terabytes. of active storage attached to running clusters. 10 Exabytes The commercial hard disk industry ships about 8 exabytes worth of drives annually.[12]IDC: Worldwide External Disk Storage Systems Factory Revenue Declines for the Second Consecutive Quarter (http://www.idc.com/getdoc.jsp?containerId=prUS24302513) Those numbers don't necessarily include companies like Google, but in any case, it seems likely that Google is a large piece of the global hard drive market. To make things worse, given the huge number of drives they manage, Google has a hard drive die every few minutes.[11]Eduardo Pinheiro, Wolf-Dietrich Weber and Luiz Andre Barroso, [Failure Trends in a Large Disk Drive Population This isn't actually all that expensive a problem, in the grand scheme of things—they just get good at replacing drives—but it's weird to think that when a Googler runs a piece of code, they know that by the time it finishes executing, one of the machines it was running on will probably have suffered a drive failure. Google tape storage Of course, that only covers storage attached to running servers. What about "cold" storage? Who knows how much data Google—or anyone else—has stored in basement archives? In a 2011 phone interview with Paul Mah of SMB Tech, Simon Anderson of Tandberg Data let slip[13]SMB Tech: Is Tape Still Relevant for SMBs? (http://www.itbusinessedge.com/cm/blogs/mah/is-tape-still-relevant-for-smbs/?cs=45557) that Google is the world's biggest single consumer of magnetic tape cartridges, purchasing 200,000 per year. Assuming they've stepped up their purchasing since then as they've expanded, this could add up to another few exabytes of tape archives. Putting it all together Let's assume Google has a storage capacity of 15 exabytes, or 15,000,000,000,000,000,000 bytes. A punch card can hold about 80 characters, and a box of cards holds 2000 cards: [Image: image] 15 exabytes of punch cards would be enough to cover my home region, New England, to a depth of about 4.5 kilometers. That's three times deeper than the ice sheets that covered the region during the last advance of the glaciers: [Image: image] That seems like a lot. However, it's nothing compared to the ridiculous claims by some news reports about the NSA datacenter in Utah. NSA datacenter The NSA is building a datacenter in Utah. Media reports claimed that it could hold up to a yottabyte of data,[14]CNET: NSA to store yottabytes in Utah data centre (http://crave.cnet.co.uk/gadgets/nsa-to-store-yottabytes-in-utah-data-centre-49304118/) which is patently absurd. Later reports changed their minds, suggesting that the facility could only hold on the order of 3-12 exabytes.[15]Forbes: Blueprints Of NSA's Ridiculously Expensive Data Center In Utah Suggest It Holds Less Info Than Thought (http://www.forbes.com/sites/kashmirhill/2013/07/24/blueprints-of-nsa-data-center-in-utah-suggest-its-storage-capacity-is-less-impressive-than-thought/) We also know the facility uses about 65 megawatts of power,[16]Salt-Lake City Tribune: NSA Bluffdale Center won’t gobble up Utah’s power supply (http://www.sltrib.com/sltrib/news/56493868-78/power-center-electricity-utah.html.csp) which is about what a large Google datacenter consumes. A few headlines, rather than going with one estimate or the other, announced that the facility could hold "between an exabyte and a yottabyte" of data[17]Dailykos: Utah Data Center stores data between 1 exabyte and 1 yottabyte (http://www.dailykos.com/story/2013/08/05/1228923/-Utah-Data-Center-stores-data-between-1-exabyte-and-1-yottabyte) ... which is a little like saying "eyewitnesses report that the snake was between 1 millimeter and 1 kilometer long." Uncovering further Google secrets There are a lot of tricks for digging up information about Google's operations. Ironically, many of them involve using Google itself—from Googling for job postings in strange cities to using image search to find leaked cell camera photos of datacenter visits. However, the best trick for locating secret Google facilities might be the one revealed by ex-Googler talentlessclown (http://www.reddit.com/user/talentlessclown) on reddit:[18]reddit: Can r/Australia help find Google's Sydney data center? Seems like a bit of a mystery... (http://www.reddit.com/r/australia/comments/1hctj4/can_raustralia_help_find_googles_sydney_data/catef4f) The easiest way to find manned Google data centres is to ask taxi drivers and pizza delivery people. There's something pleasing about that. Google has created what might be the most sophisticated information-gathering apparatus in the history of the Earth ... and the only people with information about them are the pizza delivery drivers. Who watches the watchers? [Image: image] Apparently, Domino's.

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer estimates the physical magnitude of storing modern digital data on punch cards using defensible orders of magnitude, especially bytes per card, number of cards, volume/mass/area, and comparison to real-world geographic or industrial scales.
criteria.1-2: Gives no meaningful quantitative estimate or uses wildly impossible units without recognizing scale.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that the card volume would be enormous but provides little or incorrect arithmetic.
criteria.5-6: Uses plausible card capacity and data-size assumptions but has limited or rough physical-scale calculations.
criteria.7-8: Computes credible orders of magnitude for cards, boxes, volume, mass, land area, or depth with clear assumptions.
criteria.9-10: Provides robust, internally checked scale estimates and vivid comparisons while noting sensitivity to data-size assumptions.

criteria.name: Fidelity to the counterfactual premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the premise that all digital data must be stored on punch cards, rather than slipping back into magnetic, optical, semiconductor, or cloud storage for primary storage.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the premise or continues to rely on ordinary digital storage as if unchanged.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges punch cards but repeatedly contradicts the premise with modern storage assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the premise, with some ambiguous or minor lapses about backups, caches, or transmission.
criteria.7-8: Maintains the punch-card constraint across storage, backup, indexing, and retrieval scenarios.
criteria.9-10: Applies the premise rigorously, including edge cases such as metadata, redundancy, logs, encryption keys, and temporary data.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage for storage, retrieval, and computation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the concrete mechanisms by which punch-card-only data storage would affect writing, reading, sorting, searching, updating, backing up, and computing over data.
criteria.1-2: Only says the system would be slow or impossible, with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Covers one or two mechanisms, such as storage space or read speed, superficially.
criteria.5-6: Explains several mechanisms, including read/write throughput, mechanical handling, and indexing.
criteria.7-8: Connects storage density, card readers, sorting systems, error rates, duplication, and update costs into a coherent operating model.
criteria.9-10: Deeply analyzes the full data lifecycle, including random access, distributed processing, versioning, checksums, failures, and archival workflows.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces plausible cascading effects on data centers, internet services, science, commerce, surveillance, personal devices, energy use, labor, logistics, and the environment.
criteria.1-2: Provides only an immediate observation, such as 'there would be lots of cards.'
criteria.3-4: Lists a few consequences but does not connect them causally.
criteria.5-6: Covers several downstream effects with basic causal links, such as slower internet and larger warehouses.
criteria.7-8: Develops coherent chains from physical storage limits to altered computing, economics, infrastructure, and society.
criteria.9-10: Explores broad, long-range systemic changes while distinguishing likely effects from speculative ones.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles uncertain quantities, avoids overclaiming, and keeps assumptions consistent when estimating total global or organizational data stored on punch cards.
criteria.1-2: States precise claims with no basis and contains major internal contradictions.
criteria.3-4: Includes some caveats but mixes incompatible assumptions or unjustified exact numbers.
criteria.5-6: Uses rough ranges and acknowledges uncertainty, though some assumptions remain underexplained.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates known values, estimates, and speculation; avoids most contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, tests assumptions with ranges, and maintains consistency across all calculations and causal claims.

items.model_answer:
If all digital data were stored on standard IBM-style punch cards (each holding just 80 characters), the results would be physically staggering and operationally impossible. As of 2024, the global datasphere is roughly 150 zettabytes—that’s 1.5×10²³ bytes. Storing that on punch cards demands nearly two sextillion individual cards (1.9×10²¹). Laid out flat, these would cover an area over 200,000 times the entire land surface of Earth. Stacked, the volume would exceed a million cubic miles, forming a mountain of paper far larger than any geological feature on the planet. The cards would weigh around four million billion metric tons, requiring the annual paper output of today’s industry for about ten million years to produce.

Beyond the sheer bulk, the practical side is even more absurd. Punch cards are read sequentially by electromechanical devices that handle a few hundred cards per minute. Accessing even a single modern file would involve sifting through mountainous archives, with latencies measured in days or weeks. The cards are flammable, prone to humidity damage, and wear out with handling, so data integrity would be impossible to maintain. The energy and maintenance required to operate vast warehouses of card readers, sorters, and conveyors would dwarf every existing industry. In short, this scenario is a physical and logistical nonstarter—the world would drown in paper cards long before even a tiny fraction of today’s data could be stored.

edus.text: If all digital data were stored on standard IBM-style punch cards
each holding just 80 characters
the results would be physically staggering and operationally impossible.
As of 2024, the global datasphere is roughly 150 zettabytes
that’s 1.5×10²³ bytes.
Storing that on punch cards demands nearly two sextillion individual cards
Laid out flat, these would cover an area over 200,000 times the entire land surface of Earth.
Stacked, the volume would exceed a million cubic miles
forming a mountain of paper far larger than any geological feature on the planet.
The cards would weigh around four million billion metric tons
requiring the annual paper output of today’s industry for about ten million years to produce.
Beyond the sheer bulk, the practical side is even more absurd.
Punch cards are read sequentially by electromechanical devices
that handle a few hundred cards per minute.
Accessing even a single modern file would involve sifting through mountainous archives
with latencies measured in days or weeks.
The cards are flammable, prone to humidity damage, and wear out with handling
so data integrity would be impossible to maintain.
The energy and maintenance required to operate vast warehouses of card readers, sorters, and conveyors would dwarf every existing industry.
In short, this scenario is a physical and logistical nonstarter
the world would drown in paper cards long before even a tiny fraction of today’s data could be stored.

items.question: What If You Began Rising Upward at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: Did you bring a coat? A foot per second isn't that fast—it's substantially slower than a typical elevator.[1]Otis: About Elevators (http://www.otisworldwide.com/pdf/AboutElevators.pdf) It would take you 5-7 seconds to rise out of arms' reach, depending how tall your friends are. [Image: image] After 30 seconds, you'd be 30 feet—9 meters—off the ground. Judging from What-If #44 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/44/), this is getting close to your last chance for a friend to throw you a sandwich or water bottle or something.[2]Not that it will help, ultimately. [Image: image] After a minute or two you would be above the trees. You'd still be about as comfortable as you were on the ground. If it's a breezy day, it will probably get chillier thanks to the steadier wind above the treeline.[3]For this article, I'm going to assume a typical atmosphere temperature profile. It can, of course, vary quite a bit. After 10 minutes you would be above all but the tallest skyscrapers, and after 25 minutes you'd pass the spire of the Empire State Building. [Image: image] The air at these heights is about 3% thinner than it is at the surface. Fortunately, your body handles air pressure changes like that all the time. Your ears may pop, but you wouldn't really notice anything else. Air pressure changes quickly with height. Surprisingly, when you're standing on the ground, air pressure is even measurably lower at your head than at your feet. If your phone has a barometer in it, as a lot of new Android phones do, you can download an app and actually see the pressure difference between your head and your feet. A foot per second is pretty close to a kilometer per hour, so after an hour, you'll be about a kilometer off the ground. At this point, you definitely start to get chilly. If you have a coat, you'll still be ok, though you might also notice the wind picking up. At about two hours and two kilometers, the temperature would drop below freezing. The wind would also, most likely, be picking up. If you have any exposed skin, this is where frostbite starts to become a concern.[4]National Weather Service: Wind Chill Temperature Index (http://www.nws.noaa.gov/om/windchill/images/wind-chill-brochure.pdf) Starting at this point, the air pressure would drop below what you'd experience in an airliner cabin,[5]... which are typically kept pressurized at about 70%-80% of sea level pressure, judging from the barometer in my phone. and the effects would start to become more significant, but unless you had a warm coat, the temperature would be a bigger problem. Over the next two hours, the air would drop to below-zero[6]Either unit.​[7]Not Kelvin, though. temperatures. Assuming for a moment that you survived the oxygen deprivation, at some point you'd freeze to death. But when? The scholarly authorities on freezing to death seem to be, unsurprisingly, Canadians. The most widely-used model for human survival in cold air was developed by Peter Tikuisis and John Frim for the Defence and Civil Institute of Environmental Medicine in Ontario.[8]Prediction of Survival Time in Cold Air (http://cradpdf.drdc-rddc.gc.ca/PDFS/zba6/p144967.pdf)—see page 24 for the relevant tables. According to their model, the main factor in the cause of death would be your clothes. If you were nude, you'd probably succumb to hypothermia somewhere around the five hour mark, before your oxygen ran out.[9]And frankly, this really raises more questions than it answers. If you were bundled up, you may be frostbitten, but you would probably survive ... ... long enough to reach the Death Zone. [Image: image] Above 8,000 meters—above the tops of all but the highest mountains—the oxygen content in the air is too low to support human life. Near this zone, you would experience a range of symptoms, possibly including confusion, dizziness, clumsiness, impaired vision, and nausea. As you approach the Death Zone, your blood oxygen content would plummet. Your veins are supposed to bring low-oxygen blood back to your lungs to be refilled with oxygen. But in the Death Zone, there's so little oxygen in the air that your veins lose oxygen to the air instead of gaining it.[10]Linda D. Pendleton, When Humans Fly High: What Pilots Should Know About High-Altitude Physiology, Hypoxia, and Rapid Decompression (http://www.avweb.com/news/aeromed/181893-1.html) The result would be a rapid loss of consciousness and death. This would happen around the seven hour mark; the chances are very slim that you would make it to eight. [Image: image] And two million years later, your frozen body, still moving along steadily at a foot per second, would pass through the heliopause into interstellar space—the same boundary that Voyager just crossed.[11]Again. Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto, died in 1997. A portion of his remains were placed on New Horizons spacecraft, which will fly past Pluto and then continue out of the Solar System. It's true that your hypothetical foot-per-second trip would be cold, unpleasant, and rapidly fatal. But when the Sun becomes a red giant in four billion years and consumes the Earth, you and Clyde would be the only ones to escape. So there's that. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you began rising straight up at a constant speed of one foot per second, you’d be gently lifted off the ground at about 0.3 meters per second—roughly the pace of a slow stroll. Because you aren’t accelerating, your body would feel no supporting force from the ground, so you’d experience a bizarre, persistent sensation of floating or weightlessness, even as you watch the earth recede beneath you.

**The first minutes**  
Your ears would pop almost immediately as the air pressure starts to drop. Within the first 100 feet (about a minute and a half), you’d still be breathing comfortably, but the ground would already look noticeably distant. After 10 minutes you’d be 600 feet up—higher than most skyscrapers. The temperature would still be mild, but a cool breeze might pick up.

**First hour**  
You’d climb 3,600 feet (about 1,100 meters). At this altitude, the air pressure has fallen enough that you might start feeling dizzy or lightheaded. The temperature would have dropped by roughly 7°C (13°F) from the surface, so if you started on a warm day, it might now be chilly but not yet freezing. If you’re not acclimatized, mild altitude sickness could begin.

**Two to three hours**  
Passing 7,000 to 10,000 feet, hypoxia becomes a real threat. You’d likely experience confusion, headache, nausea, and impaired judgment. In cold weather gear you’d last longer, but in typical clothing you’d soon start to shiver as temperatures dip below freezing. By three hours you’re at nearly 11,000 feet—like standing on a high mountain peak—and breathing would be labored. Without supplemental oxygen or a pressure suit, unconsciousness is likely within a few more hours.

**Five to seven hours**  
At 18,000 feet (about 5 hours), the atmospheric pressure is half what it was at sea level. Your mental and physical capabilities would degrade rapidly; you’d probably lose consciousness. By the time you passed the “Death Zone” above 26,000 feet (around 7.2 hours), you would almost certainly be unconscious and dying from oxygen deprivation. Temperatures could be –20°C (–4°F) or colder, and frostbite would set in on exposed skin.

**Beyond a day**  
If somehow protected from the cold and supplied with breathable air, you’d continue rising. In about 28 hours you’d cross the Kármán line—100 kilometers (62 miles, or about 330,000 feet)—and officially enter space. The blue sky would darken to black, the horizon would become a curved arc, and you’d see the thin layer of atmosphere glowing beneath you. But without a pressurized suit, your body would undergo severe decompression: bodily fluids would bubble, tissues would swell, and death would occur within minutes of exposure to vacuum.

**The ultimate outcome**  
Realistically, without extraordinary protection, you’d succumb to hypoxia and hypothermia long before reaching the stratosphere. The journey would begin with a curious floating sensation, transition through increasing discomfort and disorientation, and end in unconsciousness and death within a few hours—well before you ever leave the troposphere.

nodes.text: If you began rising straight up at a constant speed of one foot per second,
you’d be gently lifted off the ground at about 0.3 meters per second—roughly the pace of a slow stroll.
Because you aren’t accelerating,
your body would feel no supporting force from the ground,
so you’d experience a bizarre, persistent sensation of floating or weightlessness,
even as you watch the earth recede beneath you.
The first minutes
Your ears would pop almost immediately
as the air pressure starts to drop.
Within the first 100 feet (about a minute and a half), you’d still be breathing comfortably,
but the ground would already look noticeably distant.
After 10 minutes you’d be 600 feet up—higher than most skyscrapers.
The temperature would still be mild,
but a cool breeze might pick up.
First hour
You’d climb 3,600 feet (about 1,100 meters).
At this altitude, the air pressure has fallen enough
that you might start feeling dizzy or lightheaded.
The temperature would have dropped by roughly 7°C (13°F) from the surface,
so if you started on a warm day, it might now be chilly but not yet freezing.
If you’re not acclimatized,
mild altitude sickness could begin.
Two to three hours
Passing 7,000 to 10,000 feet,
hypoxia becomes a real threat.
You’d likely experience confusion, headache, nausea, and impaired judgment.
In cold weather gear you’d last longer,
but in typical clothing you’d soon start to shiver
as temperatures dip below freezing.
By three hours you’re at nearly 11,000 feet—like standing on a high mountain peak—
and breathing would be labored.
Without supplemental oxygen or a pressure suit,
unconsciousness is likely within a few more hours.
Five to seven hours
At 18,000 feet (about 5 hours), the atmospheric pressure is half what it was at sea level.
Your mental and physical capabilities would degrade rapidly;
you’d probably lose consciousness.
By the time you passed the “Death Zone” above 26,000 feet (around 7.2 hours),
you would almost certainly be unconscious and dying from oxygen deprivation.
Temperatures could be –20°C (–4°F) or colder,
and frostbite would set in on exposed skin.
Beyond a day
If somehow protected from the cold and supplied with breathable air,
you’d continue rising.
In about 28 hours you’d cross the Kármán line—100 kilometers (62 miles, or about 330,000 feet)—
and officially enter space.
The blue sky would darken to black,
the horizon would become a curved arc,
and you’d see the thin layer of atmosphere glowing beneath you.
But without a pressurized suit,
your body would undergo severe decompression:
bodily fluids would bubble,
tissues would swell,
and death would occur within minutes of exposure to vacuum.
The ultimate outcome
Realistically, without extraordinary protection,
you’d succumb to hypoxia and hypothermia long before reaching the stratosphere.
The journey would begin with a curious floating sensation,
transition through increasing discomfort and disorientation,
and end in unconsciousness and death within a few hours—
well before you ever leave the troposphere.

items.question: What If the Wind Reached 500 Miles per Hour?
human_answers: Absolutely! [Image: image] Some things don't work like they do in the movies. Getting shot doesn't really make someone fly backward. The vacuum of space doesn't make your skin explode. But high wind can definitely pick up a person. In fact, if you were standing in the parking lot, the wind wouldn't just pick you up—it would also peel the pavement from the ground! [Image: image] It wouldn't be strong enough to peel your skin off. Humans can survive blasts of 500 mph wind, which is important because pilots sometimes need to eject from airplanes at those speeds. In the 1940s, the US government put pilots in wind tunnels to learn how they reacted to high winds. Have you ever been curious what happens to a person's face in 457 mph winds? Well, you can watch a video of one of those wind tunnel tests here (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IU4SDDNXuUA). (That test was conducted at NASA Langley Research Center, where I worked before I started drawing internet comics for a living.) It doesn't look very comfortable—I didn't know cheeks could flap like that—but the pilot appears to stay alive. Luckily, he's strapped into that chair. He wouldn't be able to stand up in those winds! If he tried, he would go flying backward down the tunnel. High wind is really powerful. In a paper in the journal Weather, J. F. R. McIlveen showed how to calculate the force of wind on the human body.[1]McIlveen, J. F. R.. "The Everyday Effects Of Wind Drag On People. (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1256/wea.29.02/pdf)" Weather 57, no. 11 (2002): 410-413. The calculations on page 2 show how far you'd have to lean to stay upright in wind of various speeds. [Image: image] When wind speed rises above about 120 mph, it's no longer possible to stay upright no matter how far you lean; you'll start to slide backward across the ground,[2]When Hurricane Isabel hit Virginia in 2003, I had the bright idea of standing on a skateboard with a poncho held up like a sail, so the wind would blow me down the street. But the moment I got the sail up, the wind fell quiet. Later, I learned that people die from doing that (http://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-1327705/Kite-surfer-28-dies-gale-drags-100mph-beach-drops-50ft.html). Oops. then quickly go head over heels and start to tumble. You wouldn't necessarily be thrown very high. If the wind were perfectly level, you'd tumble along the surface, bouncing against the ground. However, if there were any updrafts, you could easily be lifted up and carried away. The good news is that 500 mph winds are rare. The strongest hurricanes have wind speeds around 200 mph with gusts up to 250.[3]Courtney, J.; Buchan, S.; Cerveny, R.S.; Bessemoulin, P.; Peterson, T.C.; Rubiera Torres, J.M.; Beven, J.; King, J.; Trerwin, B.; Rancourt, K.. 2012 "Documentation and verification of the world extreme wind gust record: 113.3 m s–1 on Barrow Island, Australia, during passage of tropical cyclone Olivia. (http://www.bom.gov.au/amoj/docs/2012/courtney_hres.pdf)" Australian Meterological and Oceanographic Journal, 62 (1). 1-9. Tornadoes can reach 300 mph.[4]It's difficult to get accurate measurements of surface winds since those tornadoes destroy most measuring equipment (http://www.spc.noaa.gov/faq/tornado/#History)! 300 is a far cry from 500; the force from a 500 mph wind is several times stronger than the force from a 300 mph wind. There are a few ways you could experience wind speeds faster than 500 mph. One is to stand on top of a volcano when it erupts. When Mount St. Helens exploded in 1980, the column of ash was blasted outward at 700 mph, which is close to the speed of sound.[5]Kieffer, S. W., 1981, Fluid dynamics of the May 18 blast at Mount St. Helens, in Lipman, P.W., and Mullineux, D.R., eds., The 1980 Eruptions of Mount St. Helens, Washington: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 1250, p. 379-400. Another way to experience 500 mph winds is to trigger a hypercane.[6]Limits on Hurricane Intensity (http://wind.mit.edu/~emanuel/holem/holem.html) A hypercane is an exotic type of hurricane with 500 mph winds spinning in a very tight vortex just a few miles across. Hypercanes can't exist on Earth right now. To form, they require ocean temperatures of about 50°C. No matter how much we warm the planet, we're not going to get the temperature that high any time soon. However, there's one way these storms might happen. When an asteroid or comet—coincidentally, one about the size of the recently-named 4942 Munroe (http://blog.xkcd.com/2013/09/30/asteroid-4942-munroe/)—hit Mexico 65 million years ago, it punched a hole in the crust and left behind a sea of lava.[7]Christeson, Gail L., Gareth S. Collins, Joanna V. Morgan, Sean P.S. Gulick, Penny J. Barton, and Michael R. Warner. "Mantle Deformation Beneath The Chicxulub Impact Crater (https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/bitstream/10044/1/4214/1/icpub.pdf)." Earth and Planetary Science Letters 284, no. 1-2 (2009): 249-257. When water flowed back in to fill the hole, it would have been heated by contact with the molten rock. This might have created the conditions for hypercanes to form, and one paper suggests that these storms could have lifted a large amount of dust and debris into the upper atmosphere—thus contributing to a global winter and extinction of the dinosaurs.[8]Emanuel, Kerry A., Kevin Speer, Richard Rotunno, Ramesh Srivastava, and Mario Molina. "Hypercanes: A Possible Link In Global Extinction Scenarios (ftp://texmex.mit.edu/pub/emanuel/PAPERS/hypercane95.pdf)." Journal of Geophysical Research 100, no. D7 (1995): 13755-13765. [Image: image] In short, the answer to Grey's question is yes—500 mph winds would send you flying through the air. But don't worry about that. Instead, worry about is the thing that created the 500 mph winds. Odds are, that's what's going to kill you. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Physical plausibility of 500 mph wind effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons from the 500 mph wind premise using appropriate physics, especially drag force scaling, human survivability, and object/material response.

criteria.3-4: Recognizes extreme danger but gives mostly vague or exaggerated effects with little physical basis.
criteria.5-6: Correctly states that a person would be knocked down or carried away, with some mention of force or debris hazards.

criteria.9-10: Accurately applies the physics to humans, pavement, debris, structures, and survivability, avoiding both understatement and sensationalism.

criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer traces the cascading effects of 500 mph winds from direct human impacts to environmental, infrastructural, and societal consequences.

criteria.3-4: Lists several damages but without causal sequencing or scale.
criteria.5-6: Covers humans, buildings, vehicles, and debris, but misses broader environmental or systemic consequences.
criteria.7-8: Connects immediate destruction to power failure, transport collapse, flooding or erosion, casualties, and emergency response breakdown.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent chain from aerodynamic forces through structural failure, debris missiles, infrastructure collapse, ecological damage, and long-term recovery.

criteria.1-2: Assumes 500 mph winds are normal hurricane or tornado conditions.
criteria.3-4: Notes that such winds are rare but gives inaccurate or unsupported causes.
criteria.5-6: Correctly says they exceed normal hurricanes and most tornadoes, with at least one plausible extreme source.
criteria.7-8: Compares hurricanes, tornadoes, volcanic blasts, and/or hypercanes with approximate speed ranges and formation limits.
criteria.9-10: Clearly explains that the cause of the 500 mph wind is likely more catastrophic than the wind itself, with scientifically plausible formation pathways and constraints.

criteria.name: Long-range causal coherence under the counterfactual
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer maintains a consistent timeline and scale when reasoning from the premise rather than jumping between incompatible scenarios.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise or mixes unrelated disasters without causal links.
criteria.3-4: Has some logical sequence but frequently changes scale, duration, or setting inconsistently.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly consistent scenario but leaves important transitions unexplained.
criteria.7-8: Uses a clear causal chain and distinguishes local gusts, sustained winds, vortices, and blast fronts.
criteria.9-10: Sustains a well-scoped counterfactual from initial wind exposure through regional/global aftermath, with no major causal gaps or scale errors.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer appropriately qualifies uncertain claims, avoids overprecision, and prevents contradictions with known wind records and biological limits.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident false claims, such as guaranteed instant death, global destruction, or common 500 mph storms.
criteria.3-4: Includes some correct statements but also major contradictions or unjustified certainty.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible, with modest caveats, but contains minor overclaims or imprecise comparisons.
criteria.7-8: Calibrates uncertainty about survival, lofting, structural damage, and storm formation while staying consistent with known extremes.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates known evidence from speculation, uses appropriate caveats, and avoids contradictions about hurricanes, tornadoes, ejection survival, and hypercane feasibility.

items.model_answer:
If wind speeds on Earth ever reached 500 miles per hour (about 800 kilometers per hour), the result would be an apocalypse-level event unlike anything in recorded history. For comparison, the most violent tornadoes peak at around 300 mph, and the strongest hurricane eyewall gusts are well below 250 mph. A 500 mph wind is so far beyond these extremes that it essentially becomes a sustained shockwave, pulverizing nearly everything in its path.

At that speed, the wind isn't merely a fluid flow; it's a projectile-laden blast of kinetic energy. The dynamic pressure—the force exerted on surfaces—scales with the square of the velocity. Compared to a strong 100 mph wind, a 500 mph wind exerts 25 times the pressure. A typical wall or roof designed to withstand hurricane forces would fail instantly. Reinforced concrete buildings would be stripped of their facades, then scoured down to rubble. Steel-framed skyscrapers might lose their outer cladding and windows, and their structural frames could distort or buckle under the uneven, unimaginable load. Unprotected humans would not just be blown away; they would be dismembered by the force and by debris moving like bullets. The term “missile hazard” becomes literal—gravel, glass, and wood splinters would travel at hundreds of miles per hour, shredding anything organic.

The environment would be violently re-sculpted. Trees would be uprooted and reduced to splinters; topsoil would be scoured away; vehicles, houses, and industrial equipment would tumble and fragment into high-velocity shrapnel. The roar would be deafening—akin to standing next to a rocket engine—and the pressure differential alone could rupture eardrums and internal organs. Even if you were in a bunker, the vibration and noise would be overwhelming.

Meteorologically, sustained 500 mph winds would demand a pressure gradient so extreme that it could only exist in a hyper-intensified tornado-like vortex or a completely disrupted jet stream. No natural Earth system can generate such energy, so the cause would likely be extraterrestrial—perhaps a major solar storm, a comet’s shock wave, or a theoretical "hypercane" injected with colossal heat from a supervolcano or an asteroid impact. In such an event, the windstorm would be a temporary phenomenon, but its effects would scar the planet for centuries. Coastal regions would see storm surges not in feet but in tens of meters, washing away entire landscapes. The atmospheric shock might even couple with the ground, triggering earthquakes or volcanic-like tremors.

Ultimately, a 500 mph wind would erase cities, flatten forests, sterilize topsoil, and kill virtually all exposed life. It would be a sterilizing event, not a weather event, leaving behind a barren, scoured landscape buried under pulverized debris.

edus.text: If wind speeds on Earth ever reached 500 miles per hour (about 800 kilometers per hour),
the result would be an apocalypse-level event unlike anything in recorded history.
For comparison, the most violent tornadoes peak at around 300 mph,
and the strongest hurricane eyewall gusts are well below 250 mph.
A 500 mph wind is so far beyond these extremes
that it essentially becomes a sustained shockwave, pulverizing nearly everything in its path.
At that speed, the wind isn't merely a fluid flow;
it's a projectile-laden blast of kinetic energy.
The dynamic pressure—the force exerted on surfaces—scales with the square of the velocity.
Compared to a strong 100 mph wind, a 500 mph wind exerts 25 times the pressure.
A typical wall or roof designed to withstand hurricane forces would fail instantly.
Reinforced concrete buildings would be stripped of their facades, then scoured down to rubble.
Steel-framed skyscrapers might lose their outer cladding and windows,
and their structural frames could distort or buckle under the uneven, unimaginable load.
Unprotected humans would not just be blown away;
they would be dismembered by the force and by debris moving like bullets.
The term “missile hazard” becomes literal—
gravel, glass, and wood splinters would travel at hundreds of miles per hour, shredding anything organic.
The environment would be violently re-sculpted.
Trees would be uprooted and reduced to splinters;
topsoil would be scoured away;
vehicles, houses, and industrial equipment would tumble and fragment into high-velocity shrapnel.
The roar would be deafening—akin to standing next to a rocket engine—
and the pressure differential alone could rupture eardrums and internal organs.
Even if you were in a bunker,
the vibration and noise would be overwhelming.
Meteorologically, sustained 500 mph winds would demand a pressure gradient so extreme
that it could only exist in a hyper-intensified tornado-like vortex or a completely disrupted jet stream.
No natural Earth system can generate such energy,
so the cause would likely be extraterrestrial—
perhaps a major solar storm, a comet’s shock wave, or a theoretical "hypercane" injected with colossal heat from a supervolcano or an asteroid impact.
In such an event, the windstorm would be a temporary phenomenon,
but its effects would scar the planet for centuries.
Coastal regions would see storm surges not in feet but in tens of meters, washing away entire landscapes.
The atmospheric shock might even couple with the ground, triggering earthquakes or volcanic-like tremors.
Ultimately, a 500 mph wind would erase cities, flatten forests, sterilize topsoil, and kill virtually all exposed life.
It would be a sterilizing event, not a weather event,
leaving behind a barren, scoured landscape buried under pulverized debris.

items.question: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?
human_answers: Last week, we looked at at life on a giant world (http://what-if.xkcd.com/67/). This week, let's look at a small one. [Image: image] The Little Prince, by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, is a story about a traveler from a distant asteroid. It's simple and sad and poignant and memorable.[1]For another take on the Petit Prince, scroll down to the last section of this wonderful piece (http://the-toast.net/2013/08/02/texts-from-peter-pan-et-al/) by Mallory Ortberg. It's ostensibly a children's book, but it's hard to pin down who the intended audience is. In any case, it certainly has found an audience; it's among the best-selling books in history. [Image: image] It was written in 1942. That's an interesting time to write about asteroids, because in 1942 we didn't actually know what asteroids looked like. Even in our best telescopes, the largest asteroids were only visible as points of light. In fact, that's where their name comes from—the word asteroid means "star-like." We got our first confirmation of what asteroids looked like in 1971, when Mariner 9 visited Mars and snapped pictures of Phobos and Deimos.[2]Here's (http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/imgcat/html/object_page/m09_mtvs4109_09.html) a picture of Phobos looking like the archetypical asteroid. The archived images from the mission are at the NASA Space Science Data Center (http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/masterCatalog.do?ds=PSPG-00235), but strangely, the NSSDC refers readers to someone's personal Tripod page (http://petermasek.tripod.com/mariner9.html) to browse the actual images. These moons, believed to be captured asteroids,[3]Ironically, while Phobos and Deimos look like asteroids, new research suggests they're not. See Craddock, Robert A.. "Are Phobos And Deimos The Result Of A Giant Impact? (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0019103510004100)". Icarus (2010) solidified the modern image of asteroids as cratered potatoes. [Image: image] Before the 1970s, it was common for science fiction to assume small asteroids would be round, like planets.[4]Not always; plenty of people had a good idea of what they would look like. And there were stranger ideas (http://pencilink.blogspot.com/2010/08/uncle-scrooge-29-carl-barks-art-cover.html) ... The Little Prince took this a step further, imagining an asteroid as a tiny planet with gravity, air, and a rose. There's no point in trying to critique the science here, because (1) it's not a story about asteroids, and (2) it opens with a parable about how foolish adults are for looking at everything too literally. So rather than trying to take things away from the story, let's see what strange new pieces science can add. If there really were a superdense asteroid with enough surface gravity to walk around on, it would have some pretty surprising properties. If the asteroid has a radius of 1.75 meters, then in order to have Earth-like gravity at the surface, it would need to have a mass of about 500 million tons. This is roughly equal to the combined mass of every human on Earth. If you stood on the surface, you'd experience tidal forces. Your feet would feel heavier than your head, which you'd feel as a gentle stretching sensation. It would feel like you were stretched out on a curved rubber ball, or were lying on a merry-go-round with your head near the center. [Image: image] The escape velocity at the surface would be about 5 meters per second. That's slower than a sprint, but still pretty fast. As a rule of thumb, if you can't dunk a basketball, you wouldn't be able to escape by jumping straight up. [Image: image] However, the weird thing about escape velocity is that it doesn't matter which direction you're going.[5]... which is why it should really be called "escape speed"—the fact that it has no direction (which is the distinction between "speed" and "velocity") is actually very significant here. If you go faster than the escape speed, as long as you don't actually go toward the planet, you'll escape. That means you might be able to leave our asteroid by running horizontally and jumping off the end of a ramp. [Image: image] If you didn't go fast enough to escape the planet, you'd go into orbit around it. Your orbital speed would be roughly 3 meters per second, which is a typical jogging speed. [Image: image] But this would be a weird orbit. Tidal forces would act on you in several ways. If you reach your arm down toward the planet, it would be pulled much harder than the rest of you. And if you reach down with one arm, the rest of you gets pushed upward, which means other parts of your body feel even less gravity. Effectively, every part of your body would be trying to go in a different orbit. A large orbiting object under these kinds of tidal forces—say, a moon—will generally break apart into rings. This wouldn't happen to you. However, your orbit would become chaotic and unstable. These types of orbits were investigated in an interesting paper by Radu D. Rugescu and Daniele Mortari.[6]Rugescu, Radu D., Mortari, Daniele, "Ultra Long Orbital Tethers Behave Highly Non-Keplerian and Unstable (http://www.academia.edu/3453325/Ultra_Long_Orbital_Tethers_Behave_Highly_Non-Keplerian_and_Unstable)", WSEAS Transactions on Mathematics, Vol. 7, No. 3, March 2008, pp. 87-94. Their simulations showed that large, elongated objects follow strange patterns around their central bodies. Even their centers of mass don't move in the traditional ellipses; some adopt pentagonal orbits, while others spin chaotically and crash into the planet. [Image: image] This type of analysis could actually have practical applications. There have been various proposals over the years to use long, whirling tethers to move cargo in and out of gravity wells—a sort of free-floating space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator). Such tethers could transport cargo to and from the surface of the Moon, or to pick up spacecraft from the edge of the Earth's atmosphere. The inherent instability of many tether orbits poses an interesting challenge for this kind of project. As for the residents of our superdense asteroid, they'd have to be careful; if they ran too fast, they'd be in serious danger of going into a tumble and losing their lunch. Fortunately, vertical jumps would be fine. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?

criteria.name: Counterfactual setup and quantitative anchoring
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the asteroid as tiny but ultra-massive and uses the key scale relationships needed for the scenario.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or treats the asteroid like an ordinary small rock with negligible gravity.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes strong gravity on a tiny body but gives little or incorrect quantitative support.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that extreme density/mass is required and includes roughly plausible gravity or size estimates.
criteria.7-8: Uses the core scales well: meter-sized radius, hundreds of millions of tons, Earth-like surface gravity, low escape speed.
criteria.9-10: Accurately anchors the scenario with consistent numbers and explains how small radius plus huge mass produces the unusual effects.

criteria.name: Surface gravity and tidal-force mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates explanation of how gravity would feel on a body only a few meters across, especially head-to-foot gravity gradients.
criteria.1-2: Ignores tidal effects or assumes gravity feels uniform like on Earth.
criteria.3-4: Mentions odd gravity but does not explain the gradient across a human body.
criteria.5-6: Explains that feet would feel heavier than the head and that posture/orientation would matter.
criteria.7-8: Clearly describes stretching, curvature, changing gravity with height, and why daily movement would feel strange.
criteria.9-10: Gives a physically faithful account of local gravity gradients, body forces, balance, and how different body parts experience different accelerations.

criteria.name: Movement, escape, and orbital dynamics
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces the consequences of low escape speed and nearby orbital speeds for jumping, running, and falling around the asteroid.
criteria.1-2: Claims you could move normally or fly off for the wrong reasons.
criteria.3-4: Notes that escape is possible but confuses escape speed, direction, or orbital motion.
criteria.5-6: Correctly states that fast running/jumping could launch a person into orbit or escape.
criteria.7-8: Explains that escape speed is only a few m/s, orbital speed is jogging speed, and horizontal motion can matter as much as vertical jumping.
criteria.9-10: Accurately develops the full movement chain: ramps/running, low-speed orbit, failed escape paths, unstable tumbling, and likely collisions or recontacts.

criteria.name: Habitability and downstream environmental consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of longer-range implications for actually living there, beyond the immediate gravity trick.
criteria.1-2: Provides only a superficial fantasy answer with little physical follow-through.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few survival issues but misses major consequences of the tiny surface and extreme density.
criteria.5-6: Covers several relevant effects such as tiny horizon, lack of atmosphere, anchoring, supplies, and danger of falling/orbiting.
criteria.7-8: Connects gravity, surface area, escape speed, atmosphere retention, construction, safety, and daily logistics into a plausible living scenario.
criteria.9-10: Thoroughly traces major downstream effects while separating the artificial premise from realistic survival constraints, including material impossibility or exotic matter if relevant.

criteria.name: Causal coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains internally consistent reasoning under the counterfactual and flags uncertain or impossible assumptions appropriately.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, unsupported claims, or violations of the premise.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct ideas but mixes incompatible assumptions or overstates speculative details.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, with minor contradictions or limited acknowledgement of artificial assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear causal chain and distinguishes known consequences from extrapolations.
criteria.9-10: Shows strong long-range reasoning, avoids internal conflicts, calibrates uncertainty, and explicitly handles the exotic-density premise without derailing the analysis.

items.model_answer:
If you lived on a tiny but ultra-massive asteroid, you wouldn’t live for long—and “living” in any normal sense would be impossible. Suppose this asteroid were the size of a modest house yet packed the mass of Mount Everest or even a whole planet: the surface gravity would be staggering. With a diameter of just a few meters but a mass of billions of tons, the gravitational acceleration at your feet could be millions of times Earth’s gravity. You would be instantly flattened into a smear of atoms against the surface, your body unable to support even a fraction of the force.

Even if we imagine some magical suit or force field that kept you intact, the tidal forces would be the next immediate horror. Because the asteroid is so small, the difference in gravity between your head and your feet would be enormous—you’d be stretched vertically like taffy while your sides were crushed inward. Standing upright would tear you apart. The local geometry would feel bizarre: the horizon would curve sharply upward no matter where you stood, as if you were trapped at the bottom of a steep, smooth bowl. The surface, polished to a perfectly smooth finish by the gravity, would reflect light with a flat, mirror-like sheen, and because of gravitational light-bending, the starscape would warp into bewildering arcs and halos overhead.

You couldn’t move a muscle, let alone walk. Jumping is out of the question—the escape velocity would rival that of a small planet, many kilometers per second. Any attempt to lift an arm would require superhuman strength. If the asteroid were made of something denser still, like neutron star matter, it would also be unbelievably hot and radioactive, bathing you in lethal radiation. Time would run measurably slower at your feet than at your head according to general relativity, but you’d be dead long before you could notice such an effect. In short, a tiny ultra-massive asteroid is a trap of crushing, shearing extremes—a place where ordinary matter and life have no chance.

you wouldn’t live for long—
and “living” in any normal sense would be impossible.
Suppose this asteroid were the size of a modest house yet packed the mass of Mount Everest or even a whole planet:
the surface gravity would be staggering.
With a diameter of just a few meters but a mass of billions of tons,
the gravitational acceleration at your feet could be millions of times Earth’s gravity.
You would be instantly flattened into a smear of atoms against the surface,
your body unable to support even a fraction of the force.
Even if we imagine some magical suit or force field that kept you intact,
the tidal forces would be the next immediate horror.
Because the asteroid is so small,
the difference in gravity between your head and your feet would be enormous—
you’d be stretched vertically like taffy
while your sides were crushed inward.
Standing upright would tear you apart.
The local geometry would feel bizarre:
the horizon would curve sharply upward no matter where you stood,
as if you were trapped at the bottom of a steep, smooth bowl.
The surface, polished to a perfectly smooth finish by the gravity, would reflect light with a flat, mirror-like sheen,
and because of gravitational light-bending,
the starscape would warp into bewildering arcs and halos overhead.
You couldn’t move a muscle,
let alone walk.
Jumping is out of the question—
the escape velocity would rival that of a small planet,
many kilometers per second.
Any attempt to lift an arm would require superhuman strength.
If the asteroid were made of something denser still, like neutron star matter,
it would also be unbelievably hot and radioactive,
bathing you in lethal radiation.
Time would run measurably slower at your feet than at your head according to general relativity,
but you’d be dead long before you could notice such an effect.
In short,
a tiny ultra-massive asteroid is a trap of crushing, shearing extremes—
a place where ordinary matter and life have no chance.

items.question: Could You Boil Water by Stirring It?
human_answers: No. The basic idea makes sense. Temperature is just kinetic energy. When you stir tea, you're adding kinetic energy to it, and that energy goes somewhere. Since the tea doesn't do anything dramatic like rise into the air or emit light, the energy must be turning to heat. [Image: image] The reason you don't notice the heat is that you're not adding very much of it. It takes a huge amount of energy to heat water; by volume, it has a greater heat capacity than any other common substance.[1]Hydrogen and helium have a higher heat capacity by mass, but they're diffuse gasses. The only other common substance with a higher heat capacity by mass is ammonia. All three of these lose to water when measured by volume. If you want to heat water from room temperature to nearly boiling in two minutes, you'll need a lot of power: \[1\text{ cup}\times\text{Water heat capacity}\times\tfrac{100^\circ\rm{C}-20^\circ\rm{C}}{2\text{ minutes}}=700\text{ watts}\] (Note: Pushing almost-boiling water to boiling takes a large burst of extra energy on top of what's required to heat it to the boiling point—this is called the enthalpy of vaporization (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enthalpy_of_vaporization).) Our formula tells us that if we want to make a cup of hot water in two minutes, we'll need a 700-watt power source. A typical microwave uses 700 to 1100 watts, and it takes about two minutes to heat a mug of water to make tea. It's nice when things work out![2]If they didn't, we'd just blame "inefficiency" or "vortices". 700 watts for two minutes is an awful lot of energy. When water falls from the top of Niagara Falls, it gains kinetic energy, which is converted to heat at the bottom. But even after falling that great distance, the water only heats up by a fraction of a degree.[3]\(\text{Height of Niagra Falls}\times\frac{\text{Acceleration of gravity}}{\text{Specific heat of water}}=0.12^\circ\text{C}\) To boil a cup of water, you'd have to drop it from higher than the top of the atmosphere. [Image: image] How does stirring compare to microwaving? Based on figures from industrial mixer engineering reports,[4]Brawn Mixer, Inc., Principles of Fluid Mixing (http://www.craneengineering.net/products/mixers/documents/craneEngineeringPrinciplesOfFluidMixing.pdf) (2003) I estimate that vigorously stirring a cup of tea adds heat at a rate of about a ten-millionth of a watt. That's completely negligible.[5]Tea loses heat a much higher rate than this. See: Ben Harden, Tea temperature vs. Time graph (http://www.whoi.edu/vanishingarctic/page.do?pid=48597&tid=441&cid=120786&ct=61&article=82910) The physical effect of stirring is actually a little complicated.[6]In some situations, mixing liquids can actually help keep them warm. Hot water rises, and when a body of water is large and still enough (like the ocean) a warm layer forms on the surface. This warm layer radiates heat much more quickly than a cold layer would. If you disrupt this hot layer by mixing the water, the rate of heat loss decreases. This is why hurricanes tend to lose strength if they stop moving forward—their waves churn up cold water from the depths, cutting them off from the thin layer of hot surface water that was their main source of energy. Most of the heat is carried away from teacups by the air convecting over them, and so they cool from the top down. Stirring brings fresh hot water from the depths, so it can help this process. But there are other things going on—stirring disturbs the air, and it heats the walls of the mug. It's hard to be sure what's really going on without data. Fortunately, we have the internet. StackExchange user drhodes measured the rate of teacup cooling (http://physics.stackexchange.com/a/5510) from stirring vs. not stirring vs. repeatedly dipping a spoon into the cup vs. lifting it. Helpfully, drhodes posted both high-resolution graphs and the raw data itself, which is more than you can say for a lot of journal articles. The conclusion: It doesn't really matter whether you stir, dip, or do nothing; the tea cools at about the same rate (although dipping the spoon in and out of the tea cooled it slightly faster). Which brings us back to the original question: Could you boil tea if you just stirred it hard enough? No. The first problem is power. 700 watts is about a horsepower, so if you want to boil tea in two minutes, you'll need at least one horse to stir it hard enough. [Image: image] You can reduce the power requirement by heating the tea over a longer period of time, but if you reduce it too far the tea will be cooling as fast as you're heating it. Even if you could churn the spoon hard enough—tens of thousands of stirs per second—fluid dynamics would get in the way. At those high speeds, the tea would cavitate; a vacuum would form along the path of the spoon and stirring would become ineffective. And if you stir hard enough that your tea cavitates, its surface area will increase very rapidly, and it will cool to room temperature in seconds: [Image: image] No matter how hard you stir your tea, it's not going to get any warmer.

items.model_answer: Yes, you can boil water by stirring it, at least in principle. Vigorous stirring injects mechanical energy into the water, which is converted into thermal energy through viscous friction and turbulence. If you stir fast enough and long enough—and if the container is well insulated to minimize heat loss—the water's temperature will rise until it reaches the boiling point. In practice, this requires an enormous amount of mechanical work because water has a high specific heat capacity and typical stirring methods lose much energy to the surroundings, but it has been demonstrated experimentally (e.g., using high-speed blenders under controlled conditions).

items.question: What If Humans Kept Growing at the Rate of a One-Month-Old Baby?
human_answers: Tall. According to the National Center for Health Statistics, the average newborn's height (length) is approximately 0.5 meters,[1]or 0.56 meters in heels. or a quarter of the diameter of the Death Star thermal exhaust port. [Image: image] From this initial height of 0.5 meters, they grow to about 1.5 or 2.0 meters: [Image: image] Babies grow fastest right after they're born. During their first month, infants grow about 4.4 centimeters, ten times their growth rate during their early teenage years. [Image: image] In Maria's scenario, this growth rate continues until about age 20: [Image: image] Let's follow that child's growth over the years. By its first birthday, the baby would be a meter long: [Image: image] At 2 years and 3 months, the kid would reach 169 centimeters (5'7"), the average adult height in the US. [Image: image] By age 3, we'd have a 2.08 meter (6'10") toddler, taller than Darth Vader ... [Image: image] ... and much taller than Yoda: [Image: image] By age 4, the child would be nearly nine feet tall, able to dunk a basketball without jumping.[2]A 7'8" Harlem Globetrotters player can almost dunk without jumping (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HTnC0RBXwws), so the threshold for a clear no-jump dunk is probably around 8 feet. [Image: image] A few months later, the kid would surpass Robert Wadlow (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wadlow) to become the tallest human in history. At age 5, the child would be π meters tall (10'4"): [Image: image] At age 7, the child would be 4.2 meters tall, able to stare down a T-rex: [Image: image] By age 10, the child would be 5.8 meters tall (19 feet). If we assume these giants are proportioned like adult humans, this kid would weigh over a metric ton. [Image: image] Actual humans wouldn't be able to grow to such heights. Thanks to the square-cube law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square-cube_law), our bones would be too thin to support our weight and our hearts would be unable to pump blood around our bodies. Even breathing would be difficult; we might be able to position ourselves to keep our airways opened, but to breathe in a lungful of air would require very high airflow rates; we'd experience tornado winds all the way down our airways. Our giant would reach a final height of between 10 and 12 meters, assuming growth tapered off around age 20. At that height, they'd be able to comfortably dunk a basketball while keeping one hand on the court outside the three-point line.[3]A creative NBA 2K3 mod shows us what that player might look like (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vGt10eu4XB8). [Image: image] In addition to the insurmountable health problems, someone with this rapid growth rate would face another hardship. To ride roller coasters, you have to be above a certain minimum height. However, they generally also have a maximum height. [Image: image] Bizarro, a coaster at Six Flags New England, has a minimum height of 137 cm (4'6") and a maximum height of 193 cm (6'4"). Our child would be tall enough to ride Bizarro at age 2 ... and too tall by age 3. Their coaster-riding window would last only 387 days. It's a sad truth: Roller coasters just aren't for everyone. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If humans kept growing at the same pace as a one‑month‑old baby—roughly 2.5–3 cm in length and 0.9 kg in weight per month—throughout their entire lives, we would quickly become towering giants and soon exceed the structural limits of biology.  

A typical one‑month‑old gains about 30 grams a day and elongates by around a millimeter per day. That’s a fast but not constant sprint; normally growth decelerates dramatically after infancy. If it didn’t, a person would be about 2 meters tall by age 5, close to 6.5 meters by 18, and reach 10–11 meters (35–40 feet) by 30. An 80‑year‑old would be roughly 29 meters (95 feet) high.  

Weight would balloon even faster because body mass scales with the cube of height if proportions stay the same. An 18‑year‑old at 6.5 meters would weigh over 3,800 kg (more than a small car), and a 30‑year‑old at 10 meters would tip the scales at around 15,000 kg. By mid‑adulthood the skeleton would collapse under its own mass—bone and muscle strength scale with cross‑sectional area (height squared), so they can’t keep pace with the cubed‑volume increase in bulk. Circulation would also fail: blood pressure would need to be astronomically high to pump blood up to a brain several stories above the heart. Heat dissipation would become a crisis, because surface area grows only with the square of height while metabolic heat production grows with volume.  

In short, perpetual infanthood growth would turn us into sagging, suffocating, thermally overloaded colossi long before we reached middle age. It’s a vivid reminder that growth rates are precisely timed to taper off—our survival depends on quitting the baby‑growth sprint while we’re still small.

items.question: What If a Tyrannosaurus Rex Were Released in New York City?
human_answers: About half of an adult, or one ten-year old child: [Image: image] Tyrannosaurus rex weighed about as much as an elephant.[1]This always seemed a little off to me; my mental image of elephants is that they're in the same size range as cars or trucks, whereas T-rex, as Jurassic Park showed, is big enough to stomp on cars. But a Google image search for car+elephant (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=elephant+car) shows elephants looming over cars just like the T-rex in Jurassic Park. So, great, now I'm also afraid of elephants. [Image: image] No one is totally sure what dinosaur metabolism looked like, but the best guesses for how much food T-rex ate seem to cluster around 40,000 calories per day.[2]Food calories (kcal). Sources: This (http://www.pnas.org/content/106/29/12184.full) and this (http://palaeo-electronica.org/1999_2/gigan/issue2_99.htm), and this (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2666002) with some notes from this (http://www.plosone.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0026037) and distraction from this (http://regex.alf.nu/). If we assume dinosaurs had metabolisms similar to today's mammals, they'd eat a lot more than 40,000 calories each day. But the current thinking is that while dinosaurs were more active (loosely speaking, "warm-blooded") than modern snakes and lizards, very large dinosaurs probably had metabolisms that more closely resembled komodo dragons than elephants and tigers.[3]For big sauropods, we know this must be the case, because otherwise they would overheat. However, there's a lot of uncertainty surrounding T-rex-sized dinosaurs. Next, we need to know how many calories are in a human. This number is helpfully provided, by Dinosaur Comics author Ryan North, on this wonderful t-shirt (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Store_Code=TO&Product_Code=QW-PERSON&Category_Code=QW). Ryan's shirt tells us that an 80-kg human contains about 110,000 calories of energy. Therefore, a T-rex would need to consume a human every two days or so.[4]Although a T-rex would likely be willing to eat several days to weeks worth of food in one meal, so if it has the option, it might eat a bunch of people at a time, then go for a while without eating. The city of New York had 239,736 births in 2011, which could support a population of about 1,000 tyrannosaurs. However, this ignores immigration—and, more importantly, emigration, which would probably increase substantially in this scenario. [Image: image] The 33,000 McDonald's restaurants worldwide sell something like 15 billion hamburger patties per year,[5]They stopped reporting the "x billions served" number on their signs, but this website (http://overhowmanybillionserved.blogspot.com/) has some extrapolations. for an average of 1,245 burgers per restaurant per day. 1,245 burgers is about 600,000 calories, which means that each T-rex only needs about 80 hamburgers per day to survive, and one McDonald's could support over a dozen tyrannosaurs on hamburgers alone. [Image: image] Ands if you live in New York, and you see a T-rex, don't worry. You don't have to choose a friend to sacrifice; just order 80 burgers instead. And then if the T-rex goes for your friend anyway, hey, you have 80 burgers. [Image: image]

items.model_answer: If a living Tyrannosaurus rex were suddenly released into New York City, the immediate result would be catastrophic pandemonium. The animal—roughly 40 feet long, 12 feet tall at the hips, and weighing around 8 tons—would likely be disoriented, terrified, and highly aggressive. Its first instinct would be to flee or attack anything it perceived as a threat or prey. Cars, buses, and pedestrians would be crushed underfoot, and the T. rex’s powerful jaws could easily snap through steel and concrete. The noise of the city—sirens, helicopters, shouting—would further stress the animal, fueling a rampage. Within minutes, the NYPD and eventually the National Guard would respond, but standard firearms would be largely ineffective against its thick hide and sheer bulk; only high-caliber sniper fire, military-grade weaponry, or explosives might bring it down, but not before devastating multiple city blocks and causing hundreds or thousands of casualties. Ultimately, the T. rex would be killed by sustained heavy firepower, though the chaos would completely overwhelm emergency services and leave a trail of destruction comparable to a major terrorist attack.

items.question: What If You Dumped All the World's Tea into the Great Lakes?
human_answers: Weak, bordering on homeopathic. The standard cup of tea, as described by the International Organization for Standardization in ISO 3103 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=8250), contains two grams of tea per 100 mL of water.[1]Further ISO standards concerning tea include ISO 3720 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51541) (black tea), ISO 11287 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51540) (green tea), and ISO 14502-2 (http://www.iso.org/iso/iso_catalogue/catalogue_tc/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=31357) (the difference between black tea and green tea). The Great Lakes have a volume of about 22,600 cubic kilometers, which means we would need about 450 billion tons of tea to reach proper strength. According to the Tea Board of India, one year's global tea harvest totals only about 4.8 million tons,[2]Using figures from this report (http://www.teaboard.gov.in/pdf/Tea%20Statistics%20Global%20Scenario.pdf) extrapolated forward to 2014. only 1/100,000th of what we'd require to make Great Lake Tea. If we dumped those 4.8 million tons into the lakes, the resulting tea would be about as strong as if we'd dripped two drops of tea in a bathtub.[3]Technically, calling this kind of tea "homeopathic" is an exaggeration, since substances in homeopathy are diluted way more than this. Proper bathtub tea, of course, requires one 3-kg bag. [Image: image] For better lake tea, we should find a lake with a volume of 240 million cubic meters (0.24 cubic kilometers). Wular Lake in Kashmir is one candidate. Its volume varies with the seasons, but during the winter it's just about exactly the right size.[4]Unfortunately, it's shrinking (http://www.ramsar.org/pdf/wurc/wurc_mgtplan_india_wular.pdf). (For winter volume, see the chart on page 18 of that report.) India is the world's second-largest tea producer, so it's also conveniently located. Ullswater, in the UK's Lake District, is another great candidate. With a relatively stable year-round volume of about 0.23 cubic kilometers, it would be an excellent site for brewing a global cup of tea. Of course, while neither Wular Lake or Ullswater has ever been used as a giant teakettle, something like this was—famously—attempted in my own backyard in Boston. In 1773, a group of colonists disguised as American Indians[5]They dressed up as American Indians to align themselves politically with the Americas—against Britain—invoking the popular European stereotype of the free and noble savage. The Mohawk people, the actual Indians who the protesters were mimicking, mistrusted the settlers encroaching on their land, sided with the British during the subsequent war, and afterward were driven from their homes by the Americans and fled to Canada. boarded three British ships and threw the cargo of tea—around 44 tons of it—into Boston Harbor to protest British-run tax policy. Boston Harbor has a volume of about 0.44 cubic kilometers, which means that the "tea" brewed in 1773 would have been even more dilute than our Great Lakes tea. The harbor is also somewhat larger[6]The tidal range in Boston is so large (over three meters) that the harbor's volume at high tide is nearly double what it is at low. than Wular Lake or Ullswater, so all the tea in the world would still make Boston Harbor slightly too weak. [Image: image] There's another problem: Heat. If you wanted to make tea from a lake, such as Ullswater or Wular Lake, you'd have to heat the water up. Is that even possible? There's clearly enough stored energy in the world to do it. After all, we presumably heat that amount of water for tea every year already; we just do it in small batches around the world. To heat up Ullswater to 80°C[7]Lots of people have very strong opinions on what this temperature should be. Please direct any corrections on this matter to What-If Tea-Related Complaints Dep't, c/o Her Majesty The Queen, Buckingham Palace, London SW1A 1AA. would take \(6.6 \times 10^{16}\) joules of energy—about 20 days worth of British electricity consumption. which is roughly what would be released if you dropped a water bottle full of antimatter in the lake. [Image: image] Asking Britain to go without electricity for 20 days just to fill one of their lakes with tea seems like it might be a hard sell. Fortunately, there's an easier solution. Boiling Lake in Dominica is a volcanic lake about 60 meters across. Its temperature varies, but it's often near boiling at the edges and vigorously boiling in the center. Measuring the depth of the lake is difficult, so it's hard to get an estimate of the total volume. [Image: image] Frying Pan Lake in New Zealand, on the other hand, is the largest hot lake in the world. It has a volume of about 200,000 m3, and an average temperature of around 50°C—not quite hot enough for tea, but much closer than Ullswater or Wular Lake. New Zealanders consume about 600 grams of tea per person,[8]Kerryn Pollock. 'Tea, coffee and soft drinks (http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/tea-coffee-and-soft-drinks)', Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand, updated 15-Jul-13 for a total of 2,700 tons of tea. If they waited until Frying Pan Lake got particularly hot, then dunked it all in at once ... [Image: image] ... they could brew a year's worth of tea in minutes.
