items.question: What Would Happen to a Human Body Left in Orbit?
human_answers: This isn't really relevant, but I have to ask: Is there a reason you specifically wanted your corpse to be naked? Just making things extra weird for the technicians loading up the capsule and/or throwing you out of the airlock? [Image: image] If you tried this, the first thing that would happen to your corpse would be that it would dry out. This would probably start before you made it to space; the dry, climate-controlled air in the pre-launch waiting area would help draw moisture from your body. In the Manual of Forensic Taphonomy, Franklin Damann and David Carter outline the process of human decomposition. According to them, it takes a lot of effort to keep corpses from drying out during the embalming process.[1]The citation they give for that fact is "(C. A. Wacker, pers. comm.)," which I like to think means it was shared in a conversation that totally broke up the dinner party they were both at. In extremely dry environments like the Atacama Desert in Chile, "spontaneous mummification" can occur—and space is even drier than Chile.[2]The space tourism industry has not adopted this as a slogan. Also, "Chile: Not as Dry as Space!" was probably nixed by the Chilean tourism board. Once your body made it to space, this process would ramp up quickly. Most of the "ecology" responsible for decomposing your corpse would be killed off quickly by the drying process (along with the lack of oxygen, temperature swings, and solar radiation levels), so your body wouldn't decay very much. Instead, you'd become a freeze-dried mummy, after losing about 80% of your body weight in water.[3]This is how much liquid you can remove from fresh animal tissue, according to lab experiments reported in Arthur C. Aufderheide's book The Scientific Study of Mummies. That makes sense; after all, according to that commonly-repeated piece of trivia, human bodies are around 70% water. Or is it 65%? Or 80%? The exact number is a little vague, and seems to depend on who you ask. In a footnote in her wonderful book, Stiff: The Curious Lives of Human Cadavers, writer Mary Roach mentioned that she had methodically Googled the phrase "human body is <X> percent water", for X from 0 to 100. She reported a wide range of claims, including several pages asserting that we're 98% water. It's really gratifying to know I'm not the only person who spends a lot of time carefully cataloging weird stuff like that. What happens next depends on exactly where in space you are. If you're in an orbit that passes near the Earth, your orbit will quickly decay, and before long you'll re-enter the atmosphere and burn up. If you're in a slightly higher orbit, you'll last longer, but you'd also be in the zone where space debris (http://commons.erau.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=stm) was thickest. Impacts with small bits of debris would start to leave pits and scars on your surface; they would often find these on Space Shuttle windows after a flight. Eventually, probably after a few decades, you'd probably have a violent collision with something. Higher orbits are safer. If you were some distance away from the Earth, near where geosynchronous satellites orbit, there would be less debris to run into. Furthermore, for large, dense objects, orbits out there are stable (http://www.readcube.com/articles/10.1029%2F92JE00032?show_checkout=1) for a very long time. You could spend centuries drifting among TV broadcast satellites. [Image: image] If you wanted to last even longer, you could launch yourself away from Earth completely, finding a quiet and stable orbit somewhere in interplanetary space. There, over the course of millennia, you'd be slowly baked by the Sun's radiation and pitted and powdered by micrometeorites. But if your goal is to weird out future space travelers, that might not be the best plan. Space is big; if someone randomly stumbles on your corpse, it suggests that there must be a lot of people zipping around the solar system. And if space travel has become that common, there will be lots of corpses floating around;[4]Weird that "lots of corpses floating around" is somehow an optimistic prediction about the future of space travel. discovering yours will be more archaeologically exciting than anything. You'll be stuck in a lab or museum somewhere and contribute to someone's research paper—a bland end to your exciting prank. Unless, of course, you happen to be found by the only people in space even weirder than you. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 我经常开玩笑说我希望将我的遗体送入轨道。不是“撒我的骨灰”的意思，而是“把我赤裸的尸体扔出气闸”的意思。老实说，我的主要动机是让遥远的未来的某人感到困惑，但这是一个有趣的科学问题：在几年、几十年或几个世纪的过程中，我在轨道上的身体会发生什么？

criteria.name: Immediate vacuum exposure and preservation mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately explains the body's early physical and biological changes in orbit, especially dehydration, freezing/thermal cycling, oxygen loss, radiation, and suppression of normal decomposition.
criteria.1-2: Claims ordinary Earth-like rotting, instant explosion, or other false dramatic effects with little mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions some vacuum or freezing effects but misses dehydration/mummification or misstates decomposition substantially.
criteria.5-6: Describes drying/freezing and reduced decay, with some correct causes but limited detail or minor misconceptions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains rapid desiccation/freeze-drying, microbial shutdown, oxygen absence, temperature extremes, and radiation effects.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced, mechanistic account of mummification-like preservation, water loss, tissue changes, and why normal decomposition largely stops.

criteria.name: Orbit-dependent long-term fate
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes different orbital regimes and traces how altitude and environment affect the corpse over time.
criteria.1-2: Gives one fixed outcome for all orbits, ignoring altitude, drag, and orbital stability.
criteria.3-4: Vaguely says it may fall or drift forever but does not connect outcomes to orbital conditions.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes low orbit decay versus higher orbit persistence, but with weak timing or incomplete distinctions.
criteria.7-8: Explains low-Earth reentry, longer survival in higher orbits, debris-rich regions, and more stable high/geosynchronous orbits.
criteria.9-10: Accurately compares LEO, higher Earth orbit, GEO-like regions, and escape/interplanetary trajectories with plausible timescales and causal drivers.

criteria.name: External space environment impacts over decades to millennia
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream effects from debris, micrometeorites, solar radiation, thermal stress, and possible atmospheric reentry.
criteria.1-2: Omits long-term environmental interactions or invents implausible effects unrelated to orbit.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one long-term hazard, such as burning up or radiation, without explaining cumulative effects.
criteria.5-6: Covers several hazards but treats them shallowly or with unclear sequencing.
criteria.7-8: Connects debris pitting, micrometeorite erosion, radiation damage, heating/cooling cycles, and reentry where applicable.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent long-range degradation pathway from initial preservation to eventual collision, erosion, reentry, or prolonged drifting depending on location.

criteria.name: Causal chain coherence and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a consistent cause-effect chain under the counterfactual premise of a human body left in orbit.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, such as simultaneous rapid decay and permanent perfect preservation, or impossible orbital behavior.
criteria.3-4: Has a recognizable chain but frequent inconsistencies or unsupported leaps.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, though some steps are underexplained or mildly contradictory.
criteria.7-8: Sequences events logically from exposure to preservation to orbital/environmental fate with few inconsistencies.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a tightly reasoned, physically consistent chain across immediate, medium-term, and long-term consequences.

criteria.name: Uncertainty, assumptions, and plausibility calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer appropriately qualifies uncertain details such as exact orbit, body condition, clothing/container status, timescales, and probability of collisions.
criteria.1-2: Presents precise but unsupported claims or ignores critical assumptions entirely.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges uncertainty superficially while still overcommitting to specific outcomes.
criteria.5-6: States some assumptions and gives broadly plausible but imprecise estimates.
criteria.7-8: Clearly conditions conclusions on orbit, exposure, and timescale, using cautious probability language.
criteria.9-10: Expertly calibrates uncertainty, avoids false precision, and separates robust mechanisms from scenario-dependent outcomes.

items.model_answer:
If a human body were left in orbit without a spacesuit, the individual would lose consciousness within about 10–15 seconds due to oxygen deprivation and would die within a minute or two. The immediate hazards are the vacuum and lack of breathable atmosphere, not explosive decompression as often depicted. Gases trapped in the lungs would expand rapidly, so holding one’s breath would cause fatal lung rupture; any air remaining in the digestive tract would force its way out. Bodily fluids exposed to vacuum—saliva, tears, moisture on the skin—would boil off in a process called ebullism, causing localized swelling and evaporative cooling, but the skin and circulatory system would largely contain internal pressure, preventing the body from bursting.

After death, the body would undergo a complex, long-term transformation driven by the extreme thermal, radiative, and vacuum environment. In direct sunlight, the side facing the Sun would heat to over 120°C (250°F), while the shaded side would plunge to around -150°C (-238°F). This temperature gradient would freeze-dry the body: water would sublimate from tissues, gradually desiccating and mummifying the remains. Ultraviolet and ionizing radiation would break down skin and soft tissues, darkening and eroding them over months to years. Micrometeoroids and orbital debris would pummel the body, causing pitting and fragmentation. Unless actively preserved, the body would not decompose microbially in the normal sense, as most internal bacteria would be killed by radiation and extreme conditions, though some spores might survive.

Orbital decay determines the ultimate fate. In low Earth orbit (e.g., ISS altitude ~400 km), the tenuous atmosphere would gradually slow the body down. Over months to a few years, drag would lower its orbit until it entered the denser atmosphere, where frictional heating would incinerate it, leaving only charred fragments if any reached the surface. In a higher, more stable orbit, the desiccated, radiation-blasted corpse could remain circling Earth for centuries or millennia, becoming a slowly eroding piece of human-made space debris.

items.question: What If You Dug Straight Down at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: This question is the reverse of question #64 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/64/), which asked how you'd die if you rose steadily at a foot per second. Digging at the same rate would kill you more quickly. [Image: image] After you get through the surface layers,[1]See question #132 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/132/) for more on that. temperatures rise pretty steadily as you go deeper, a trend that continues all the way to the core. In some areas, where the hot magma[2](Lava (http://xkcd.com/1405/).) is closer to the surface, the ground gets hotter more quickly. The Southern Methodist University Geothermal Lab has produced some superb maps (http://www.smu.edu/Dedman/Academics/Programs/GeothermalLab/DataMaps/TemperatureMaps) showing the temperature of deep rocks in different parts of the United States. If you look at the map of the 3.5 km layer (http://www.smu.edu/~/media/Site/Dedman/Academics/Programs/Geothermal%20Lab/Graphics/TemperatureMaps/SMU_2011_35kmTemperature.ashx?la=en), you see that at that depth, most of the US is colored greenish-yellow, representing temperatures somewhere around 100°C—with one glaring exception. In northwest Wyoming, there's a circle of ground colored bright red, where the rock is much hotter than normal. That circle is the Yellowstone supervolcano (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_Caldera). [Image: image] The SMU maps show that even if you avoided digging in Yellowstone, you'd quickly encounter temperatures too hot for an unprotected human. The ground typically gets hotter at an average of about 35°C per kilometer, so at a rate of a foot per second, you'd encounter lethal heat within an hour or two. But wait a moment. Let's say your hole is about a meter wide. At the rate you're digging, you have to remove roughly half a ton of material every second. No human would be capable of lifting that first foot of material out of the hole so quickly, and it only gets worse after that. After a minute of digging, you'd be 60 feet down, and would have to lift all that rock and dirt a huge distance vertically to get it out of the hole. The power required to do that lifting—just after the first minute—would be roughly 150 horsepower. [Image: image] Even if you're not doing the lifting yourself, the way your question is worded makes it pretty clear that you are in this hole. Whatever process you're using is going to require huge amounts of energy to lift all that rock, and that energy is inevitably going to result in the hole being heated somehow. Even if the layer you're digging through wasn't hot when you started, it will be. What if we assume you're protected against the heat from the ground (and the digging mechanism)? Well, in that case, the pressure would become a problem. As you go deeper, air pressure increases. Below about 5 km, the pressure is high enough that oxygen (http://www.scuba-doc.com/oxygentox.html) becomes toxic (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LOZuxwVk7TU). So what if you're protected against the heat, pressure, and the digging process? Well, at that point, we've redefined the rules so much that I'm not sure it makes sense to try to calculate an answer. The question—"what would kill you if you kept digging downward"—has left the realm of physics and become fantasy. Which, come to think of it, makes the answer perfectly clear. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you could somehow dig straight down through the entire Earth at a constant speed of one foot per second, the journey from one side of the planet to the other would take about **1.33 years** (roughly 485 days). In reality, you’d be dead from unimaginable heat and pressure long before you got more than a few miles deep — but let’s explore the hypothetical physics.

**Time and distance**  
Earth’s diameter is about 7,918 miles, or 41.8 million feet. Moving at 1 ft/s, you cover 86,400 feet per day, so:  
41,800,000 feet ÷ 1 ft/s = 41,800,000 seconds ≈ 484 days (1.33 years).  
If you started on the surface, passed through the center, and stopped when you reached the antipodal point, you’d need a little over a year and four months, assuming you never pause.

**What you’d feel: gravity**  
At 1 ft/s, gravity doesn’t act like the famous “free-fall through the Earth” scenario. You’re not in free fall; you’re boring your way down, so your weight changes gradually.

- At shallow depths, gravitational pull is almost unchanged. In the real Earth, gravity actually increases slightly in the upper mantle (due to the dense core) before it begins to drop.
- Once inside the mantle, gravity roughly declines linearly toward zero at the center, if we imagine uniform density. The real profile is more complex, but you would feel lighter and lighter, reaching weightlessness at the very center.
- As you ascend the other side, gravity builds back up, pulling you downward toward the center (which now feels like “up” relative to your direction of motion). You’d need to actively pull yourself along or dig against that growing force to maintain 1 ft/s.

**Rotation and the Coriolis effect**  
Earth rotates. If the shaft were truly straight (along a diameter), the Coriolis force would push you into the side of the hole because your angular velocity must increase to match the rotation of the material around you as you go deeper. At constant speed, you’d be scraped against the wall unless you continuously steered or braced. In a free-fall gravity train, you’d build up huge sideways speed; here, your slow pace would make the effect mild but persistent, causing a constant sideways drift you’d have to fight.

**The fatal environment**  
Long before the weird gravity, you’d be killed by the Earth’s interior:

- **Temperature**: Just 10 miles down, the ambient rock is well over boiling point. The geothermal gradient (~25°C per km) means that at 100 km depth, temperatures exceed 2,500°C. You’d be incinerated within hours of digging, even if your suit could withstand the pressure.
- **Pressure**: At the center, pressure is roughly 360 gigapascals (3.6 million atmospheres). At 1 ft/s, you’re crawling through solid rock, then liquid outer core (you’d be swimming/molten), then solid inner core. The hole would collapse instantly behind and ahead of you, and your body would be crushed to a smear long before you left the lithosphere.

**Why it’s impossible even hypothetically**  
No material can remain open against the immense lithostatic pressure at mantle depths. The tunnel would self-seal in an instant, and the heat would melt any drilling apparatus. The constant 1 ft/s isn’t a physical limit — it’s just a narrative rate that highlights how enormous Earth is. At walking speed, it would take you well over a year of nonstop digging to reach the other side, but you’d never survive the first few dozen miles.

So, the short answer: it would take 1.33 years to travel through the Earth at 1 ft/s, but the planet’s internal heat and pressure make any such journey instantly lethal and the shaft physically unsustainable.

edus.text: If you could somehow dig straight down through the entire Earth at a constant speed of one foot per second,
the journey from one side of the planet to the other would take about 1.33 years (roughly 485 days).
In reality, you’d be dead from unimaginable heat and pressure long before you got more than a few miles deep
but let’s explore the hypothetical physics.
Earth’s diameter is about 7,918 miles, or 41.8 million feet.
Moving at 1 ft/s, you cover 86,400 feet per day,
so 41,800,000 feet ÷ 1 ft/s = 41,800,000 seconds ≈ 484 days (1.33 years).
If you started on the surface, passed through the center, and stopped when you reached the antipodal point,
you’d need a little over a year and four months,
assuming you never pause.
At 1 ft/s, gravity doesn’t act like the famous “free-fall through the Earth” scenario.
You’re not in free fall;
you’re boring your way down,
so your weight changes gradually.
At shallow depths, gravitational pull is almost unchanged.
In the real Earth, gravity actually increases slightly in the upper mantle (due to the dense core)
before it begins to drop.
Once inside the mantle, gravity roughly declines linearly toward zero at the center, if we imagine uniform density.
The real profile is more complex,
but you would feel lighter and lighter,
reaching weightlessness at the very center.
As you ascend the other side, gravity builds back up,
pulling you downward toward the center
(which now feels like “up” relative to your direction of motion).
You’d need to actively pull yourself along or dig against that growing force
to maintain 1 ft/s.
Earth rotates.
If the shaft were truly straight (along a diameter),
the Coriolis force would push you into the side of the hole
because your angular velocity must increase to match the rotation of the material around you as you go deeper.
At constant speed, you’d be scraped against the wall
unless you continuously steered or braced.
In a free-fall gravity train, you’d build up huge sideways speed;
here, your slow pace would make the effect mild but persistent,
causing a constant sideways drift
you’d have to fight.
Long before the weird gravity, you’d be killed by the Earth’s interior:
Just 10 miles down, the ambient rock is well over boiling point.
The geothermal gradient (~25°C per km) means that at 100 km depth, temperatures exceed 2,500°C.
You’d be incinerated within hours of digging,
even if your suit could withstand the pressure.
At the center, pressure is roughly 360 gigapascals (3.6 million atmospheres).
At 1 ft/s, you’re crawling through solid rock, then liquid outer core (you’d be swimming/molten), then solid inner core.
The hole would collapse instantly behind and ahead of you,
and your body would be crushed to a smear long before you left the lithosphere.
No material can remain open against the immense lithostatic pressure at mantle depths.
The tunnel would self-seal in an instant,
and the heat would melt any drilling apparatus.
The constant 1 ft/s isn’t a physical limit
it’s just a narrative rate that highlights how enormous Earth is.
At walking speed, it would take you well over a year of nonstop digging to reach the other side,
but you’d never survive the first few dozen miles.
So, the short answer:
it would take 1.33 years to travel through the Earth at 1 ft/s,
but the planet’s internal heat and pressure make any such journey instantly lethal
and the shaft physically unsustainable.

items.question: What If You Dropped a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: Nope! Jupiter's pressure, density, and temperature curves are different from ours. At the point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the density is high enough for a submarine to float, the pressure is high enough to crush the submarine,[1]Which makes it more dense. and the temperature is high enough to melt it.[2]Which makes it harder to drive. [Image: image] But there's another problem: Jupiter is a gas giant, but submarines—as you can figure out from etymology—go under water. [Image: image] Air and water are different. This seems straightforward enough, but they're also the same in a lot of ways. They're both "fluids," and some of the same rules apply to each. In some sense, when you look up at the sky (http://xkcd.com/1556/), you're looking up from the bottom of a deep sea of air. Things float when they're less dense than the fluid around them. This works the same for balloons in air and boats in water. The late Terry Pratchett wrote a truly beautiful passage about this, in the prologue to his book Going Postal. He says that since water is in many respects a wetter form of air,[3]Sounds reasonable enough to me. as ships sink, eventually they reach a point where the water was too dense to sink any further. This layer forms an underwater surface on which shipwrecks collect, drifting around beneath the waves but far above the sea floor:It’s calm there. Dead calm.Some stricken ships have rigging; some even have sails. Many still have crew, tangled in the rigging or lashed to the wheel.But the voyages still continue, aimlessly, with no harbour in sight, because there are currents under the ocean and so the dead ships with their skeleton crews sail on around the world, over sunken cities and between drowned mountains, until rot and shipworms eat them away and they disintegrate.Sometimes an anchor drops, all the way to the dark, cold calmness of the abyssal plain, and disturbs the stillness of centuries by throwing up a cloud of silt. I love that passage. It's also completely wrong. Ships sink all the way to the bottom. (Sir Terry knew this, as the rest of the passage makes clear, but he's describing how ships work on Discworld, not Earth.) Air follows the ideal gas law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_gas_law). The more pressure you put on it, the smaller (and denser) it gets. Water, on the other hand, is pretty much incompressible. When you dive into the ocean, the pressure increases as you go deeper (rising by one atmosphere every 10 meters or so) but the water's density barely changes all the way down to the sea floor. Buoyancy depends on density, not pressure. There's a point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the pressure is equal to a little more than an Earth atmosphere—which is the pressure a submarine is used to—but the air there is barely a tenth as dense as ours. A submarine in that layer would fall even faster than it would in the air on Earth. [Image: image] To reach a depth where it could "float" in Jupiter, the submarine would have to go halfway to the center of the planet, where the intense pressure turns the air into a metallic soup (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_hydrogen) that's hotter than the surface of the Sun. The pressure there would be so high that not only would the submarine be crushed, the substances that make it up would probably be converted into new and exciting forms. It's hard to create those kinds of conditions in a lab, so we don't know a lot about how materials behave with that much pressure pushing down on them. [Image: image] In the sea, on the other hand, the density of the fluid stays relatively constant. That means the submarine can find its appropriate pressure range and float there. In other words, submarines only work because water doesn't follow the ideal gas law. But there's one more twist: Water sort of does obey the ideal gas law. The equations governing water under normal pressure are similar to (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1311.0534.pdf) the equation for a gas under about twenty thousand atmospheres of pressure. In a sense, this is why water seems incompressible to us—it behaves as if it's already compressed so much that an extra atmosphere or two hardly makes a difference. So, in some ways, water and air are more similar than they seem, but in the ways that matter for a submarine, they really are different. Which, of course, brings us back to why it's called a submarine—it operates under a "mare". A vehicle designed to operate beneath a sea of air would be called a subaerine.[5]The "gas" in "gas giant" is from the Greek word for void (χάος, kháos), so maybe a vessel (σκάφη, skáphē) that travels through a gas giant's atmosphere would be a khaoskaphe. Which, come to think of it, is a perfectly good description of a car. [Image: image]

items.model_answer: If you dropped a submarine into Jupiter, it would plunge into an atmosphere that has no true surface—just an ever-thickening mixture of hydrogen and helium. Within minutes, the pressure would far exceed what any Earth-built submarine is designed to withstand. Even the strongest military subs have crush depths of a few hundred atmospheres; Jupiter’s atmosphere reaches that pressure only a few hundred kilometers below the visible cloud tops. The submarine would implode violently, its hull collapsing long before reaching the deeper layers. As it fell, it would also be subjected to rapidly rising temperatures—from frigid ammonia-ice clouds at the top to thousands of degrees—causing the metal and any remaining organics to melt and vaporize. The debris would then mix with the planet’s interior, sinking until its atoms become part of the dense, fluid metallic hydrogen that makes up most of Jupiter’s bulk. In short, there is no ocean to float in, only a bottomless sky where the submarine would be crushed, incinerated, and absorbed.

items.question: What Would It Be Like to Ride a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: We don't know! We've only flown spacecraft into a gas planet's atmosphere twice (both Jupiter). One had no cameras, and one went in at night (and was being disposed of, so wasn't taking pictures anyway). If you took a submarine to Jupiter, it would burn up. Jupiter has a deep gravity well; after falling down toward it from space, you're going very fast. There's no easy way to shed that speed other than slamming into the atmosphere and letting it slow you down, but the entry is about four times faster than the Space Shuttle or Apollo Earth reentries. Only the Galileo probe has survived a Jupiter atmospheric entry. [Image: image] The Galileo probe survived by being a bullet with a big heat shield, and several inches of the shield were burned away before it finished slowing down and started falling vertically by parachute. The probe only sent back about half a megabyte of data to the Galileo orbiter, and had no camera, so we don't know what it saw. We could, I guess, try to do the same thing with a submarine—by mounting a giant heat shield on the front—but it would probably qualify as the most Kerbal (https://youtu.be/vwrLR2kv5KA?t=1119) vehicle ever built. [Image: image] If our submarine survived, what would we see?[1]I mean, submarines don't usually have a lot of windows, but we at least have a periscope, right? The best pictures we have of Jupiter's atmosphere are probably these carefully processed mosaics (http://www.planetary.org/blogs/emily-lakdawalla/2010/2644.html) of the Great Red Spot, but they're still taken from very far away. At those resolutions, a huge Earth thunderstorm would appear as roughly one pixel. Trying to figure out what Jupiter's clouds would look like from those pictures is like using this (http://visibleearth.nasa.gov/view.php?id=78314) to reconstruct these (http://stormandsky.smugmug.com/Thumbnail-Galleries). By combining the pictures with other science data, we've been able to put together a pretty good idea of what Jupiter's atmosphere is like, but there are some pretty big questions still unanswered which make it hard to be too confident about what it would actually look like. For example, you know the Great Red Spot? We don't know what all that red stuff is. [Image: image] Author Michael Carroll has done a lot of thinking about planetary atmospheres, and his book Drifting on Alien Winds (http://www.amazon.com/Drifting-Alien-Winds-Exploring-Weather/dp/1441969160) vividly describes of what it would be like to descend through Jupiter's clouds. He was also kind enough to answer some of my questions about Jupiter. Here's a rough sketch of what you'd see as you descended through the clouds; for more, definitely check out his book (http://www.amazon.com/Drifting-Alien-Winds-Exploring-Weather/dp/1441969160). [Image: image] Jupiter's upper atmosphere (the part we would see before we died (http://what-if.xkcd.com/138/)) has three main layers—an upper layer of haze and ammonia clouds, similar to cirrostratus (https://www.google.com/search?q=cirrostratus&tbm=isch) clouds on Earth. Below that is a thick, reddish-brown ammonium hydrosulfide cloud layer. The lowest layer consists of white water clouds, which occasionally rise into towering thunderstorms that occasionally push through the middle layer. Between these cloud layers, the air is probably pretty clear. At those levels, it would be less dense than the air on Earth, so you could see a long way. Thanks to Rayleigh scattering (https://xkcd.com/1145/), the sky would be blue, and objects far off in the distance would fade to blue just like they do on Earth (http://thehelpfulartteacher.blogspot.com/2010/11/landscapes-continuedatmospheric.html). But since Jupiter is so huge, we might not see the clouds disappear over the horizon; the towers might just fade off into the distance. We don't really know how accurate these pictures are, though, until we send a camera to fly down into Jupiter's atmosphere and send pictures back. Juno, scheduled to reach Jupiter next year, carries a pretty nice camera (http://www.msss.com/all_projects/junocam.php),[2]Thank you to Emily Lakdawalla for her helpful background about various spacecraft cameras, including her many thorough spreadsheets. which should give us slightly better-resolution pictures, but it still won't really give us a sense of what the cloud decks look like from within them. For that, we need to send in a probe with a camera—and there's nothing like that on the horizon. There's certainly more science value in visiting Europa than in satisfying our curiosity about the Jovian sky. But with interplanetary cubesats (http://www.nasa.gov/directorates/spacetech/niac/staehle_interplanetary_cubesats.html) soon to make their debut, who knows—maybe someone out there will put together a camera, heat shield, and parachute, and hitch a ride on the next outer planets mission. And then, finally, we'll get to look at Jupiter's clouds from both sides (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v9j_j-cUwKc). [Image: image]

criteria.name: Entry and Survival Physics
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons from the premise of bringing a submarine to Jupiter through the unavoidable high-speed atmospheric entry, heating, deceleration, and structural survival issues.
criteria.1-2: Treats Jupiter entry like ordinary diving or flight; ignores orbital/fall speed, heating, pressure, or the submarine's likely destruction.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger or crushing/burning vaguely but gives little causal explanation or uses Earth-ocean analogies incorrectly.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that the submarine would probably burn up or be destroyed during entry, with some reference to high speed, atmosphere, or pressure.
criteria.7-8: Explains the long-range chain from Jupiter's gravity well to very fast entry, intense heating, need for extreme heat shielding, deceleration, then later pressure/temperature hazards.
criteria.9-10: Accurately compares Jupiter entry to extreme spacecraft reentry, notes Galileo-like heat-shield requirements, and clearly separates entry heating, deceleration, parachute/fall dynamics, and later atmospheric crushing/heating.

criteria.name: Jovian Atmospheric Structure and Visual Experience
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of what a surviving observer might plausibly see while descending through Jupiter's cloud layers, including haze, ammonia clouds, ammonium hydrosulfide clouds, water clouds, storms, visibility, and sky color.
criteria.1-2: Describes an ocean, solid surface, or generic darkness with no Jupiter-specific atmospheric features.
criteria.3-4: Mentions clouds or storms but with little distinction between layers or with major misconceptions such as liquid water seas.
criteria.5-6: Covers some plausible Jovian visuals, such as colored clouds, storms, haze, or limited visibility, but omits important layering or scale effects.
criteria.7-8: Describes multiple cloud decks and likely visual effects, including upper haze/ammonia, reddish-brown middle clouds, lower water clouds, storm towers, and clear regions between layers.
criteria.9-10: Gives a vivid but scientifically grounded descent sequence, including blue Rayleigh-scattered sky in clearer layers, enormous cloud towers fading into distance, uncertain colors, and lack of a solid surface view.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a coherent sequence from approach to entry to descent to deeper atmospheric fate without skipping or contradicting necessary intermediate mechanisms.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims or impossible jumps, such as instantly diving into a Jovian sea or safely touring the planet.
criteria.3-4: Has a rough sequence but major causal gaps, e.g., ignores how the submarine slows down or why conditions worsen with depth.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly ordered narrative from entry to descent to destruction, though some transitions are shallow or underspecified.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear causal progression: gravity-driven acceleration, atmospheric braking, heat-shield survival problem, cloud-layer descent, increasing pressure/temperature, communications/visibility limits.
criteria.9-10: Integrates all major stages into a tightly reasoned chain, showing how each physical constraint determines the next and why even a modified submarine would only briefly function as a probe.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Evidence Use
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer distinguishes known science from speculation, reflects the limited direct observations of Jupiter's atmosphere, and uses relevant probes or missions appropriately.
criteria.1-2: States speculative visuals as certain facts or invents unsupported details without acknowledging observational limits.
criteria.3-4: Includes a token caveat but mostly overclaims what we know about views inside Jupiter's atmosphere.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty and mentions limited observations or spacecraft data, but does not connect this to specific visual or atmospheric claims.
criteria.7-8: Correctly notes that only limited probes have entered Jupiter, that imagery from within the atmosphere is lacking, and that cloud appearance is partly inferred.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates confidence throughout, referencing Galileo/Juno or remote imaging limits where relevant, and frames the submarine-view description as plausible extrapolation rather than settled fact.

criteria.name: Contradiction Control and Counterfactual Discipline
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer preserves the counterfactual premise without introducing contradictions about submarines, Jupiter, or planetary physics.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts basic facts, such as giving Jupiter a normal ocean floor, breathable air, survivable open hatches, or submarine propulsion working normally.
criteria.3-4: Avoids some obvious errors but still includes incompatible claims, such as both immediate destruction and extended normal exploration without modification.
criteria.5-6: Mostly respects the premise and physics, with minor inconsistencies about buoyancy, pressure, windows, propulsion, or survivability.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes an ordinary submarine's fate from a heavily modified probe-like version and avoids claims of solid-surface landing or oceanic navigation.
criteria.9-10: Consistently handles the absurd premise by explaining what must be modified, what remains impossible, and what observations could occur only under tightly qualified survival assumptions.

items.model_answer:
Riding a submarine into Jupiter would quickly transform from an ethereal, alien cruise into a crushing, incinerating plunge into one of the most hellish environments imaginable.

Your journey begins in the upper atmosphere, where your pressure hull provides a cozy bubble of Earth-like conditions. Outside, you’d first encounter a thin, cold haze of ammonia crystals at about -150°C, stretching into delicate cirrus-like cloud decks. The gravity is a crushing 2.4 times Earth’s, pressing you into your seat. As you descend slowly, the view through the porthole turns a more dramatic palette: high-altitude hazes give way to the unmistakable tan, orange, and reddish-brown bands of ammonium hydrosulfide clouds, and eventually the brilliant white peaks of ammonia clouds—the “surface” we see from space. The submarine’s buoyancy, designed for water, would behave oddly in hydrogen and helium; you’d need to adjust ballast constantly as the atmospheric density increases.

But the beauty is fleeting. Very quickly—within mere tens of kilometers—the pressure mounts exponentially. The ambient light fades, and sunlight is swallowed by the ever-thickening gases, plunging you into a perpetual brown–black twilight. The gentle turbulence of the cloud tops gives way to violent, supersonic wind shear that would batter your vessel as it crosses between latitudinal bands where winds rip at hundreds of meters per second. The hull groans; the temperature begins to climb.

By the time you reach a depth of just 150 kilometers below the visible cloud tops—a tiny fraction of the planet’s 70,000-kilometer radius—the pressure outside is over 20 times Earth’s atmospheric pressure, and the temperature soars past 300°C. The submarine as we know it would already be a crushed, melting wreck. But suppose you’re in a magical, indestructible craft. The hydrogen around you, still mostly molecular, gets denser and hotter, turning the view into an orange-black, supercritical fluid—neither gas nor liquid—where the concept of a “surface” is meaningless. You’re now in a vast, roiling ocean of liquid metallic hydrogen, electrically conducting, churning with enormous currents that generate Jupiter’s intense magnetic field. The temperature exceeds 10,000°C, hotter than the surface of the Sun, and the pressure is millions of times Earth’s atmospheric pressure—so extreme that even atoms are pressed into a quantum degenerate state.

At the core, if there is one, your craft would finally meet a rocky and icy center perhaps a few Earth-masses in size, buried in that seething metallic hydrogen soup. By then, the descent would have been long, dark, and silent except for the ominous creaks and shrieks of a hull subjected to forces that no material can withstand. The entire journey would be a one-way ticket into a crushing abyss where your spacecraft, you, and all your atoms become part of the planet’s forbidding interior—a testament to the sheer, indifferent power of a gas giant.

edus.text: Riding a submarine into Jupiter would quickly transform from an ethereal, alien cruise into a crushing, incinerating plunge into one of the most hellish environments imaginable.
Your journey begins in the upper atmosphere,
where your pressure hull provides a cozy bubble of Earth-like conditions.
Outside, you’d first encounter a thin, cold haze of ammonia crystals at about -150°C,
stretching into delicate cirrus-like cloud decks.
The gravity is a crushing 2.4 times Earth’s,
pressing you into your seat.
As you descend slowly,
the view through the porthole turns a more dramatic palette:
high-altitude hazes give way to the unmistakable tan, orange, and reddish-brown bands of ammonium hydrosulfide clouds,
and eventually the brilliant white peaks of ammonia clouds—the “surface” we see from space.
The submarine’s buoyancy, designed for water, would behave oddly in hydrogen and helium;
you’d need to adjust ballast constantly as the atmospheric density increases.
But the beauty is fleeting.
Very quickly—within mere tens of kilometers—the pressure mounts exponentially.
The ambient light fades,
and sunlight is swallowed by the ever-thickening gases,
plunging you into a perpetual brown–black twilight.
The gentle turbulence of the cloud tops gives way to violent, supersonic wind shear
that would batter your vessel
as it crosses between latitudinal bands
where winds rip at hundreds of meters per second.
The hull groans;
the temperature begins to climb.
By the time you reach a depth of just 150 kilometers below the visible cloud tops—a tiny fraction of the planet’s 70,000-kilometer radius—
the pressure outside is over 20 times Earth’s atmospheric pressure,
and the temperature soars past 300°C.
The submarine as we know it would already be a crushed, melting wreck.
But suppose you’re in a magical, indestructible craft.
The hydrogen around you, still mostly molecular, gets denser and hotter,
turning the view into an orange-black, supercritical fluid—neither gas nor liquid—
where the concept of a “surface” is meaningless.
You’re now in a vast, roiling ocean of liquid metallic hydrogen,
electrically conducting,
churning with enormous currents
that generate Jupiter’s intense magnetic field.
The temperature exceeds 10,000°C, hotter than the surface of the Sun,
and the pressure is millions of times Earth’s atmospheric pressure—
so extreme that even atoms are pressed into a quantum degenerate state.
At the core, if there is one,
your craft would finally meet a rocky and icy center
perhaps a few Earth-masses in size,
buried in that seething metallic hydrogen soup.
By then, the descent would have been long, dark, and silent
except for the ominous creaks and shrieks of a hull subjected to forces that no material can withstand.
The entire journey would be a one-way ticket into a crushing abyss
where your spacecraft, you, and all your atoms become part of the planet’s forbidding interior—
a testament to the sheer, indifferent power of a gas giant.

items.question: What If All Sunlight Reaching Earth Were Bundled into a 1-Meter Beam?
human_answers: Here's the situation Max is describing: [Image: image] If you were standing in the path of the beam, you would obviously die pretty quickly. You wouldn't really die of anything, in the traditional sense. You would just stop being biology and start being physics. When the beam of light hit the atmosphere, it would heat a pocket of air to millions of degrees[1]Fahrenheit, Celsius, Rankine, or Kelvin—it doesn't really matter. in a fraction of a second. That air would turn to plasma and start dumping its heat as a flood of x-rays in all directions. Those x-rays would heat up the air around them, which would turn to plasma itself and start emitting infrared light. It would be like a hydrogen bomb going off, only much more violent. [Image: image] This radiation would vaporize everything in sight, turn the surrounding atmosphere to plasma, and start stripping away the Earth's surface. But let's imagine you were standing on the far side of the Earth. You're still definitely not going to make it—things don't turn out well for the Earth in this scenario—but what, exactly, would you die from? The Earth is big enough to protect people on the other side—at least for a little bit—from Max's sunbeam, and the seismic waves from the destruction would take a while to propogate through the planet. But the Earth isn't a perfect shield. Those wouldn't be what killed you. Instead, you would die from twilight. [Image: image] The sky is dark at night[citation needed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flunixin)] because the Sun is on the other side of the Earth.[citation needed (http://library.williams.edu/citing/game/)] But the night sky isn't always completely dark. There's a glow in the sky before sunrise and after sunset because, even with the Sun hidden, some of the light is bent around the surface by the atmosphere. If the sunbeam hit the Earth, x-rays, thermal radiation, and everything in between would flood into the atmosphere, so we need to learn a little about how different kinds of light interact with air. Normal light interacts with the atmosphere through Rayleigh scattering. You may have heard of Rayleigh scattering as the answer to "why is the sky blue." This is sort of true, but honestly, a better answer to this question might be "because air is blue." Sure, it appears blue for a bunch of physics reasons, but everything appears the color it is for a bunch of physics reasons.[2]When you ask, "Why is the statue of liberty green?" the answer is something like, "The outside of the statue is copper, so it used to be copper-colored. Over time, a layer of copper carbonate formed (through oxidation), and copper carbonate is green." You don't say "The statue is green because of frequency-specific absorption and scattering by surface molecules." When air heats up, the electrons are stripped away from their atoms, turning it to plasma. The ongoing flood of radiation from the beam has to pass through this plasma, so we need to know how transparent plasma is to different kinds of light. At this point, I'd like to mention the 1964 paper Opacity Calculations: Past and Future (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022407364900202), by Harris L. Mayer, which contains the single best opening paragraph to a physics paper I've ever seen:Initial steps for this symposium began a few billion years ago. As soon as the stars were formed, opacities became one of the basic subjects determining the structure of the physical world in which we live. And more recently with the development of nuclear weapons operating at temperatures of stellar interiors, opacities become as well one of the basic subjects determining the processes by which we may all die. Compared to air, the plasma is relatively transparent to x-rays. The x-rays would pass through the plasma, heating it through effects called Compton scattering (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compton_scattering) and pair production (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanical_scattering_of_photon_and_nucleus), but would be stopped quickly when they reached the non-plasma air outside the bubble. However, the steady flow of x-rays from the growing pocket of superhot air closer to the beam would turn a steadily-growing bubble of air to plasma. The fresh plasma at the edge of the bubble would give off infrared radiation, which would head out toward the horizon (along with the infrared already on the way), heating whatever it finds there. [Image: image] This bubble of heat and light would wrap around the Earth, heating the air and land as it went. As the air heated up, the scattering and emission from the plasma would cause the effects to propogate farther and farther around the horizon. Furthermore, the atmosphere around the beam's contact point would be blasted into space, where it would reflect the light back down around the horizon. Exactly how quickly the radiation makes it around the Earth depends on many details of atmospheric scattering, but if the Moon happened to be half-full at the time, it might not even matter. When Max's device kicked in, the Moon would go out, since the sunlight illuminating it would be captured and funneled into a beam. Slightly after the beam made contact with the atmosphere, the quarter moon would blink out. [Image: image] When the beam from Max's device hit the Earth's atmosphere, the light from the contact point would illuminate the Moon. Depending on the Moon's position and where you were on the Earth, this reflected moonlight alone could be enough to burn you to death ... [Image: image] ... just as the twilight wrapped around the planet, bringing on one final sunrise.[3]Here's an image which is great for annoying a few specific groups of people: [Image: image] [Image: image] There's one thing that might prevent the Earth's total destruction. Can Max's mechanism actually track a target? If not, the Earth could be saved by its own orbital motion. If the beam was restricted to aiming at a fixed point in the sky, it would only take the Earth about three minutes to move out of the way. Everyone on the surface would still be cooked, and much of the atmosphere and surface would be lost, but the bulk of the Earth's mass would probably remain as a charred husk. The Sun's death ray would continue out into space. Years later, if it reached another planetary system, it would be too spread out to vaporize anything outright, but it would likely be bright enough to heat up the surfaces of the planets. [Image: image] Max's scenario may have doomed Earth, but if it's any consolation, we wouldn't necessarily die alone.

rubrics.question_focus: What If All Sunlight Reaching Earth Were Bundled into a 1-Meter Beam?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise and Energy-Scale Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets the premise as essentially all solar power normally intercepted by Earth concentrated into a roughly 1-meter beam, and reasons from the resulting extreme power density rather than treating it as ordinary sunlight or a laser of arbitrary strength.
criteria.1-2: Misreads the premise or treats the beam as merely bright sunlight with minor heating effects.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes a dangerous concentrated beam but gives little sense of the enormous total solar power involved.
criteria.5-6: Correctly identifies planet-scale energy concentration and predicts catastrophic heating, with limited quantitative or scale-based support.
criteria.7-8: Uses appropriate order-of-magnitude reasoning to connect Earth's intercepted sunlight to extreme beam intensity and rapid destruction.
criteria.9-10: Precisely maintains the counterfactual setup, energy scale, and implications of concentrating Earth's full solar input into a 1-meter beam throughout the reasoning.

criteria.name: Initial Beam-Atmosphere Interaction Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the first physical consequences when the beam hits Earth: rapid atmospheric heating, plasma formation, x-ray/thermal emission, blast-like effects, and vaporization of nearby air, surface, and observers.
criteria.1-2: Omits atmospheric interaction or claims the beam simply drills a clean hole with little secondary effect.
criteria.3-4: Mentions burning or explosion near impact but lacks mechanisms such as plasma, radiation, or atmospheric coupling.
criteria.5-6: Describes severe local vaporization and atmospheric heating, but with incomplete or vague radiation/plasma dynamics.
criteria.7-8: Explains plasma formation, high-energy radiation, thermal re-emission, and rapid local devastation coherently.
criteria.9-10: Gives a causally detailed account of the impact region, including plasma opacity/transparency, x-rays, infrared emission, shock/heating, and surface stripping.

criteria.name: Global Propagation and Far-Side Lethality
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reasons beyond the impact site to how effects reach the night side or far side of Earth through atmospheric scattering, plasma emission, horizon-wrapping radiation, reflected light, and delayed seismic or material effects.
criteria.1-2: Assumes only the beam path is affected or that the far side remains safe indefinitely.
criteria.3-4: Predicts global death but attributes it only to vague explosion, earthquakes, or instantaneous heat without a credible propagation path.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that radiation or atmospheric heating spreads around Earth, but the causal chain is thin or partially confused.
criteria.7-8: Coherently explains twilight-like atmospheric propagation and radiation wrapping around the planet before slower mechanical effects dominate.
criteria.9-10: Captures the key long-range mechanism: x-rays/thermal radiation create expanding plasma and infrared/scattered light that reaches beyond the horizon, potentially killing far-side observers before seismic effects.

criteria.name: Downstream Planetary and Astronomical Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates treatment of longer-range consequences such as atmospheric loss, surface ablation, possible total planetary destruction versus charred remnant, Moon illumination/reflection, and the role of Earth's orbital motion or beam tracking.
criteria.1-2: Stops at immediate local death and gives no meaningful downstream consequences.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Earth is destroyed but without distinguishing atmosphere, surface, Moon, orbital motion, or duration of exposure.
criteria.5-6: Covers some planetary-scale effects such as atmosphere loss or surface vaporization, but omits important conditional outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Discusses major downstream effects, including global heating, atmosphere stripping, and possible dependence on whether the beam tracks Earth.
criteria.9-10: Thoroughly integrates planetary aftermath, Moon/reflected-light effects, orbital escape from a fixed beam, and the fate of the beam after Earth moves or is destroyed.

criteria.name: Causal Coherence, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a logically consistent causal timeline, distinguishes robust conclusions from uncertain details, and avoids contradictions with the premise or known physics.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible timelines, or unsupported claims that undermine the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible statements but mixes incompatible mechanisms or overstates uncertain details as certain.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent causal sequence, with minor contradictions or weak calibration of uncertain atmospheric/radiative details.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear timeline from beam impact to global effects and flags uncertain rates or geometry-dependent outcomes appropriately.
criteria.9-10: Provides a tightly consistent long-range causal chain, explicitly calibrates uncertainties such as scattering speed and Moon geometry, and avoids unsupported or premise-breaking assumptions.

items.model_answer:
If all 173 petawatts of sunlight that normally bathe the Earth were focused into a single 1‑meter‑wide beam, the result would be a catastrophe unlike anything in Earth’s history. The beam’s intensity would be roughly 2.2 × 10¹⁷ W/m²—over 3 billion times the intensity at the Sun’s surface. Everything in its path would be instantaneously vaporized, and the effects would tear the planet apart on multiple fronts.

**What happens at the impact point**  
The beam delivers the energy equivalent of about 40 megatons of TNT *every second* onto a single square meter. Rock, soil, water, and air would be turned into a high‑temperature plasma in microseconds. The continual blast would excavate a crater hundreds of meters deep almost immediately, and within minutes the beam would bore through the Earth’s crust and into the mantle. A permanent, incandescent plume of vaporized rock and plasma would shoot into the sky, acting like a continuous volcanic eruption. The radiation pressure alone—over 7 × 10⁸ pascals—would physically blast material aside, deepening the hole even faster.

**Global climate and the dark side**  
While that one spot endures an endless explosion, the rest of the planet would receive *zero* sunlight. Within days the surface would begin to freeze; within weeks the oceans would be covered by a thick layer of ice. Photosynthesis would stop, causing a total collapse of most food chains. The temperature contrast between the blazing beam‑site (tens of thousands of degrees) and the rapidly cooling dark hemisphere would generate hyper‑hurricane winds, shrieking across the planet as the atmosphere desperately tries to redistribute heat.

**Atmospheric and orbital consequences**  
The super‑heated plasma column would carry air and water vapour high into the upper atmosphere and even into space, potentially stripping away much of the atmosphere over time. The beam’s continuous thrust on the Earth is tiny in terms of orbital change (about 578 million newtons, which is negligible for a planet of 6 × 10²⁴ kg), but its focused pressure on the ground is immense. If the beam is stationary relative to the Earth, it would drill a hole completely through the mantle in a matter of weeks, possibly triggering massive earthquakes, tsunamis, and secondary volcanism as magma finds new paths to the surface.

If the beam instead remains fixed in space while Earth rotates and orbits, it would carve a searing trench across entire continents and oceans, flashing every material to vapour as it passes. No life would survive anywhere on the surface, and the planet would quickly become a frozen, blackened rock with a perpetual glowing scar—a world utterly sterilized by its own concentrated sunlight.

items.question: What If You Built a Siphon from Europa's Ocean to Earth?
human_answers: No, but I like where you're going with this. [Image: image] Siphons are neat—they let you pump water up and over a barrier using just a tube and gravity. You can use siphoning to empty swimming pools, fill awkwardly-shaped containers, or get up to all kinds of trouble.[1]I asked some friends to suggest which thing in their house they'd be most upset to find someone siphoning water into. Answers included: Spice drawer, gumball machine, tea collection, bottle of vitamins, watercolor paint set, bag of rice with a cell phone in it, mint-condition instant oatmeal collection, carefully tuned musical glasses, ice hotel, prizewinning sand castle, sodium action figure collection, gremlin cage, Martian soil sample, dehydrated astronaut ice cream, and rack of those water-sensing self-inflating lifeboats. [Image: image] It's not necessarily obvious at first glance, but siphoning works because of air pressure. Before we answer the Europa question, it may help to go over how siphons work. If you take a tube full of water and point the ends down, gravity will try to pull the water down, making it fall out of both sides. If the water did start to fall out, a vacuum would form in the middle, since there's no way for air to get in to fill the gap. Each column of water would then have a vacuum on one side and air on the other, which means it would be pushed back up into the tube. [Image: image] In reality, this doesn't happen; the air pressure stops the vacuum from opening up in the first place, and the water just sits there in the tube. Or, at least, it would if it were perfectly balanced. If the water in one end is slightly lower than the other, then the column of water on that side pushes down harder against the air than the column on the other side. This imbalance causes the water to "tip" and run out of the heavier end. [Image: image] To siphon something, you can just keep feeding more water into the tube on the higher side. As long as the surface of that water is higher up than the place where the water is coming out, the siphon will keep running. [Image: image] If the column of water is more than about 34 feet[2]10 meters​[3]2 giraffes high, the pressure from the weight of the water becomes too strong for Earth's air pressure to counteract, and the water does fall out from both sides and briefly create a vacuum.[4]Although as the pressure drops, the water boils away to fill it, so you can't actually get too close to a pure vacuum this way. However, if you use something like olive oil (or mercury), you can get much closer. This means that on Earth's surface, you can't siphon water over a barrier that's more than 34 feet high. In Denver, where the air pressure is lower, the limit is 28 feet (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%28air+pressure+at+altitude+of+denver%29+%2F+%28water+density+*+earth+gravity%29). In a vacuum—in theory—you can't siphon at all.[5]In practice, it turns out siphons do work in a vacuum, at least a little bit (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8F4i9M3y0ew), because the "stickiness" of the water keeps it from pulling apart in the middle. Europa has barely any atmosphere, so you won't be able to do much siphoning. But you also can't siphon water out of the atmosphere from a planet in general. A column of atmosphere, which is miles high, pushes down only as hard as a column of water 34 feet high. The water column is smaller because water is much denser than air. As long as the stuff on top is less dense than the liquid below it, you can't use the pressure from the stuff on top to siphon the liquid up above the stuff on top.[6]Most of the time, things sort themselves into layers, with the denser ones on the bottom. Occasionally, in the Earth, layers of dense rock will end up above layers of less-dense oil. This is why—when oil wellheads break—oil can sometimes come spurting out without any help from the pumps. Even if you could generate a lot of pressure, pumping water from Europa's surface would take some work. Europa's gravity is weaker than Earth's, which means lifting something up from the surface of Europa takes less energy, but it's still not easy. The energy required to "climb out of Europa's gravity well" is the same as the energy required to climb up 209 kilometers (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=Newton%27s+constant+*+europa+mass+%2F+%28earth+gravity+*+europa+radius%29) against Earth's surface gravity. (Earth's gravity well, by comparison, is about 6,379 kilometers "deep"—click on this comic (http://xkcd.com/681/) for an illustration.) Once you've lifted the water out of Europa's gravity well, you then have to lift it the rest of the way out of Jupiter's, which is a lot deeper. Then, you have to do more work to push the water on a trajectory where it intercepts Earth. In terms of energy, the whole task is roughly equivalent to lifting the water about 2,500 kilometers in Earth gravity: [Image: image] You could send the water to Earth by launching it from the surface of Europa at about 7 km/s. Conveniently, since Europa has no atmosphere, you don't need to use inefficient (http://what-if.xkcd.com/38/) rockets to climb up to space. You can launch the water directly from the surface using something simpler, like a coilgun (http://www.coilgun.info/theorymath/ieee/induction_1995.pdf). When the water reaches Earth, it can use atmospheric braking to slow down, and the individual bottles could be steered directly to their targets. Timing the deliveries would be tricky, sure, but it sure would be impressive if you got it right. Plus, you could totally one-up Amazon's drone delivery scheme. [Image: image] At current electricity prices, the launch would cost a minimum of 50 cents (US) per bottle. Of course, getting electricity on Europa is probably a bit more expensive than getting it on Earth,[7]Or would need an awfully long cord. and setting up the purification plant and bottling operation on Europa wouldn't be cheap, to put it mildly. All in all, you're going to have to charge an awful lot per bottle to break even on this whole operation. And if it turns out Europa's water has some weird alien pathogen in it, you might accidentally kill all your customers.[8]And, possibly, everyone else. This may sound like your plan is pretty impractical and unrealistic, especially since there's no point to it all. Water is water. Once you've purified the water on Europa to make it drinkable, it won't be much different from water here on Earth. On the other hand, we ship water around the world from Fiji (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiji_Water) for no reason, so who knows. Maybe, with the right marketing, this idea could work. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
Building a siphon from Europa’s ocean to Earth is impossible for many physical reasons, but let’s break down the main ones.

A siphon works by creating a continuous liquid column between two reservoirs, where gravity pulls the liquid from the higher end down to the lower end, and atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid up the short leg. For Europa to Earth, you’d need a tube spanning over 600 million kilometers (on average) through the vacuum of space. The moment the tube exits Europa’s icy crust and enters the near-zero pressure of space, the water would instantly boil and vaporize—no continuous liquid column can exist across that vacuum. Even if you tried to keep the tube pressurized, Earth’s gravity and Europa’s gravity are pulling in different directions around a common center of mass (the Sun), not along a simple “higher-to-lower” gravity gradient like a hill. There is no single “up” or “down” that would allow a siphon to function across interplanetary distances. Additionally, the tube would need to be strong enough to withstand tidal forces and orbital dynamics, and the flow would be disrupted by the fact that Europa orbits Jupiter, not Earth, so the endpoints are constantly moving at different speeds. In short, the siphon principle fundamentally cannot operate in space on that scale.

items.question: What If You Tried to Start a Fire with Moonlight and a Magnifying Glass?
human_answers: At first, this sounds like a pretty easy question. A magnifying glass concentrates light on a small spot. As many mischevious kids can tell you, a magnifying glass as small as a square inch in size can collect enough light to start a fire. A little Googling (http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/badastronomy/2012/08/27/bafact-math-the-sun-is-400000-times-brighter-than-the-full-moon/) will tell you that the Sun is 400,000 times brighter than the Moon, so all we need is a 400,000-square-inch magnifying glass. Right? [Image: image] Wrong. Here's the real answer: You can't start a fire with moonlight[1]Pretty sure this is a Bon Jovi song. no matter how big your magnifying glass is. The reason is kind of subtle. It involves a lot of arguments that sound wrong but aren't, and generally takes you down a rabbit hole of optics. [Image: image] First, here's a general rule of thumb: You can't use lenses and mirrors to make something hotter than the surface of the light source itself. In other words, you can't use sunlight to make something hotter than the surface of the Sun. There are lots of ways to show why this is true using optics, but a simpler—if perhaps less satisfying—argument comes from thermodynamics: Lenses and mirrors work for free; they don't take any energy to operate.[2]And, more specifically, everything they do is fully reversible—which means you can add them in without increasing the entropy of the system. If you could use lenses and mirrors to make heat flow from the Sun to a spot on the ground that's hotter than the Sun, you'd be making heat flow from a colder place to a hotter place without expending energy. The second law of thermodynamics says you can't do that. If you could, you could make a perpetual motion machine. [Image: image] The Sun is about 5,000°C, so our rule says you can't focus sunlight with lenses and mirrors to get something any hotter than 5,000°C. The Moon's sunlit surface is a little over 100°C, so you can't focus moonlight to make something hotter than about 100°C. That's too cold to set most things on fire. "But wait," you might say. "The Moon's light isn't like the Sun's! The Sun is a blackbody—its light output is related to its high temperature. The Moon shines with reflected sunlight, which has a "temperature" of thousands of degrees—that argument doesn't work!" It turns out it does work, for reasons we'll get to later. But first, hang on—is that rule even correct for the Sun? Sure, the thermodynamics argument seems hard to argue with,[3]Because it's correct. but to someone with a physics background who's used to thinking of energy flow, it may seem hard to swallow. Why can't you concentrate lots of sunlight onto a point to make it hot? Lenses can concentrate light down to a tiny point, right? Why can't you just concentrate more and more of the Sun's energy down onto the same point? With over 1026 watts available, you should be able to get a point as hot as you want, right? Except lenses don't concentrate light down onto a point—not unless the light source is also a point. They concentrate light down onto an area—a tiny image of the Sun.[4]Or a big one (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=sunspotter+solar+telescope)! This difference turns out to be important. To see why, let's look at an example: [Image: image] This lens directs all the light from point A to point C. If the lens were to concentrate light from the Sun down to a point, it would need to direct all the light from point B to point C, too: [Image: image] But now we have a problem. What happens if light goes back from point C toward the lens? Optical systems are reversible, so the light should be able to go back to where it came from—but how does the lens know whether the light came from B or to A? In general, there's no way to "overlay" light beams on each other, because the whole system has to be reversible. This keeps you from squeezing more light in from a given direction, which puts a limit on how much light you can direct from a source to a target. Maybe you can't overlay light rays, but can't you, you know, sort of smoosh them closer together, so you can fit more of them side-by-side? Then you could gather lots of smooshed beams and aim them at a target from slightly different angles. [Image: image] Nope, you can't do this.[5]We already know this, of course, since earlier we said that it would let you violate the second law of thermodynamics. It turns out that any optical system follows a law called conservation of étendue. This law says that if you have light coming into a system from a bunch of different angles and over a large "input" area, then the input area times the input angle[6]Note to nitpickers: In 3D systems, this is technically the solid angle, the 2D equivalent of the regular angle, but whatever. equals the output area times the output angle. If your light is concentrated to a smaller output area, then it must be "spread out" over a larger output angle. [Image: image] In other words, you can't smoosh light beams together without also making them less parallel, which means you can't aim them at a faraway spot. There's another way to think about this property of lenses: They only make light sources take up more of the sky; they can't make the light from any single spot brighter,[7]A popular demonstration of this: Try holding up a magnifying glass to a wall. The magnifying glass collects light from many parts of the wall and sends them to your eye, but it doesn't make the wall look brighter. because it can be shown[8]This is left as an exercise for the reader. that making the light from a given direction brighter would violate the rules of étendue.[9]My résumé says étendue is my forté. In other words, all a lens system can do is make every line of sight end on the surface of a light source, which is equivalent to making the light source surround the target. [Image: image] If you're "surrounded" by the Sun's surface material, then you're effectively floating within the Sun, and will quickly reach the temperature of your surroundings.[10](Very hot) If you're surrounded by the bright surface of the Moon, what temperature will you reach? Well, rocks on the Moon's surface are nearly surrounded by the surface of the Moon, and they reach the temperature of the surface of the Moon (since they are the surface of the Moon.) So a lens system focusing moonlight can't really make something hotter than a well-placed rock sitting on the Moon's surface. Which gives us one last way to prove that you can't start a fire with moonlight: Buzz Aldrin is still alive. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
You can't start a fire with moonlight and a magnifying glass—physics won't allow it.

A magnifying glass concentrates light, but the fundamental limit is that it can't make the target hotter than the surface of the light source itself (a consequence of the second law of thermodynamics and the conservation of étendue). The sun's surface is around 5,500°C, so focused sunlight can easily ignite paper or wood at a few hundred degrees. The moon, however, shines by reflecting sunlight, and its surface temperature is only about 100°C. Even if you perfectly focused all the moonlight you collected, you couldn't exceed that temperature, which is far below the ignition point of typical materials. Plus, moonlight is about 400,000 times dimmer than direct sunlight, so even the raw intensity isn't enough. In short, the moon simply isn't a hot enough or bright enough light source for passive optics to start a fire.
